            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee to submit
the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Seventy-first Report on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) relating to the Ministry of Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions.
 
2.         The Committee heard the concerned officers of the Ministry in its sittings held on 28 March and 10 April, 2001.
 
3.         The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations has mainly relied upon the following:-
 
(i)
                 Presentations made by the concerned officers of the Ministry;
(ii)                Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2000-2001;
(iii)              Detailed Demands for Grants of the Union Public Service Commission for the year 2001-2002;
(iv)              Explanatory Note on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) received from the Ministry;
(v)               Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 2001-2002;
(vi)              Annual Report of the Union Public Service Commission for the year 1998;
(vii)            Annual Report of the Central Bureau of Investigation for the years 1997, 1998 and 1999;
(viii)           Central Bureau of Investigation Crime Manual;
(ix)              Annual Report of the Central Vigilance Commission for the year 1998;
(x)               Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Sixtieth Report on the Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the
Ministry
(xi)              Written replies furnished by the Ministry on the Questionnaire sent to it by the Secretariat; and
(xii)            Written clarifications to the points/issues raised by the Members in the meetings of the Committee.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on 11 April, 2001.
 
5.         For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of
the Report.

R E P O R T
CHAPTER – I
Introductory
 
            The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the joint responsibility of the Ministries of Home Affairs (Services
and Establishment Wing) and Finance (Establishment Division) with Union Public Service Commission playing an important advisory role. The
Establishment Officer to the Government of India, functioning under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under the
Government of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified  Central direction.
 
2.         To plug this organisation loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha in its 93
rd Report (April 1966) observed that “the ever expanding
role of the government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large civil service calls for effective personnel control through a single agency”.
The Administrative Reforms Commission too urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel, to be placed directly under the Prime
Minister to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel functions of the Government.
 
3.         The Union Government accepted this recommendation and as a consequence the ‘Department of Personnel’ was set up in August, 1970 and placed
within the Cabinet Secretariat. In February, 1973, the Department of Administrative Reforms, till then with the Ministry of Home Affairs, was amalgamated
with the Department of Personnel and the newly created department was christened, the ‘Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms’. In 1977, this
department was transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In March, 1985 a full fledged ‘Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions’ was
created.
 
4.0       The Ministry is the coordinating agency of the Central Government in personnel matters specially issues concerning recruitment, training, career
development, staff welfare as well as the process of responsive people–oriented modern administration.  The Ministry comprises three Departments, namely: -
 
(i)                  Department of Personnel and Training.
(ii)             Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare.
(iii)
               Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
 
4.1       The Ministry has under its administrative control  four attached offices and four other offices, namely: -
 
            (i)            Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI);
(ii)
                Staff Selection Commission (SSC);
(iii)              Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM); and
(iv)              Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA).
 
 
The other offices under the administrative control of the Ministry are: -

(i)                 Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), a constitutional body;
(ii)                Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), proposed to be converted into a statutory body;
(iii)              Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), a statutory quasi-judicial body; and
(iv)              Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB), a body set up by the resolution of Government.
 
5.         The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister, assisted by two Ministers of State – one for the Department of Personnel and Training
and Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare and the other for the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances. All the three
Departments are functioning under the charge of the Secretary (Personnel) assisted by four Additional Secretaries and three Joint Secretaries and other
supporting officers and staff.
 
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING AND THE VARIOUS AGENCIES UNDER ITS ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL
 
6.0       The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided into two parts.  In its larger nodal role, it acts as the formulator of
policy and the watch dog of the Government ensuring that certain accepted standards and norms, as laid down by it, are followed by all
Ministries/Departments in the recruitment, regulation of service conditions and deputation of personnel as well as other related issues.  Towards this end,
guidelines are issued by it for the benefit of all Ministries/Departments and it monitors the implementation of these guidelines.  It also advises all
organisations of the Central Government  on issues of personnel management.  At a more immediate level, the Department has the direct responsibility of
being the cadre controlling authority for the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS).  The Department also operates the
Central Staffing Scheme under which suitable officers from  All India Services and Group ‘A’ Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at the
level of Deputy Secretary, Director and Joint Secretary on the basis of tenure deputation.  The Department also deals with cases of appointment to posts of
Chairmen, Managing Directors, full-time functional Directors/Members of the Board of Management of various public sector undertakings/enterprises,
corporations, banks and financial institutions.  It also deals with the assignment of Indian experts to various developing countries.
 
Recruitment Agencies
6.1       The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of personnel for the Government are the Union Public Service Commission
(UPSC) and the Staff Selection Commission (SSC). The former is constituted under a provision of the Constitution and is responsible for conducting
examinations for appointment to the higher civil services and civil posts under the Union Government, including recruitment to the All India Services. There
is a mandatory provision for consulting the Commission on all matters relating to methods of  recruitment, principles to be followed in making promotions
and transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The SSC is responsible for making recruitment for Group ‘B’ non-gazetted posts of
Assistants, Stenographers, etc.
 
Training Institutions
6.2       Two major training institutions directly under the administrative control of the Department are the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of
Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie and the Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. The former   is   mainly   responsible  
for   providing   induction   training   to  recruits   to  the Indian Administrative Service and other All India Services and Central Services. The Institute of
Training and Management provides induction as well as in-service training to members of the Central Secretariat Service.
 
Senior Appointments under the Government of India
6.3       All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the approval of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet
(ACC) are processed through the Establishment Officer as Secretary to the ACC.  These include board level appointments to Central Public Sector
Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries/Departments. In addition, all appointments by
promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also processed through the Establishment Officer.
 
Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
 
6.4       The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board
level posts of Chief Executive and functional Directors and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Undertakings.
 
Administrative Vigilance
 
6.5       The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the maintenance of integrity of the public services and eradication of
corruption and coordinates the activities of various Ministries/Departments in that area.
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)
6.6       Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commission. It has jurisdiction and power in respect of all matters to which the
executive power of the Union Government extends. The Commission is also entrusted with the supervision of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). The
Commission enjoys the same measure of independence and autonomy as the Union Public Service Commission.
 
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
 
6.7       The Central Bureau of Investigation is the premier investigating agency of the country to investigate complex and important cases particularly relating
to internal security, espionage, sabotage, narcotics, economic offences, cybercrimes and cases  registered under Preventing   Corruption  Act.
 
Joint Consultative Machinery
6.8       The Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) is three-tier machinery consisting of the National Council, the Departmental Council and the Regional/Office
Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the generality of employees or specific groups of them are dealt with by this machinery.
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)

6.9       In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by Government decisions, the Government has set up the Central
Administrative Tribunal  (CAT) in 1985, which now deals with all cases relating to service matters which were previously dealt with by Courts upto and
including the High Courts. 
 
Staff Welfare
 
6.10     The Department supports various programmes, which are provided in various Ministries/Departments, Central Government Employees Welfare
Coordination Committee in Central Government offices located outside Delhi, Residents’ Welfare Associations/Area Welfare Officers; Benevolent Fund and
Departmental Canteens.  Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for three registered societies set up  for the welfare of the Government
employees and their families.  These societies are the Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board, Grih Kalyan Kendra and Kendriya Bhandar. 
 
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
7.         The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare is the nodal agency of the Government of India for formulation of general policy on pension and
other retirement benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on retirement benefits.  The Department was set up in 1985 as a part of Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions and has been rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then.  Department has taken a number of steps over the
years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater convenience and welfare of the pensioners.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
8.         The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well
as redressal of public grievances relating to the State in general and grievances pertaining to  Central Government agencies in particular. The Department
disseminates information on important activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through Management
Publications and Documentation.  This Department also acts as the nodal agency in regard to Organisation and Methods activities and offers advice to the
Ministries/Departments. It also undertakes activities in the field of international co-operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms.
 
CHAPTER-II
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY
 
9.0       The overall Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2001-2002 are Rs.270.26crores both for plan and non-plan.
 
9.1       The detailed Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Ministry were laid in Lok Sabha on 20 April 2001.

SCHEME FOR ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS
 
12.0     The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the Government of India of administrative reforms as well as
redressal of public grievances relating to the State in general and grievances pertaining to the Central Government agencies in particular.
 
12.1     In the Plan Budget of the Department for the year 2000-2001, a new programme/scheme entitled “Scheme for Administrative Reforms” has been
approved with a provision of Rs. 45 lakhs.  It is proposed to undertake, through empanelled consultancy organisations/professional consultants etc., projects in
the area of administrative reforms such as evaluation of Citizens’ Charters, Information and Facilitation Counters etc., pilot e-governance initiatives,

SMART Administration
 
13.0            SMART is acronym for Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive and Transparent. The Ministry has initiated several measures towards achieving
the goal of operationalising SMART administration. The conference of Chief Ministers  held in New Delhi on 29 May, 1997 represented the culmination of
the National Debate on Effective and Responsive Administration. The Action Plan prepared for the conference dealt with three themes, namely, making
administration accountable and citizen-friendly, ensuring transparency and Right to Information and taking measures to cleanse and motivate Civil Services.
The following are the major components of the aforesaid action plan, which are also being operationalised:-
 
(i)
                 Citizen’s Charter;
(ii)                Information and Facilitation Counters (IFCs);
(iii)              Redress of Public Grievance;
(iv)              Review of Laws, Regulations and Procedures;
(v)               Transparency in Government and Right to Information; and
(vi)              A minimum Agenda for e-governance.
 
13.1     The Ministry of Statistic and Programme Implementation ensure overall monitoring of  Twenty Point Programme relating to Responsive
Administration. The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions monitors measures taken by Ministries/Departments under point 20 of Twenty
Point Programme relating to Responsive Administration. The areas under point 20 of above Twenty Point Programme relates to simplification of rules and
procedures, delegation of authority, enforcement of accountability and redressal of public grievances.
 
CITIZEN’S CHARTER
 
14.0     The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances coordinates the efforts to formulate and operationalise citizen’s/user’s charter by
the Central Government Ministries/Departments and their PSUS/autonomous/statutory bodies in areas in which they provide services to the members of the
public. The Department also coordinates the efforts of formulating and operationalising citizen’s charter in various States/Uts.
 
14.1            Citizen’s charter has been modelled on pattern of charters prevalent in the United Kingdom but the Indian citizen’s charter has an additional
component of “expectations of the service providers from the users”. All other components, namely, (i) statement of the services provided (ii) standards of
service (time norms, locations, costs etc.) (iii) grievance redress mechanism (iv) mechanism of feedback are same under both the models.
 
14.2     The Committee wanted to know whether any specific time frame has been given to Ministries/Departments/Organisations and States/Uts for
formulation of citizen’s charters. The Ministry in its reply has stated that although no specific time frame has been given, yet the Department constantly
persue with these organization as a result of which the number of citizen’s charters formulated by Central Ministries/Departments/ Organisations have
increased from 61 to 68. Simarily, the number of charters formulated by 19 States/Union Territories have witness an increased trend from 200 to 313 during
the financial year 2000-2001.
 
14.3     To a question how the Government ensure involvement and participation of Members of Parliament, and State legislatures and opinion makers on the
evaluation/review of citizen’s charters to make them citizen-friendly, the Ministry has replied that Ministries/Departments/Organisations and States/UTs have
been advised to consult representatives of Consumer Groups, members of public, experts and representatives of the people at the time of  formulation of the
charter. It has been  further stated by the Ministry that the concerned organization is advised to set up a task force assisted by field agencies and
representatives of Consumer Groups to identify the nature of work and the client groups, nature of service provided and cost involved at the formulation time
of charter. Further the concerned organization are also advised by the Ministry to monitor/review/evaluate the citizen’s charter by internal as well as external
agencies such as consumer groups, NGOs and representatives of the charter.
 
14.4     From the replies of the Ministry elaborated in the previous paras, it seems that directions of the Ministry to ensure participation of Members of
Parliament, State Legislatures and opinion makers exist at the formulation stage and not at the evaluation stage of the citizen’s charter. The Committee
recommends that the feedback of the users must be assessed by the organizations providing services in the light of suggestion received from the
representatives of the people. The concerned organization must strive to find methods to ensure the participation of representatives of people in formulation as
well as evaluation of citizen’s charter.

14.5     The Committee wanted to know the modes of receipt of feedback from public and representatives of people to review the citizen’s charter. The
Committee is given to understand that the one of  the main  criteria of the charter is that it should contain in-built provision for on-going monitoring of its
effectiveness and a fixed review date. Accordingly, the Ministries/Departments/Organisations have been advised by the Ministry of Personnel to provide a
feedback mechanism in the charter and a fixed schedule for review of its implementation, preferably once a year.
 
14.6     The Ministry’s reply amply proves that the  feedback mechanism is the vital component of citizen’s charter but the reply is not expressive as to the
mode of receiving feedback. The Committee is of the view that review of implementation of charter is not given proper attention and, therefore, recommends

14.7     About the publicity of citizen’s charter, the Committee wanted to know whether the charter is being made available in any regional languages. The

has also been intimated that the concerned organization are advised to give wide publicity about their citizen’s charter through electronic media, newspaper

available in the website of the NIC (http://goidirectory.nic.in
). NIC has been requested to put all the  charters on the website.
 
14.8     The Ministry has intimated that it has published the names, addresses telephone/fax numbers of contact officers for citizen’s charter and information
and facilitation counter in February/March, in 2001 under the caption titled ‘Towards Effective and  Responsive Administration. 
 
14.9     The Committee feels that publicity of charters is very essential to make the general public aware about its existence and utility, which would help in

INFORMATION AND FACILITATION COUNTERS
 
15.0            Information and Facilitation Counter (IFC) is the visible face/physical manifestation of citizen’s charter formulated by an organization. IFCs are
setup outside the security zone of each office with a view to facilitating the dissemination of the information to the citizen/user at one place without the hassle
of getting an entry pass. Information is disseminated through print-outs, brochures, book-lets, display boards and sometimes telephonically too.
 
15.1            Computerised Information and Facilitation Counters have been set up in various Ministries/Departments/Organisations, etc. of the Government of
India to provide information and assistance to the public regarding the schemes and procedures of the organization concerned and also to acknowledge and to
apprise status report of individual applications and grievances.
 
15.2     The Ministry admits the fact that like formulation of citizen’s charter, setting up of IFCs is an on-going process. However, due to the constant
persuasion by the Department of AR&PG, the number of IFCs has risen to 65 from 45 during this year.
 
15.3     N.I.C. has been imparting training to the Staff  manning IFCs.  To avoid  rotation of trained staff, the Ministry/ Department  have also  been  advised
not to transfrer the staff  which have been trained.
 
15.4     The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry to plug the deficiencies  in the structure and functioning of IFCs in different 
Ministries/Department.  The Committee  understands three organization which  have  Citizen’s Charter but have not set up IFCs,  should be  urged to take
steps for setting up of IFCs as  Citizen’s Charter appears to  be meaningless without its physical manifestation.
 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL
 
16.0     The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances  issues  various  guidelines  from  time to time  to reduce number of public
grievances,  during the year the same Department has published  a booklet  titled  “Guidelines for Grievances Redress Mechanism in Government of India” in
English which contains  detailed guidelines on Redressal  of public grievances.  A provision of Rs.50 lakhs  has been kept under BE (2001-2002)  to publish
the same in Hindi.
 
16.1.0  The organizational set up for handling public grievances  in Government of India are as follows:-
 
(i)
                 The Public Wing of the  Prime Minister’s Office (PMO)
(ii)                The  Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions
(iii)              The Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions
(iv)              Directorate of Public Grievances, Cabinet Secretariat
 
The Public wing of PMO
 
16.1.1  The Public Wing is placed in the charge of an Officer on Special Duty.  The petitions received are properly  segregated in the PMO and forwarded to
the concerned Ministries/Departments for further necessary action.  Handling  of cases are fully computerized.
 
Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances
 
16.2       The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public  Grievances is the Chief coordinating  agency  for redressal of public grievances arising from
the work of Ministries/Departments and other organisations of the Government of India.  According to the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961, the main
functions of the Department  in the sphere  of redressal of public grievances are as follows:-

Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare
 
16.3.0  The Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare, being a policy formulation agency  pertaining to pensions and retirement  benefits of
Government official, takes upon itself those cases  wherein any policy matter is invovled.  All other grievances received in Department of Pensions are 
transferred to the concerned Ministry /Department   for settling  their grievances, since the payment of pensions and retirement  dues is decentralized.
 
16.3.1  The Secretary has informed the Committee that a grievance redressal   cell  under the supervision of an officer of the rank of Deputy Secretary has
been created to monitor pension related cases  till their final disposal.  An automated reminder mechanism  has been  introduced in the Department.  A
consumer friendly  website  has been put on internet.  Furthermore, a web- enabled grievance mechanism  is also being developed to enable pensioners to
interact with the Department of Pensions and getting feedback on their grievances.
 
Directorate of  Public Grievances, Cabinet Secretariat
 
16.4.0  As per the Government resolution  dated  25 March 1988,  Directorate  of Public Grievances came into being w.e.f.  1 April 1988.   So far the
Directorate is looking into  grievances relating to 14 Ministries/Departments, which are given at Annexure –I
 
16.4.1  Under the aforesaid resolution the following  functions  in relation to redressal  of public grievances have been assigned to the Directorate of Public
Grievances:-
 
(i)         The Directorate is an  Appellate  Body investigating grievances selectively and particularly those where a complainant has failed to get redress
at the hands of the internal machinery and the hierarchical authorities.
(iii)
              It has authority to call for relevant files/papers from the Ministries/Departments concerned with a view to examining whether the grievance
has been dealth with in a fair, objective and just manner and whether a decisions containing reasons has been communicated to the complainant
within a reasonable time.  The concerned Ministries are required to furnish the documents/files asked for within a period of six weeks.
 
(iv)
              Where the Directorate is satisfied that the grievance has not been dealt with in a fair, just and objective manner, it makes suitale
recommendations for consideration and adoption by the concerned Ministries/Departments.  The recommendations made by the Directorate are
required to be implemented within a period of one month.
 
(v)               The Directorate does not concern, itself with policy matters or where a grievance has already been disposed of at the level of Minister.  It also
does not entertain grievances relating to service matters (excluding those relating to payment of terminal benefits like gratuity, provident fund,
etc., commercial contracts or cases which are sub-judice or where quasi-judicial procedures are prescribed for decision making.
 
Internal Grievance Redressal Machinery within each Ministry/Department
 
16.5.0.            Redressal of grievances has been decentralized as a result of which each Ministry/Department has its own internal grievance redressal
mechanism for settling grievances pertaining to it.   An officer of the rank Joint Secretary or above has been designed as Director of Grievances, who has been
vested with the powers to call for files/papers relating to public grievances in the cases in which a decision is pending for more than three months and take a
decision, with the approval of the Secretary/head of the Department of the Ministry/ Department concerned.
 
16.5.1.The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances gives wide publicity to  the existence of the decentralized grievance redress
machinery in the Central Ministries/Departments annually in major dailies.  A list of containing names, addresses of 48 designated Public Grievances officers
is given at Annexure-II.  This apart, 33 Ministries/Departments have reported to have published their own grievance machinery through newspaper.      
 
External Grievance Redressal Machinery in the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
 
16.6.    The Department of AR&PG acts as an external monitoring agency and review periodically the performance of Ministries/Departments with respect to
redressal of public grievances.  The grievances received in the Department are gone through and sent to the concerned Ministry/Department for appropriate
action.  An acknowledgement is sent to the complainant and he is also informed that his grievances has been sent to the specifically mentioned Department
which would send him a reply about the complaint.  Even in cases where the petition does not contain a grievance and no action is warranted by this
Department, a reply is sent to the petitioner.  Quarterly review meetings are held with Directors of Public Grievance/Staff Grievances Officers.  The
Department also carries out periodic evaluation of grievance redressal machinery set up in selected Ministries/Department having large interface with the
public.  In the process of dealings with public grievances the Department also identifies the systemic deficiencies and takes up studies of grievance-prone
areas with a view to suggesting reform.
 
16.7.    A list containing gist of the guidelines from the booklet ‘Guidelines for Grievance Redress mechanism in Government of India’ has been put as
Annexure– III.
 
Public Grievance Commission
 
16.8.0.A Public Grievance Commission is in the offing.  The Ministry has submitted in its written reply that the proposal for setting up a Public Grievance
Commission’ has been prepared for consideration of the Committee of Secretaries.
 
16.8.1.When asked about the details of the proposed Commission, the Ministry has mentioned in its replies that there is a proposal to set up a independent
Central Grievance Commission (CGC) to function on the lines of Ombudsman in matters relating to public grievances within the jurisdiction of the Cabinet
Secretariat or as an autonomous body, which will carry out the tasks of policy formulation for grievance redressal, monitoring and evaluation of grievance
redressal mechanisms of the Central Government, suggesting measures for systemic changes in relation to grievance-prone areas and ensuring disposal of

jurisdiction over the Grievance Redress Mechanisms of all Central Ministries/Departments/Organisations.  It may also suggest measures to strengthen the
grievance redress mechanism of Central Government Organisations, appointment of Ombudsman like institutions in organization with a large public interface

grievances relating to the State Governments.  It may also be the nodal agency for all matters relating to Citizen’s Charters.
 
16.9.    The Committee understands that there  would be two  policy-formulators with regard to public grievance redressal with the institution of the Central
Grievance Commission (CGC) i.e. Department of AR&PG and CGC.  There would also be two appellate bodies . The Directorate of Public Grievances in
Cabinet Secretariat for the 14 Ministries/Departments and the CGC for the rest Ministries/Departments.  Further, the grievances pertaining to State
Government would be in the hands of the Department of AR&PG.  With the proliferation of grievance redressal bodies and apparent over-lapping of functions
between those may entail confusion in the minds of the complainants.  Moreover many bodies for the same work would also have the direct bearing on the
Government exchequer.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Committee of Secretaries while giving shape to the CGC must clearly define the role
and scope of other existing grievance redressal mechanisms with a view to avoid undue over-lapping .

GOOD GOVERNANCE
 
18.0.    One of the main themes identified for good governance is rightsizing of Government.  The size of Government machinery is critical for the success of
any drive for efficiency and economy in Government. On being asked to elaborate on the plan/scheme being implemented/contemplated to rightsize/downsize
the Government, the Ministry has stated in its written replies that in August, 1999, instructions were issued to all the Ministries/Departments inter-alia to
undertake a review of all the posts which were lying vacant in the Ministries/Departments and in their attached and subordinate offices, etc., in consultation
with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure).  The instructions envisage that till the review is completed, no vacant posts will be filled up except
with the approval of Department of Expenditure of the Ministry of Finance.  Approximately, 1.83 lakhs posts pertaining to different Groups, have been
abolished in various Ministries/Departments as a result of this exercise.  The Departments, namely, Department of Industrial Development, Department of
Sugar and Edible Oils, and the Department of Supply have been abolished/merged.  In addition, the Department of Telecom Services and Telecom Operations
have been corporatised w.e.f. 10 October 2000.
 
18.1.    In the budget speech in the Parliament on 28 February, 2001, the Finance Minister has inter-alia proposed that “All requirements of recruitment will be
scrutinized to ensure that the fresh recruitment is limited to 1 percent of total civilian staff strength.  As about 3 percent staff retire every year, this will reduce
the manpower by 2 percent per annum, achieving a reduction of 10 percent in five years………The surplus pool under the Department of Personnel will be
streamlined and equipped to redeploy and retrain surplus staff.  Employees in the surplus pool will also be offered an attractive VRS package.”

CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
 
19.0.            Pursuant to the provision of Article 323A of the India Constitution, the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1985 was enacted by Parliament to set up
Administrative Tribunal for adjudication of disputes and complaints with regard to recruitment and condition of services of persons appointed to public
services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union and the States.
 
19.1.            Administrative adjudication, which is quasi-judicial in nature, is the main function of Administrative Tribunals.  The basic objective of enacting

71st Report of COmmittee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/71streport.htm[30-06-2016 17:38:46]
the Administrative Tribunal Act was:
 
(i)                 to relieve congestion in the ordinary set of courts; and
(ii)                to provide for speedy disposal of disputes relating to service matters.
 
19.2.    The Central Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 provides that the Tribunal shall not be bound by the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908 but shall be guided by the principle of natural justice and subject to the other provisions of Administrative Tribunals Act and rules made by
the Central Government.  The Tribunal shall have power to regulate its own procedure including the fixing of places and times of enquiry.  As a result of the
judgement of the Supreme Court in the case of L. Chandra Kumar dated 18 march, 1997, the appeals against the orders of an Administrative Tribunals lie
before the Division Bench of the concerned High Court.
 
19.3.            Administrative Tribunals are distinguishable from the ordinary courts with regard to their jurisdiction and procedure.  They are free from the
shackles of many of the technicalities of the ordinary courts.  The litigant(s) has to submit an application in paper book form prescribed by rule 4 of Central
Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1985.  It means that every application should be accompanied by a proper    containing the following:-
 
(i)
                 Certified copy of the order against which the application has been filed.
(ii)                All documents relied upon by the applicants and mentioned in the application;
(iii)              Details of the crossed Demand Draft or crossed Indian Postal Order representing the application fee of Rs. 50/- and
(iv)              Index of documents.
 
The aggrieved person can appear before the court personally.  Government can also present its case through its departmental officers or legal practitioners.
19.4.    At present CAT has 17 regular benches, 15 of which operate at the principal seats of High Courts and the remaining two at Jaipur and Lucknow. 
These Benches also hold circuit sittings at other seats of High Courts.  A statement showing the location of CAT Benches, and Circuit Benches, the dates of
their establishment and the number of courts in each of these benches is given at Annexure-VI.
 
19.5.    The Tribunal consists of a Chairman, Vice-Chairman and Members.  The Members are drawn from both judicial as well as administrative streams so
to give the Tribunal the benefit of expertise both in legal and administrative spheres.  The present sanctioned strength of Chairman, Vice-Chairman and
Members of the CAT is as below:-

19.10.1            The Committee wanted to  know as to how many times  the respondents have sought adjournments  vis-à-vis  the litigants of the  pending cases
as on 31.12.2000 in different Benches of CAT.
 
19.10.2  The Ministry has stated in the written submission such information is not being centrally maintained  either by the CAT or  the Department of
Personnel and Training.  But the Ministry has maintained  that the adjournments in the case(s) is/are granted by the Tribunal in its judicial capacity taking into
account the circumstances  of case(s).  The Ministry has in that context, has  quoted the rule position envisaged  in the Administrative Tribunals  Act, 1985
and the Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1987 which are as below:-
 
Section 30 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985  provides that “ All proceedings   before a Tribunal shall be deemed to be judicial proceedings
within the meaning of sections 193, 219 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code.”
 
Rule 14(3) of the Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1987 provides that “The  Tribunal shall have the power to decline an
adjournment and also to limit the time for oral arguments.”
 
Rule 15 provides that when an applicant fails to appear on appointed day, the Tribunal may, in its discretion, either dismiss the application for default
or hear and decide it on  merit.  However, a protection has been given to the applicant to file an application within 30 days from the date of dismissal
to restore the same after satisfying the Tribunal for non-appearance.  Where a final decision has been given, the applicant can file an application for
review.
 
Rule 16 provides that when a respondent  fails to appear on appointed day, the Tribunal may, in its discretion, adjourn the hearing or hear and decide
the application ex-parte.  The respondents may apply within 30 days from the date of the  order to the Tribunal  for an order to set it aside and if such
respondent/s satisfy  the Tribunal   that the  notice was not duly served, or that he or they  were  prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing
when application came up for hearing, the Tribunal may make an order setting aside the ex-parte order  as against  him or them, upon such terms as it
thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the application.
 
Rule 19 further provides that the Tribunal may, if sufficient cause is shown  at any stage  of proceedings, grant  time to the parties or any of them, and 
adjourn the hearing of the application.  The Tribunal may make such  order as it thinks fit with respect to the costs occasioned by the adjournments.
 
As is evident from the above, the adjournments in the case/s is/are granted by the Tribunal in its judicial  capacity taking into account the
circumstances  of the case/s and  Government as a matter of policy does not issue directions related  to the judicial functioning of CAT as that may
construe interference in their judicial functioning.
 
19.10.3 The Ministry maintains that the Government as a matter of policy does not issue directions related to judicial functioning of CAT as that may be
construed as   interference in their judicial functioning.  It  states that  instructions have been issued to all the Ministries/Departments in January, 1994 at the
level of Cabinet Secretary, impressing upon the Secretaries the obligation to dispose  of the case within time and requesting them that necessary steps may be
taken to review pending cases so that not only they are properly and effectively defended before the Tribunal but also a system is put in place for handling
such cases in a  systematic and effective manner  so as to help the Tribunal in disposing the cases within the time limit.
 
19.10.4 The Ministry   holds the view that the CAT may issue order as it think fit to charge cost of adjournments from the litigants, if sought unnecessary by
them.  The Committee sought details thereof, which could not be supplied to it as so such information is maintained by CAT & DOPT.

same, the Ministry has stated in its written submission that there is no separate rule  to  regulate the cases of litigants  on the verge of

19.11   The CAT’s functioning and the role played by it in arresting the reduction of pendency of service-related cases is not satisfactory.  Further, the
decision of the CAT can be  challenged   in the Division Bench of High  Court has put the deliverance  of inexpensive  and speedy  justice to the Government
employees in question.  The Committee feels that serious  thinking  on the functioning of the CAT has to be taken and in that context  takes into account   the
following suggestions of Law  Commission on the functioning  and structure  of the CAT in its 162nd Report.
 
(i)         The present practice of appointing retired or about to retire District Judges as  Judicial  members is not entirely satisfactory.  Since they did not
deal service matters earlier and there  is no time and in some of them,  inclination to learn  the service   jurisprudence.  Therefore, members of
Bar of the age  of 45  to 50 having experience  in service matters may be recruited for the initial period of ten years which required amendment 
of Section 8 of the A.T. Act, 1985.
(ii)        Administrative Member should not be appointed as Chairman/Vice-Chairman of CAT.
(iii)
              Constitution of a National Appellate  Administrative  Tribunal to entertain appeals against the orders  passed by the Administrative Tribunals
on the lines of the National Consumer Dispute  Redressal Commission created by the Consumers Protection Act, 1986.
(iv)              Selection  of Judicial Members from legal officers holding  atleast three years the post of Joint Secretary  and its equivalent through a process
of a high standard written examination.
(v)               Grouping of judgements pronounced by Courts for expeditious  disposal of cases by the CAT for which a Research Officer will be  appointed 
to assist  the Tribunal in increasing the expertise and efficiency of the CAT/SAT.
(vi)              Constitution of Benches of retired Members   of the   tribunal for disposal of pending cases.
(vii)            A proper litigation policy and machinery should be evolved by the Government/Public Sector Undertakings to curb litigation.
(viii)           Cost of raising frivolous defences to  be quantified by the Tribunal.
(ix)              Need to evolve  a mechanism for nipping in the bud the conflicting  interpretations  by the CAT/High Court.
(x)               Need for reform of the administrative  justice system  in order to ensure better standards of independence, accessibility/openness, expertise,
representativeness, efficiency and accountability.
 
19.12   The Committee strongly recommends to the Government to take an early decision on the above suggestions of Law Commission to make CAT a
viable instrument in providing speedy and inexpensive  justice to the Government employees.
 
19.13   The Committee in its Sixtieth Report on the Demands for Grants (2000-2001)  of the Ministry had inter alia   recommended  that the Ministry should
take a holistic approach to use Joint Consultative Machinery  (JCM) and Board of Arbitration (BOA)  to check filing of cases in CAT.
 
19.14.  In the ATR to the recommendation contained  in  the aforesaid Report of the Committee, the Ministry has stated that individual cases of service
grievances do not come within the purview of JCM  and BOA  as they are created for different  purposes.
 
19.15   In that background, the Committee wanted to know whether JCM  and BOA have been effective in arresting cases pertaining to group of employees
and in that context  sought data  of   cases  of group  of employees instituted with CAT since its inception.
 
19.16   The Ministry in its written submission has stated that JCM scheme is an additional forum for Central Government employees and plays an important
role when individual employees as well as service Associations are free to approach the CAT.   296 Service related cases of Group of employees have been
instituted since its inception out of which 207 cases have been disposed.  The Ministry also  states that JCM scheme is also effective in solving cases of group
of employees since its inception in 1966.  In Railway Ministry, there is  Permanent  Negotiation Machinery (PNM)  in addition to  JCM.  Out of 242 cases
decided by the Board of Arbitration, most of the awards were in  favour of the Government servants.
 
19.17   The Committee is informed that service related cases of group of employees are  also instituted in the CAT in addition to individual cases  and
understands that 87 such cases  are still pending  with  the CAT.  The Committee wanted to know whether the JCM & BOA machinery   was used  in the
aforesaid pending cases to get relief.  The Committee, in view of the reply of the Ministry, reiterates its earlier stand to take a holistic approach  to solve group
as well as individual service related cases through JCM and BOA before allowing them to approach CAT straightway.

23.3     The Committee, further, wanted to know steps taken to reduce pendency of cases under the investigation of the CBI not covered under the Prevention

23.4     The Ministry further informed that the CBI has drawn up an Action Plan for achieving a 10 percent reduction in cases pending investigation and 20

(i)
                  All the Regional DIGs to prepare a list of cases pending investigation for over two years in respect of their Region.
(ii)                Depending upon the nature of the case and the extent of investigation required to be conducted a team of Investigating officer(s)/Law Officer, be

23.5     The Ministry informed that whenever cases of faulty investigation or dereliction of duty on the part of Investigating Officers/Prosecuting Officers

23.6     The Committee is not convinced by the reply of the Ministry equating criminal cases with corruption cases as the provision of Special Courts are not
available for criminal cases under the investigation of the CBI.  In spite of extant rules for monitoring of cases as available in the CBI Crime Manual, the
cases pending trial between 15-20, 8-15 and 5-8 years as on 31.1.2000 are 488, 1458 and 1162, respectively.  Thus, the Committee strongly feels that the
Government should make serious efforts with a view to reducing the pendency of the cases in both the categories.
 
23.7     The Committee feels that the CBI is over-burdened with all sorts of cases.  In this context, the Committee is of the considered opinion that the CBI
should conduct investigations in complex cases and in such cases as provided in the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946.
 
23.8     The Committee has been informed that in order to strengthen inner mechanism of the CBI, an Independent Review Committee (IRC) was constituted
by the Government of India in September, 1997, inter alia, to examine the structure and working of CBI.  The IRC comprised Shri B.G. Deshmukh, former
Cabinet Secretary, Shri N.N. Vohra, the then Pincipal Secretary to the Prime Minister and Shri S.V. Giri, the then Central Vigilance Commissioner.  Based on
the recommendations of the IRC, The Supreme Court in Vineet Narain case gave certain directions to insulate CBI from extraneous influences and improve
its functioning.  The Supreme Court, inter alia, directed that the CBI shall report to the CVC about cases taken up by it for investigation, progress of
investigation, cases in which charge-sheets are filed and their progress, and the CVC shall review the progress of all cases moved by the CBI for sanction of
prosecution of Public Servants.  The Court also gave directions for conferring statutory status upon the CVC, vesting the CVC with powers to exercise
superintendence over CBI, process to be followed for selection of Director, CBI, ensuring minimum tenure of Director, CBI, induction of professionals to
strengthen in-house expertise of CBI, etc.  The Court also directed that the CVC shall have a separate section in its Annual Report on the CBI functioning
after the supervisory function of the CBI is transferred to it.
 
23.9     In pursuance of the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, as stated above Government has initiated action to accord statutory status to the Central
Vigilance Commission and to vest it with powers to exercise superintendence over CBI in so far as it relates to investigation of cases under the Prevention of
Corruption Act.  The Government has also constituted a CBI Selection Board on May 20
th, 1998 to make recommendations for appointment of Director, CBI
and other senior level posts of SP and above.  A panel of lawyers of impeccable reputation has been prepared for engagement as Special Counsels in
significant cases.  The Government has also sanctioned 183 posts, including technical posts to strengthen in-house expertise by inducting professional from
the revenue, banking and security sector.
 
23.10   Apart from the above exercise, the CBI has been restructured from time to time to strengthen its inner mechanism as and when the need was felt and as
result the organization evolved as follows:
 
(i)
                  1944 – The Special Police Establishment (SPE) was set up to investigate offences of bribery and corruption in the War and Supply Department
of the Government of India.
(ii)                1948 – The Special Police Establishment Act was passed and the jurisdiction was extended to investigate cases of bribery and corruption in all
Departments of Government of India.  The superintendence of SPE transferred to the Home Department.
(iii)               1963 – Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) was created vide a Government of India Resolution dated April 1, 1963 to investigate all cases
relating to corruption of Central Government employees and Departments, breach of Central fiscal laws and major frauds relating to Government
of India Departments.  The Special Police Establishment was made a Division of the CBI.
(iv)              1964 – A Special Economic Offences Division was added as the role of CBI had become multi-dimensional.
(v)                1987 – Based on the recommendation of the Committee headed by the Cabinet Secretary, a Special Crime Division was created.
(vi)              1994 – Due to increased work load relating to bank fraud and economic offences, an Economic Offences Division was added and functioning of
Anti-Corruption Division was decentralized with the creation of Zonal Joint Directors.
 
23.11   The Committee understands that the CBI Crime Manual was last revised in 1991.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the CBI Crime Manual
should be updated and revised from time to time.
 
PUBLIC ENTERPRISES SELECTION BOARD
 
24.0     Public Sector Enterprises (PSE) under the control of the Central Government play a vital role in the development of the national economy.  In order to
evolve a sound managerial personnel policy for the Public Sector Enterprises and, in particular, to advise Government on appointments to the top management
posts, the Government of India constituted a Public Enterprises Section Board (PESB) by a Resolution dated 30 August, 1974.  Consequent upon the shift of
the secretariat of the PESB from the Department of Public Enterprises to the Department of Personnel & Training from 9 July 1986, a comprehensive review
of the policy relating to the functions, membership, methodology for selection and infrastructure of the PESB  was made by Resolution dated 3 March 1987
of  Ministry of Personnel, PG & Pensions.  Amendments have been made to the Resolution from time to time.
 
24.1     The PESB functions as a professional body with a large measure of autonomy.  Its function are:
 
(i)
                  to be responsible for the selection and placement of personnel in the posts of Chairman, Managing Director or Chairman-cum-Managing
Director (Level I), and Functional Director (Level II) in PSEs as well as in posts at any other level as may be specified by the Government;
(ii)                to advise the Government on matters relating to appointment, confirmation or extension of tenure and termination of the services of personnel of
the above mentioned levels;
(iii)               to advise the Government on the desired structure at the Board level, and for senior mangement personnel, for each PSE or group of PSEs;
(iv)              to advise the Government on a suitable performance appraisal system for both the PSEs and the managerial personnel in such enterprises;

71st Report of COmmittee on Home Affairs

(v)                to build a data bank containing data relating to the performance of PSEs and its officers;
(vi)              to advise the Government on formulation and enforcement of a Code of Conduct and Ethics for managerial personnel in PSEs;
(vii)             to advise the Government on evolving suitable training and development programmes for management personnel in PSEs.
 
24.2     The PESB  consists of one part-time or full-time Chairperson and three full-time Members.  The Chairperson and Members shall be persons who have
had a long and distinguished career in management of public or private corporations or public administration and have a proven record of achievements,
preferably, in the field of personnel, finance, production or marketing.  The three full time members of the PESB shall be:
 
(i)
                  A distinguished serving or former Chief Executive of a Public Sector or Private Sector or Joint Sector Enterprise;
(ii)                A distinguished person with experience in selection of top management personnel;
(iii)               A distinguished serving or former civil servant with experience in management of PSEs or in areas of finance, industry or economic affairs.

Members of PESB:-

24.6     The Committee understands that one of the main functions of PESB is to build a data bank on PSEs and its officers.  The Committee recommends that

24.7     As per the instructions issued by the Department of Public Enterprises, the temporary vacancies of Chairmen and Managing Directors of Public

24.8     The Committee recommends  that the PESB must ensure early compliance of guidelines issued by DOPT in  regard to filling up the posts of Chairmen

24.9     From a perusal of papers submitted by the Ministry to the Committee, it notes that the PESB functions as a professional body with large measure of

CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION
 
25.0     The Central Vigilance Commission is an apex body exercising general superintendence and control over vigilance matters in administration of
Ministries/Department/Organisations of  Central  Government was conceptualized under Government of India Resolution dated 11 February, 1964.  The
Commission is headed by the Central Vigilance Commissioner who is assisted by a Secretary who is of the rank of Additional Secretary to the Government of
India, two Additional Secretaries of the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India and other supporting Officers and staff.  There are thirteen
Commissioners of Departmental Inquiries (CDI) who conduct oral inquiries relating to major penalty proceedings on behalf of the disciplinary authorities in
serious and important disciplinary cases.
 
25.1     In pursuance of Supreme Court judgement in Vineet Narain case in 1997, the Government introduced  the Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 1999 to
make it statutory body but the same could not be passed due to dissolution of Twelveth  Lok Sabha following which Ordinances were promulgated.  The
Central Vigilance Commission Ordinances dated 25 August, 1998, 27 October, 1998 and 8 January 1999 lapsed after expiry of the prescribed period.  The

Central Vigilance Commission is presently continuing on the basis of the Government of India Resolution dated 4 April 1999, as a non-statutory body,
pending enactment of an Act of Parliament which is under process. 
 
25.2     On being asked about the action plans envisaged by the CVC to improve viligance administration of Ministries/Departments/Organisations  of Central
Government so as to evolve good governance based on transparency, integrity and accountability, the Ministry has enumerated the following steps envisaged
by the CVC:
 
(i)
                  That the Agreed List and List of Officers of doubtful integrity should be finalized early and it should be ensured that officers appearing on those
lists are not posted in sensitive areas;
(ii)                That the complaints should be investigated expeditiously.  The Commission had observed that a large number of complaints forwarded by it to
the CVOs were pending for reports.  As on 22.02.2001, the reports were awaited on 2045 complaints, which included 498 complaints pending for
more than five years.
(iii)               The Commission has also put on its web site the age-wise pendency of cases with administrative authorities for action on its advice.  As on
22.02.2001, 3973 cases were pending for implementation of its first stage advice for initiation of major/minor penalty proceedings, which
included 631 cases pending for more than five years.  Likewise, there were 1332 cases pending implementation of its second stage advice for
imposition of major/minor penalty, which included 202 cases pending for more than five years.  The Commission has since initiated a special
drive for the departments to ensure that the cases pending implementation of the Commission’s second stage advice for more than three years are
disposed of in next three months.
 
(iv)
              The Commission has also put on its web site the names of officers against whom it has advised launching of criminal proccedings or imposition
of major penalty since 1.1.1990.
 
(v)                The Commission, in order to reduce the level of corruption, has issued a number of instructions to the administrative authorities regarding
electronics clearance system, computerization of the branches, action on anonymous/pseudonymous complaints, negotiations regarding tenders,
etc.
 
25.3     From the perusal  of statistics of the CVC, it appears that the advice of CVC is yet to be considered  in more than 800  cases  which are pending for
more than  five years.  Further  criminal  action/ major penalties  have  been  suggested against many officers by the CVC.  The detailed status of action taken 
by the Government may be  submitted  to the Committee.  Steps should also be expedited  to take  appropriate  action  against  officers  against  whom major
penalties /criminal proceedings have been suggested.
 
25.4     The Central Vigilance Commission has issued several instruction, some of which are enumerated below:
 
(i)
                  Creating a culture of honesty: Junior employees who initiated any proposal relating to vigilance matters could endorse a copy directly to the
CVC by name and such reference would not be treated as an act of indiscipline unless a false or frivolous complaint was made.
(ii)                Greater transparency in administration: All organizations under the CVC’s purview should publish details of all cases relating to acceptance of
tenders, out-of-turn allotments or discretion exercised in favour of an employee/party on the notice board and in the organisation’s regular
publications.  This would provide an automatic check on corruption-induced decisions or undue favours.  In addition in cases of disciplinary
proceedings, the Commission’s first and second stage advice should be made available to the concerned employees along with a copy of the
charge sheet served on him or along with the Inquiry Officer’s report as the case may be.
(iii)
               Speedy departmental inquiries: Retired officers may be appointed as Inquiring Authorities so as to complete departmental inquiries within a
period of 6 months from the date of appointment of the Inquiry Authority.  The Commission has also a panel of retired officers who can be
appointed as Inquiring Authorities, which is now available on its web site.  The Commission has also stipulated model time schedule for
observance by the Inquiring Authorities.
(iv)
              Tenders: The Commission has banned post-tender negotiations with effect from 18.11.1998, except with the lowest tenderer.
(v)                Electronics clearance system and computerization of bank branches: Instructions have been given to banks accordingly.
(vi)              Sensitising the public about corruption:  The Commission has directed all organizations under its purview to prominently display a notice board
at the Reception In English and other languages asking the public not to pay bribes and in case they are victims of corruption, they could
complain to the Head of the Department of CVO or the CVC.  The names, addresses and telephone numbers of the concerned officers are also to
be placed on the notice Board.  In addition, the Commission has advised that the week beginning 31 October every year to be observed as
Vigilance Awareness Week.
(vii)
             Action on anonymous/pseudonymous complaints: The Commission has directed that such complaints be filed.
(viii)           Effective punishment to corrupt employees through traps: The number of traps conducted by the police officials under the provisions of the PC
Act were not commensurate with the level of corruption in the country.  The Commission has directed the CVOs to take initiative in arranging
traps if a person gives a written complaint or a source information to him.
(ix)              Special Chapter on vigilance management in public sector Banks and public sector enterprises, and
(x)                Strengthening vigilance and anti-corruption work.
 
       
25.5     The Ministry is fully alive to the need to eradicate corruption at all levels of public services.  A three pronged strategy of surveillance, Prevention and
Punitive/Deterrent action is followed by the Government.
 
25.6     Under the strategy of Preventive Vigilance, steps have been taken to ensure transparency in public administration and initiate measures of
administrative reforms such as – framing of Citizen’s Charter, setting  up of  Information Facilitation Counter for dissemination of information and review of
simplification of laws, rules and procedures and  the latest being the introduction of Freedom of Information Bill.
 
25.7     The punitive action is being taken under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 duly supported by various rules governing the service conditions of
public servants and also act as a deterrent against corruption.  The drive against corruption in public services is a continuing process.
 
ROTATION OF OFFICERS IN SENSITIVE POST
 
26.0     In accordance with existing instructions, various Minsitries/Departments/Organisations are required to prepare lists of public servants of Gazetted

71st Report of COmmittee on Home Affairs

status of doubtful integrity.  The purpose of the lists is to keep Ministries/Departments/Undertakings concerned informed about such officers to ensure that
they are not posted to sensitive assignments.  Further, ‘Agreed lists’ are also required to be prepared of officers of gazetted status against whose honesty or
integrity there are complaints, doubts or suspicions after consultation between officers of the Departments concerned and the CBI.  Further, CVC guidelines
regarding rotations of officers who are working in sensitive posts  every two/three years to avoid developing vested interest.  The Ministry has taken action to
rotate such officers after each five years.
 
26.1     The Ministry has informed the Committee that six IAS officers have been prematurely retired from service during the last five years.
 
26.2     Rule 16(3) of the All India Services (Death-cum-Retirement Benefit) Rules, 1958 provides that the Central Government may, in consultation with the
concerned State Government and after giving a member of the service at least three months’ previous notice in writing or three months’ pay and allowances in
lieu of such notice, require that member to retire from service in public interest on the date on which such member completes 30 years’ of qualifying service
or attains 50 years of age or any date thereafter as may be specified.  The objective of this Rule is to provide a mechanism for weeding out officers who have
proven to be of doubtful integrity or who have a track record of inefficiency and have become ‘deadwood’ in the system.
 
26.3     All State Governments are required to conduct a review of the career records and the character rolls of members of the service due to complete 30
years’ of qualifying service or attain 50 years of age.  The recommendations of Review Committees which conduct such reviews are then forwarded by the
State Government concerned to the Central Government with their recommendations in the matter.  Final orders in this regard are issued by the Central
Government.
 
26.4     The Committee has been informed that Ministry has formulated a 'Rotation Policy for CSS officers' vide OM No. 31/23/98-EO(MM-I) dated 24.12.99
as per which CSS Officers of US and above grades will be transferred to other Ministries / Department on completion of a fixed tenure of 7 years in the grade
for US and 5 years in the grades of DS/Directors/JS.  Accordingly, as replied by the Ministry to Rajya Sabha Starred Question No. 394 on 22.3.2001, transfer
orders for 224 officers of US has been issued.  But it is noticed that some officers have not been relieved as on the date of reply of the Rajya Sabha Question. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure strict compliance of orders, as any deviation will defeat the very purpose of rotation policy.  The
Ministry should also ensure timely preparation of lists of officers required to be transferred every year.  The Committee further recommends that the Section
Officers promoted to Under Secretary  on in situ basis shall also be subjected to transfer as per rotation policy.  It has also been brought to the notice of the
Committee that participating Ministries/Department of CSS are not strictly following the instruction of the CVC issued from time to time on rotational
transfer of the CSS officers in the Ministries/Departments.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry shall devise a mechanism for proper
monitoring of rotational transfer of the CSS officers within Ministries/Departments and urge them to fix responsibility for non compliance of instructions of
CVC.
 
26.5     The Committee appreciates  the steps taken  by the CVC  to root out corruption from the Government  Departments, however, it feels that a lot more is
required  to be done.  The Committee recommends that CVC should vigorously pursue its instructions   and proper monitoring  mechanism be evolved to
ensure compliance  of instructions  by all the Ministries/Departments etc.
 
26.6    The Central Vigilance Commission Bill, which has been examined and reported upon by this Committee and Joint Select Committee is pending in Lok
Sabha.  The Committee urges upon the Government to expedite the consideration and passage of the Bill.                    
 
 
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
DOMESTIC FUNDING FOR FOREIGN TRAINING
 
*          The Committee observes that Foreign Travel Expenses usually comes under the non-plan head.  Leaving aside the aforesaid new provision of Rs. 10
crores under plan outlay, a total amount of Rs. 1.19 crores have also been kept for Foreign Travel Expenses under non-plan outlay. The Committee is
at a loss to understand the rationale for keeping substantial amount of Rs. 10 crores under plan outlay instead of  non-plan.  In this connection, the
Committee is constrained to point out that the Ministry has not responded to the specific query in that regard.                                                             
                                                                                                    (Para 10.6.0)
*          The Committee strongly feels that the amount in the plan-outlay could have been augmented gradually keeping in view the cost-benefit aspect of
domestic funding of foreign training, instead of requesting the Planning Commission to allocate such a high amount of Rs. 10 crores in the Annual
Plan of the Ministry beginning from the year 2001-2002.
                                                                                                                          (Para 10.6.1)
            NON-PLAN OUTLAY/EXPENDITURE
                                             
*          The Committee while taking note of a decision not to publish the booklet already
available at Ministry’s website, desires that the publication of revised Manual of Office Procedure may be completed at the earliest.
                                                                                                                           (Para 10.8.9)
*          The Committee appreciates the measures taken to reduce administrative expenditure as projected under the BE (2001-2002).  The Committee desires
that the tempo of cut in administrative expenditure should well be reflected at RE stage and the BE of the next year budget so that the cut could be
diverted to plan outlay for modernization of Government offices.
                                                                                                                        (Para 10.8.10)
                DEMAND NO. 94 (UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION)
 
*          The Committee notes the justifications offered by the Ministry for the hike of administrative expenses of the UPSC for the coming year.
    (Para 11.5)
            CITIZEN’S CHARTER
 
*          From the replies of the Ministry elaborated in the previous paras, it seems that directions of the Ministry to ensure participation of Members of
Parliament, State Legislatures and opinion makers exist at the formulation stage and not at the evaluation stage of the citizen’s charter. The Committee
recommends that the feedback of the users must be assessed by the organizations providing services in the light of suggestion received from the
representatives of the people. The concerned organization must strive to find methods to ensure the participation of representatives of people in
formulation as well as evaluation of citizen’s charter.
      (Para 14.4)

*          The Ministry’s reply amply proves that the feedback mechanism is the vital component of citizen’s charter but the reply is not expressive as to the
mode of receiving feedback. The Committee is of the view that review of implementation of charter is not given proper attention and, therefore,
recommends that evaluation aspect of implementation of charters from customer-point of view must be given due stress and importance.
                                                                                                                                         (Para 14.6)
*          The Committee feels that publicity of charters is very essential to make the general public aware about its existence and utility, which would help in
soliciting their feedback for its evaluation. The Committee desires that citizen’s charter movement in India must be given adequate publicity, if
required, open discussions with the users of services of organizations may be resorted to make it a viable instrument for achieving responsible and 
responsive administration.
                                                                                                                                          (Para 14.9)
            INFORMATION AND FACILITATION COUNTERS
 
*          The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry to plug the deficiencies         in the structure and functioning of IFCs in different 
Ministries/Department.  The Committee  understands three organization which  have  Citizen’s Charter but have not set up IFCs,  should be  urged to
take steps for setting up of IFCs as  Citizen’s Charter appears to  be meaningless without its physical manifestation.
                             (Para 15.4)           
            PUBLIC GRIEVANCE COMMISSION
 
*          The Committee understands that there  would be two  policy-formulators with regard to public grievance redressal with the institution of the Central
Grievance Commission (CGC) i.e. Department of AR&PG and CGC.  There would also be two appellate bodies . The Directorate of Public
Grievances in Cabinet Secretariat for the 14 Ministries/Departments and the CGC for the rest Ministries/Departments.  Further, the grievances
pertaining to State Government would be in the hands of the Department of AR&PG.  With the proliferation of grievance redressal bodies and
apparent over-lapping of functions between those may entail confusion in the minds of the complainants.  Moreover many bodies for the same work
would also have the direct bearing on the Government exchequer.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Committee of Secretaries while
giving shape to the CGC must clearly define the role and scope of other existing grievance redressal mechanisms with a view to avoid undue over-
lapping .
                  (Para 16.9)
*          The Committee notes the action taken in respect of the grievances appearing in newspapers.  The Committee understands that the issue of settling the
grievances lies with the concerned Ministry/Department to which the newspaper clippings  have been forwarded by the Department of AR&PG.  The
Committee feels that the grievances appearing in newspaper should be settled within a given time-frame; the status of the grievances must be
communicated to the ‘writers of the letters to editors’, in case the concerned Ministry takes time to settle the matter.  The Committee recommends that
action must be taken to give due publicity to the existing grievance mechanisms and mode of handling/settling grievances by the
Ministries/Departments in Government of India.
            (Para 16.10.4)
            MODERNISATION OF GOVERNMENT OFFICES
 
*          The Committee notes the steady progress made in the modernization in some of the Government offices.  Initiatives must now be taken to modernize
all Government offices on the lines of the models of modernizations, which will facilitate faster decision making process and lesser
grievances.                                                                                         
      (Para 17.7)
            GOOD GOVERNANCE
 
*          The Committee notes that the Secretary level posts have increased from 117 to 159 from 1 January, 1998 to 1 January, 2000 with the
proliferation/bifurcation of Ministries/Departments.  The Committee, however. feels that downsizing of the Government should be reflected at all
levels of posts without compromising the efficiency and accountability of the civil service.                       
     (Para 18.3)
            CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
 
*          The Committee strongly recommends to the Government to take an early decision on the above suggestions of Law Commission to make CAT a
viable instrument in providing speedy and inexpensive  justice to the Government employees.                            
    (Para 19.12)
 
*          The Committee is informed that service related cases of group of employees are  also instituted in the CAT in addition to individual cases  and
understands that 87 such cases  are still pending  with  the CAT.  The Committee wanted to know whether the JCM & BOA machinery   was used  in
the aforesaid pending cases to get relief.  The Committee, in view of the reply of the Ministry, reiterates its earlier stand to take a holistic approach  to
solve group as well as individual service related cases through JCM and BOA before allowing them to approach CAT straightway.                            
                                                                                                                    (Para 19.17)
            STATE ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
 
*          The Committee recommends  that steps should be taken to complete  the process  of establishing   SATs in Gujarat, Punjab and Tripura.  The
Committee also recommends the Ministry to  issue necessary  instructions/guidelines  to the State Governments to dispose of service-related cases
pending before SATs/other Tribunals expeditiously.                                                                              (Para 21.3)
 
 
CENTRAL SECRETARIAT SERVICE
 
*          The various aspects pertaining to the service matters of Central Secretariat Service have been engaging the attention of the Committee for quite some
time. In its successive Reports on Demands for Grants of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, the Committee have made detailed
observations/recommendations on the Central Secretariat Service. During the examination of  Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of Ministry of
Personnel by the Committee in its sitting held on 28 March, 2001, several members referred to the on-going agitation by CSS Forum, and in that
context, several issues relating to CSS were raised. In its sitting held on 29 March, 2001 members raised the said matter again.  After some discussion,
the Committee decided to have a separate sitting to discuss all the aspects relating to service conditions of CSS. It was also decided that Secretary
(Personnel) would be requested to be present in that sitting to respond to queries/questions of the members. Accordingly, the Committee in its sitting
