consideration.  It heard the views of Prof. A.K. Sharma, Head of Department, Department of Transport and Centre for Transport Studies and
Traffic Laboratory, School of Planning and Architecture, New Delhi and Dr. T.S. Reddy, Deputy Director (Traffic and Transportation),
Central Road Research Institute, New Delhi, on the subject in its meeting held on 30 March 2001.
57.       Prof. A.K. Sharma, in his presentation focused on major issues concerning the problems of traffic in Delhi.  The most important was
the functional distribution of work related to the traffic management in Delhi.  These functions were planning, engineering and management. 
The role of traffic police came under the ambit of management especially in terms of enforcement and regulation of traffic.  So far as
engineering and planning inputs was concerned, Delhi Police had no mechanism in their cadres.  He stated that there existed multiplicity of
authorities to take care of traffic management. Agencies like DDA, MCD, NDMC, State Transport Authority, etc. were responsible for traffic
management in Delhi. This multiplicity of authority had resulted into the disintegration of transport planning functions. He suggested that
there should be one nodal agency for performing the planning functions which should be under the jurisdiction of
 
Government of Delhi. This agency should have an expert group who could sensitise other agencies regarding the future policies, programme
implementation and execution. The enforcement, however, should remain with Delhi Police.  The next major issue was that of road safety
which was intrinsically linked to licensing of drivers and the use of road space within the city. He suggested for stringent procedures for issue
of licenses which should inter alia have a mandatory requirement of minimum level of literacy, six months compulsory training   from a
driver training institute, etc. Referring to the safety of school children of the roads, he stated that a proper system of school transportation
needed to be evolved. He felt that there was an urgent need to have a dedicated transport system for school children. Touching upon the issue
of enforcement, he stated that a high-end technology and traffic surveillance system should be put in place. He opined that dedicated
technologies could help in controlling traffic. Another important aspect was training of traffic personnel. In his view, most of the traffic
personnel were not trained in traffic management, which was a specialized subject of study. He felt that rotation of traffic personnel was not
going to produce any results. Sustained involvement of traffic personnel  was key to the success. He was of the view that improvement in the
functioning of traffic police relied on the inputs of local agencies responsible for traffic management.
58.       Another traffic expert, Dr. T.S. Reddy stated that the worsening traffic situation was largely due to the total negligence of planning.
The transport system had not been planned properly. He opined that three Es-engineering, education and enforcement were the most
important aspects of traffic management.  Of these, engineering was the most neglected as a result of which traffic was being controlled
manually by traffic personnel. He felt that there was need for a selective and strategic enforcement drive to discipline the behaviour of
motorists on the roads. This apart, a tremendous thrust should be given for bringing about an attitudinal change in the traffic police. In fact,
there was need for systematic traffic training school. He further stated that a comprehensive parking policy was also needed. As for the
training aspect, he felt that it was the most important thing for personnel managing the traffic.
59.       The worsening traffic scenario of the capital has attracted the attention of the Committee primarily because of its negligence by the
authorities concerned.  There is no gainsaying the fact that it is not too easy a problem to be dealt with.  A city with close to four million
vehicles with an almost static road network definitely poses huge challenges for its traffic managers.  However, it is interesting to note that in
spite of having so many challenges to grapple with, there is no unified authority to take them on.  There seem to be as many authorities as
there are challenges.  This is probably the reason why things are pulling in different directions.  There is no unity of command nor there is any
coordination among the agencies responsible for the management of overall traffic scenario.  At a time when situation warrants concerted,
well-coordinated and unified measures to be taken, the system lacks the required mechanism to see it through.  Though a slew of other
agencies such as DDA, MCD, NDMC, STA etc. are also responsible for the traffic management of the city either this way or the other, the
onus of receiving the brickbats for the traffic woes lies purely with the Delhi Traffic Police.  To put the whole blame on Traffic Police will
mean closing eyes to the reality.  Delhi has acquired the dimensions of being billed as one of the fastest expanding megapolises of the world. 
The deterioration of traffic scenario is nothing but the reflection of an over-stretched civic infrastructure.  Therefore, the need of the hour is to
see how best can the limited civic infrastructure of this over-populated and over-crowded city be managed. 
59.1     In the opinion of the Committee there is an urgent need for setting up a Unified Traffic Management Authority, which should be
responsible for the overall planning, and management of traffic scenario of Delhi.  This body may consist of noted experts with proven
expertise on traffic management, senior officers of traffic police, representatives of local civic agencies and public representatives.  It should
be vested with adequate powers.  Besides, there should be clear division of work.  Ideally, there should be three functional units one each for
enforcement, education and training and engineering.  Enforcement should remain with Delhi Traffic Police whereas for education and
training and engineering two separate units should be created.  These three functional units should be placed within the jurisdiction of the
proposed Authority.  In such a set up it should be the sole responsibility of the Authority to plan, implement and monitor a comprehensive
traffic management plan based on present as well future requirements.
60.       Enforcement plays a crucial role in managing traffic on the roads.  For a city like Delhi, which has the largest number of vehicles in
the country, enforcement of traffic rules is an extremely difficult task.  Manual enforcement cannot match with the scale at which
enforcement is required to be done.  Therefore, state-of-the art technological devices should be pressed into service for the rescue of traffic
enforcement personnel.  The growing number of traffic violations in Delhi makes it abundantly clear that enforcement through primitive
methods has lost its efficacy.  The use of latest gadgets and technology alone can reduce the number of violations.  This can be illustrated
with the successful use of red light camera by Delhi Traffic Police which helped to reduce the rate of traffic violations quite considerably.  In
the light of the experience of successful use of red light camera by Delhi Traffic Police, it is imperative that such need-based technological
devices are made available so as to restore sanity on the roads.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Delhi Traffic Police should be
provided with adequate number of state-of-the art technological devices such as Red Light Speed Cameras, CCTV Cameras, Radar Guns,
Alco meters and Interceptors so as to enable it to discipline the behaviour of errant motorists.  Top most priority should be accorded to the
acquisition of these devices by finding suitable financial ways and means.

60.1     Apart from enforcement, another key area which requires attention is the need for educating the public about traffic rules and
regulations. The Delhi Traffic Police should lay special emphasis on creating awareness among people for behaving in a disciplined manner
on the roads as it was in their own interest. The awareness campaign in this regard should be a constant exercise instead of being an
occasional one. Traffic personnel, while enforcing traffic rules, should also focus on educating the public about the dangers of not adhering to
traffic rules.  
61.       Another important aspect that requires immediate attention is the training of traffic personnel.  Any number of technological devices
will fail to produce desired results unless the persons responsible for traffic management have requisite professional skills to make use of
them.  Traffic personnel should have a flair for their professional duties.  Adequate orientation towards the calling of their job is essential. 
Enforcement of traffic rules should not be treated as a mere policing job.
62.       Keeping in view the significance of having a skilled and fully trained manpower for managing traffic in Delhi, the Committee
recommends that a comprehensive curriculum covering all the aspects of traffic management should be prepared for being imparted to the
personnel of Delhi Traffic Police.  Besides, the Committee is also of the view the recruitment policy needs a re-look.  Recruitment of
personnel on conventional pattern may no longer be in tune with present day requirements.  People with adequate professional background
and a natural flair for the job, alone should be recruited. 
63.       Of late, Delhi has witnessed a large number of accidents in which a number of school children have died.  These accidents have
mainly occurred due to rash and negligent driving by the drivers of school buses.  These accidents have brought to the fore the need to focus
attention on this hitherto totally neglected area of traffic management.  The safety of school children is the shared responsibility of school
authorities, traffic authorities, drivers/conductors of the buses and parents.  Therefore, all of them need to be sensitized about their role in this
shared responsibility.  Apart from this, the need for a dedicated fleet for school transportation is of paramount importance.
64.       The Committee is of the considered view that a set of guidelines should be framed whereby the role and responsibility of every person
concerned with the transportation of school children should be clearly defined.  Cooperation and coordination among all concerned should be
the hallmark of managing the affairs pertaining to the school transportation.  The Committee hopes that with the creation of a dedicated fleet
of buses for school transportation, framing of clear-cut guidelines and their strict compliance will help save the lives of innocent school
children.  To ensure the compliance and strict adherence to the guidelines, a school level monitoring body should be set up in which local
traffic personnel may be associated.

67.       North Eastern Council came into being as an inter-state structural entity to provide a functional framework for ensuring all-round and
balanced development of the North Eastern region.  The concept of having a regional organization for the seven sister States was aimed at
providing an institutional platform to discuss the matters of common interest in the field of economic and social planning, transport &
communication and power and flood control.  It was also aimed at infusing a sense of cooperation and coordination among all the States of
the region so as to enable them to be part of national mainstream.  However, a look at the over-all performance of the NEC ever since it
started functioning, reveals that it has not been able to live up to the high expectations.  It is now in the 29
th year of its existence but its
performance record is not as impressive as it should have been.  Its contribution lies in adding a mere 247.50 MW of power to the installed
capacity, 1887 kms. of power transmission lines and 4800 kms. of roads.  This apart, it has built two major bridges across the Brahmaputra at
Tejpur and Jogigopa.  In addition to this, it has established 5 regional institutes for development of manpower and improvement of health
care    facilities.  The   achievements    of  the Council have belied the high expectations with
which it was set up.  Almost all projects of NEC have suffered from cost and time over-runs.  For instance, 31 road projects have experienced
cost over-run to the tune of Rs.840.84 crore and are still going on.  Similarly, Ranganadi Hydro-Electricity Project (405 MW) is already
delayed by 7 years and has experienced cost over-run to the tune of Rs.1133.31 crore.  Besides, Ranganadi Transmission Lines project will be
late by 9 years with a cost over-run of Rs.113.09 crore.  Given the way NEC has performed, it raises doubts about its efficacy and puts a
question mark on the continuation of its very existence in its present form.
68.       The Governors and Chief Ministers of all the seven States of North Eastern region are members of North Eastern Council (NEC).  The
Committee is of the considered view that it should be made more broad based so as to enable it to have a much wider perspective vis-à-vis
over-all development of the member States.  The involvement of elected representatives of the people in the decision making process of the
Council can help it generate a sense of belonging among the people of the region towards it.  For, it is very significant to take the people
along in the developmental process.  People, in general, should not feel alienated and isolated from the process, which in effect, is aimed at
their welfare.  The association of their representatives with a body which exists for the all-round development of their States, will definitely
lead to the identification of a common man’s aspirations with the actions of that body.  Therefore, the Committee is of the opinion that at least
one MP from each North Eastern State should be member of NEC so that he can present the people’s viewpoint before the Council vis-à-vis
its various projects/plans. 
69.       As mentioned in the preceding paragraphs, almost all projects of NEC have had cost and time over-runs.  Although these projects are
sponsored by NEC, their execution remains with the concerned States.  Since most of these projects have an inter-State character which
means the involvement of various agencies, the progress of work would always remain tardy especially in the absence of a single monitoring
agency.  Therefore, in the view of the Committee, the execution of the projects/plans sponsored by NEC should also be included in its
mandate.  The recommended widening of the mandate of the NEC, the Committee hopes, will help it reduce cost and time over-runs to a large
extent.
70.       Construction of inter-State roads is part of NEC’s mandate.  Ever since its inception, it has added 4800 kms. of road length to the
network of roads in the North Eastern Region.  Despite that, the condition of roads in almost all States of the region remains pathetic. 
Apparently, the quality of construction and maintenance of roads is very poor due to which roads have a very short span of life.  In the
opinion of the Committee, road projects of NEC should be executed by an agency with a creditable performance record having strict quality
controls.  Border Roads Organisation (BRO) is one such agency which could deliver the desired results in this regard.  Therefore, the
Committee recommends that NEC projects involving construction and maintenance of roads should be entrusted with the Border Roads
Organisation (BRO).
71.       The Committee notes that the North Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill, 1998 is pending in Rajya Sabha.  It recommends that the
proposed restructuring of NEC should be done expeditiously keeping in view present day ground realities and requirements.

of not adhering to traffic rules.  
(Para 60.1)
*          Another important aspect that requires immediate attention is the training of traffic personnel.  Any number of technological devices
will fail to produce desired results unless the persons responsible for traffic management have requisite professional skills to make use
of them.  Traffic personnel should have a flair for their professional duties.  Adequate orientation towards the calling of their job is
essential.  Enforcement of traffic rules should not be treated as a mere policing job.
(Para 61)
*          Keeping in view the significance of having a skilled and fully trained manpower for managing traffic in Delhi, the Committee
recommends that a comprehensive curriculum covering all the aspects of traffic management should be prepared for being imparted to
the personnel of Delhi Traffic Police.  Besides, the Committee is also of the view the recruitment policy needs a re-look.  Recruitment
of personnel on conventional pattern may no longer be in tune with present day requirements.  People with adequate professional
background and a natural flair for the job, alone should be recruited. 
(Para 62)
*          Of late, Delhi has witnessed a large number of accidents in which a number of school children have died.  These accidents have
mainly occurred due to rash and negligent driving by the drivers of school buses.  These accidents have brought to the fore the need to
focus attention on this hitherto totally neglected area of traffic management.  The safety of school children is the shared responsibility
of school authorities, traffic authorities, drivers/conductors of the buses and parents.  Therefore, all of them need to be sensitized about
their role in this shared responsibility.  Apart from this, the need for a dedicated fleet for school transportation is of paramount
importance.
(Para 63)
*          The Committee is of the considered view that a set of guidelines should be framed whereby the role and responsibility of every person
concerned with the transportation of school children should be clearly defined.  Cooperation and coordination among all concerned
should be the hallmark of managing the affairs pertaining to the school transportation.  The Committee hopes that with the creation of
a dedicated fleet of buses for school transportation, framing of clear-cut guidelines and their strict compliance will help save the lives
of innocent school children.  To ensure the compliance and strict adherence to the guidelines, a school level monitoring body should
be set up in which local traffic personnel may be associated.
(Para 64)
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL
*          North Eastern Council came into being as an inter-state structural entity to provide a functional framework for ensuring all-round and
balanced development of the North Eastern region.  The concept of having a regional organization for the seven sister States was
aimed at providing an institutional platform to discuss the matters of common interest in the field of economic and social planning,
transport & communication and power and flood control.  It was also aimed at infusing a sense of cooperation and coordination among
all the States of the region so as to enable them to be part of national mainstream.  However, a look at the over-all performance of the
NEC ever since it started functioning, reveals that it has not been able to live up to the high expectations.  It is now in the 29
th year of

73rd Report of Committee on Home affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/73rdreport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:49]
its existence but its performance record is not as impressive as it should have been.  Its contribution lies in adding a mere 247.50 MW
of power to the installed capacity, 1887 kms. of power transmission lines and 4800 kms. of roads.  This apart, it has built two major
bridges across the Brahmaputra at Tejpur and Jogigopa.  In addition to this, it has established 5 regional institutes for development of
manpower and improvement of health care facilities.  The achievements of the Council have belied the high expectations with which it
was set up.  Almost all projects of NEC have suffered from cost and time over-runs.  For instance, 31 road projects have experienced
cost over-run to the tune of Rs.840.84 crore and are still going on.  Similarly, Ranganadi Hydro-Electricity Project (405 MW) is
already delayed by 7 years and has experienced cost over-run to the tune of Rs.1133.31 crore.  Besides, Ranganadi Transmission Lines
project will be late by 9 years with a cost over-run of Rs.113.09 crore.  Given the way NEC has performed, it raises doubts about its
efficacy and puts a question mark on the continuation of its very existence in its present form.
(Para 67)
*          The Governors and Chief Ministers of all the seven States of North Eastern region are members of North Eastern Council (NEC).  The
Committee is of the considered view that it should be made more broad based so as to enable it to have a much wider perspective vis-
à-vis over-all development of the member States.  The involvement of elected representatives of the people in the decision making
process of the Council can help it generate a sense of belonging among the people of the region towards it.  For, it is very significant
to take the people along in the developmental process.  People, in general, should not feel alienated and isolated from the process,
which in effect, is aimed at their welfare.  The association of their representatives with a body which exists for the all-round
development of their States, will definitely lead to the identification of a common man’s aspirations with the actions of that body. 
Therefore, the Committee is of the opinion that at least one MP from each North Eastern State should be member of NEC so that he
can present the people’s viewpoint before the Council vis-à-vis its various projects/plans. 
(Para 68)
*          As mentioned in the preceding paragraphs, almost all projects of NEC have had cost and time over-runs.  Although these projects are
sponsored by NEC, their execution remains with the concerned States.  Since most of these projects have an inter-State character
which means the involvement of various agencies, the progress of work would always remain tardy especially in the absence of a
single monitoring agency.  Therefore, in the view of the Committee, the execution of the projects/plans sponsored by NEC should also
be included in its mandate.  The recommended widening of the mandate of the NEC, the Committee hopes, will help it reduce cost and
time over-runs to a large extent.
(Para 69)
*          Construction of inter-State roads is part of NEC’s mandate.  Ever since its inception, it has added 4800 kms. of road length to the
network of roads in the North Eastern Region.  Despite that, the condition of roads in almost all States of the region remains pathetic. 
Apparently, the quality of construction and maintenance of roads is very poor due to which roads have a very short span of life.  In the
opinion of the Committee, road projects of NEC should be executed by an agency with a creditable performance record having strict
quality controls.  Border Roads Organisation (BRO) is one such agency which could deliver the desired results in this regard. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends that NEC projects involving construction and maintenance of roads should be entrusted with
the Border Roads Organisation (BRO).
(Para 70)
*          The Committee notes that the North Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill, 1998 is pending in Rajya Sabha.  It recommends that the
proposed restructuring of NEC should be done expeditiously keeping in view present day ground realities and requirements.
(Para 71)
PERSONNEL POLICIES FOLLOWED IN CISF
*          The grievances of the direct recruit Group ‘A’ officers of CISF have been engaging the attention of the Committee for quite some time
now, as part of its larger study of personnel policies being followed in respect of the Central Para-military Forces.  In its successive
reports on Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Committee has made detailed observations/recommendations on
the subject.  In the sitting of the Committee held on 28 March, 2001, members raised issues relating to the grievances of the direct
recruit Group ‘A’ CISF Officers, when the Secretary (Personnel) was present in connection with the examination of the Demands for
Grants (2001-2002) of his Ministry.  In the next sitting of the Committee held on 29 March 2001, members raised the matter again. 
After some discussion, the Committee decided to have a separate sitting to discuss at length all the aspects relating to the grievances of
the said officers.  It was also decided that Home Secretary and Secretary (Personnel) would be requested to be present in that sitting to
respond to the questions/queries of the members.  Accordingly, the Committee in its sitting held on 10 April 2001 discussed the
subject in detail.  The Home Secretary and Secretary (Personnel) made brief presentations.  They also replied to some of the
points/queries raised in the meeting.  As a large number of points/suggestions were raised/made, the Home Secretary was requested to
submit at an early date written responses of the Government thereto for further consideration of the Committee.  Keeping in view the
deliberations held in the Committee, it has decided to present a separate report in the matter to Parliament.
(Para 72)

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
 
RAJYA SABHA
DEPARTMENT-RELATED PARLIAMENTARY
STANDING COMMITTEE ON HOME AFFAIRS
SEVENTY FOURTH REPORT
ON
 
THE CONSTITUTION (NINETY-FIRST AMENDMENT) BILL, 2000
 
(PRESENTED TO RAJYA SABHA ON 26th APRIL, 2001)
(LAID ON THE TABLE LOK SABHA ON 26th APRIL, 2001)
 
REPORT
            The Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Bill, 2000 (See Annexure-I) seeks to amend altogether six Articles of the
Constitution (55, 81, 82, 170, 330 and 332) to remove the distortions and disparities caused due to uneven growth of
population/electorate in territorial constituencies for Lok Sabha/Legislative Assemblies, while sustaining the measure to boost
family planning norms.
1.1              To achieve the foresaid objective, the Bill has the following enabling provisions:-
(i)                  extending the constitutional embargo on undertaking fresh delimitation of constituencies from the year 2000 to
2026;
(ii)                readjustment and rationalization of Parliamentary constituencies in the States without altering the number of seats
allotted to each State in the House of People, including the Schedule Caste and the Scheduled Tribe constituencies,
on the basis of 1991 population census;
(iii)               readjustment and rationalization of Assembly constituencies in the States without altering the number of seats
allotted to each State in their Legislative Assemblies, including the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribe
constituencies, on the basis of 1991 population census; and
(iv)              refixing the number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the House of the
People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States on the basis of 1991 population census.
2.0       The amendment to the aforesaid seven Articles has been necessitated mainly due to the following two facts:-
(i)                  the constitutional embargo on the delimitation of territorial constituencies (both Parliamentary and Assembly),
imposed by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, will expire after the publication of first census
after the year 2000 AD, the process of which has already been set in motion; and
(ii)
                the growth of population is not uniform in the country.  The unbalanced and uneven growth of population as well
as continuous migration of people from one place to another, especially from rural to urban areas have resulted in
strikingly different sizes of electoral constituencies even within the State.  The most glaring example is outer Delhi
Parliamentary constituency, which had approximately 29.3 lakhs population whereas the Chandni Chowk
Parliamentary Constituency had a population of 3.7 lakhs (both 1998 figures).
2.1       The last delimitation of territorial constituencies was done on the basis of decennial population census of 1971 by the
Delimitation Commission, constituted for the purpose by the Delimitation Act, 1972 (See Annexure-II).  The Commission took
roughly four years to complete the delimitation work on that occasion, after which the delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly
Constituencies Order, 1976 came into force. 
2.1.1    The ban on the delimitation was imposed by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment)Act, 1976 with a specific aim to
boost family planning norms.  It was thought at that time that the States which did not control their population should not get
rewarded through the delimitation process and that by the year, 2000, the progress of implementation of family planning would,
more or less be uniform throughout the country.
2.1.2    But it is found that the population growth since 1971 census is quite haphazard and uneven.  The said uneven growth is

74th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/74threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:50]
attributed mainly to the fact that some States have gone slow in arresting population explosion whereas some States especially
those in the South have achieved  comparative success in the implementation of family planning programme.
2.1.3    Delimitation on the basis of 2001 population census, in effect, would mean that States which are successful in arresting
population growth to a large extent, would be in disadvantageous position vis-à-vis the States which have gone slow in the
implementation of family planning programme, in the inter-State allocation of seats in the House of the People.
2.2.0    Keeping in view the rationale narrated in the previous para, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has recommended
(See Annexure-III) extending the current freeze up to the year 2026  as by that time the replacement level of fertility would be
expected to be achieved at national level.  In other words, the population growth in the country would be comparatively even by
the year 2026.
2.2.1    The Government as a part of the National Population Policy, 2000 strategy have also decided to extend the current freeze
on undertaking fresh delimitation upto the year 2026 AD as a motivational measure to enable State Governments to pursue the
agenda for population stabilization fearlessly.
2.2.2    The Law Commission of India in its Report on Reform of Electoral Laws has inter-alia recommended (See Annexure-IV)
extending the freeze on the delimitation till the year 2025.
2.2.3    Similar suggestions have also been received from the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
3.0       In spite of constitutional embargo till 2000, demands for taking up fresh delimitation of constituencies have been raised in
both the Houses of Parliament from time to time.  The issue have also been discussed in the meetings with major political parties
by the Government on 23 July, 1996 and 22 May, 1998 (See Annexure-V for the minutes of the meetings).
3.1.0    The provisions in the proposed legislation owe their origin to the Dinesh Goswami Committee Report on Electoral Reforms
and host of previous legislative attempts by the Government to give effect to some recommendations of the Goswami Committee.
3.1.1    The Goswami Committee (in May, 1990) had inter-alia recommended for:
(i)
                  fresh delimitation on the basis of 1981 census; and
(ii)                rotation of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes but the manner of  achieving the object of rotation of seats
should be left to the Delimitation Commission and the Parliamentary Law to be made for the purpose.
3.1.2    On the basis of above recommendations of Goswami Committee Report, the Constitution (Seventy-first Amendment) Bill,
1990 (See Annexure-VI) was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 30 May, 1990 to facilitate delimitation on the basis of 1981 census
without increasing the total number of seats allocated to various States on the basis of 1971 population census.  The Bill had also
enabling provision for rotation of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes on the basis of their population in the constituencies. 
The Bill was referred to a Select Committee of Lok Sabha (See Annexure-VII  for the Report of the Select Committee) after being
passed by the Rajya Sabha on 29 April, 1992.  However, the Bill was withdrawn in June, 1994, while it was awaiting its
consideration and passage by the Lok Sabha.
3.1.3    Again, another Bill i.e. the Constitution (Eightieth Amendment) Bill, 1996 (See Annexure-VIII ), containing provision for
fresh delimitation of Parliamentary as well as Assembly constituencies on the basis of 1991 population census without affecting
the existing number of seats allocated to various States, was introduced in Lok Sabha on 25 July, 1996.  But the same  lapsed upon
the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
3.1.4    A comparison of the three legislative proposals including the present one shows that the Constitution (Seventy-first
Amendment) Bill, 1990 had explicit provision for the introduction of the scheme of rotation for the constituency reserved for the
Scheduled Castes only, as Clause 5 of that Bill intended to amend Article 327 of Constitution.  But the scheme of rotation was/is
omitted in the other two Bills. 
3.1.5    Another striking difference between the Bill introduced in 1990 and 1996 on the one hand and the present Bill on the other,
is that there was no need to extend the freeze on undertaking delimitation of seats  in the former Bills since freeze was in force till
2000 under the proviso to clause (3) of Articles 81 and 170 of Constitution.  But the present legislation has a provision to extend
the freeze till 2026 as  it may become necessary to increase the number of seats in the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies on the
basis of 2001 census figures, which are  expected by the end of the year 2002.
3.2       The Election Commission had interactions with major political parties on 29 April and 13 May, 2000 on the issue. 
Although, there is convergent view amongst political parties on the issue of extending the constitutional embargo, divergent views
were expressed  on other issues pertaining to the proposed legislation.
4.0       The Secretary in his presentation before the Committee on the Bill under consideration  had briefly outlined  the salient
features of the Bill.  He had stated that under clause (2) of Article 368 of the Constitution, the amendments proposed by the Bill
would require ratification by not less than one-half of the State Legislatures before the same is presented to the President for his
assent. The Secretary further informed the Committee that after the Bill is enacted a new Delimitation Commission would have to
be established to give effect to the proposals contained therein i.e. readjustment/rationalization of Parliamentary and Assembly
constituencies as well as refixation of number of the Schedule Caste and the Scheduled Tribe constituencies on the basis of 1991
population census within the overall limit of seats.  In this connection the Secretary stated that  the number of the Scheduled Caste
and the Scheduled Tribe seats might undergo change.

5.0       In that context, the Committee noted that although the size of the electorate differed from one constituency to another, the
election expenditure ceiling for a candidate and the amount provided under  MPLAD scheme for an M.P. remained uniform.  Thus
the Committee was of the view that readjustment/rationalization of territorial constituencies was the need of hour.
5.1.0    A view was also expressed in the Committee that since the process of decennial census of 2001 had been set in motion, it
would be better if the Government consider to rationalize/readjust constituencies on the basis of 2001 population census which is
expected by the end of the year 2002.
5.1.1    The Ministry in its written submission has stated that, going by past experience associated with the process of delimitation
of territorial constituencies on the basis of 1971 population census, the process of delimitation is expected to be completed by
2005, if the figure of 2001 population census are to be relied upon. In the meantime, if any contingency arises for any elections, the
proposed rationalization of constituencies would not be completed if the figure of the current census are to be relied upon.
Therefore, the present Bill would be helpful in rationalizing the constituencies on the basis of the figures of 1991 census instead of
waiting for new census figures.
  5.2     A point was also raised that the proposed refixation of seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as mentioned in
paragraph 4 of Statement of Objects and Reasons is not explicitly mentioned in the clauses of the Bill.  However, it was clarified to
the Committee that rationalization/readjustment of seats would entail refixation of seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled
Tribes on the basis of the proportion of their population to the total population under Articles 330 and 332 of Constitution.
5.3       Apprehension was raised in the Committee that refixation of seats as mentioned in  paragraph 4 of the Statement of Objects
and Reasons may affect the number of general seats, which was endorsed by the Ministry in the written responses submitted to it.
5.4       Another point was raised whether refixation  amounted  to rotation.  The Ministry had replied  in the negative  yet another
point was raised  whether the existing  seats reserved  for the Scheduled Castes would continue to be reserved.  The Ministry in the
written submission  had stated  that in the present  Bill, the Government  has not proposed any specific  provision for a change in
the present  status of reserved seats  unless  demographic  changes so warrant.
5.5       Attention of the Committee was drawn to Section 9 (1) (c ) and (d) of the Delimitation Act, 1976 wherein the basis of the
reservation of constituencies for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes have been  spelt.  As per the said provision of the
Act, the constituencies are reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes if the proportion of their population to the
total are ‘comparatively large’ and ‘largest’, respectively. In that context, it was pointed out that the Scheduled Tribe seats are
located where their concentration is highest ( i.e.tribal belt of the State).  As such, the Committee feels that the scheme of
refixation envisaged  in the Bill would hardly change the number of seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes within the overall limit of
the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.  The Committee also anticipates that it would be difficult to rotate
those seats, in case the scheme of rotation is introduced at a later stage.
5.6       In the context of the above, some Members of the Committee expressed a view that the seats reserved for the Scheduled
Castes may be  rotated instead of  being refixed, which would also give a chance to the general candidates to contest election in the
constituencies  which are reserved since 1950 and that it would not affect the number of general seats.

2.         The Committee took up for consideration the draft Report on the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Bill, 2000.
2.1       A Member drew the attention of the Committee to the provisions contained in Section 22(2)(b) of the Uttar Pradesh
Reorganisation Act, 2000 relating to delimitation of constituencies in the Legislative Assembly of Uttaranchal which stipulated
that all constituencies shall, as far as practicable, be geographically compact areas and in delimiting them, regard shall be had to
physical features, existing boundaries of administrative units, facilities of communication and conveniences to the public.  In that
context he stated that from the perusal of the Bill, it appeared that the sole criterian for readjustment of territorial constituencies is
on the basis of 1991 population census. A question was, therefore, posed whether the criteria laid down in the aforesaid provision
of the Act would be made applicable at the time of undertaking readjustment of constituencies in the newly created state of
Uttaranchal  as it had its unique geographical features, culture etc. which needed to be preserved.
2.2       With reference to the point raised by the Member, the Chairman observed that certain temporary arrangements relating to
delimitation of territorial constituencies in the newly created States of Uttaranchal, Jharkhand and Chhatisgarh should be merged
with the general arrangement as proposed in the Bill under consideration of the Committee because each State had its unique geo-
political history, culture, ethos and the sacrifices made by the people  of the respective regions for attaining statehood.
2.3       The Committee then decided that a suitable para may be added in the Report recommending to Government to ensure that
the criteria mentioned in the Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh Reorganisation Acts, 2000 for delimitation of
constituencies, should be taken into consideration while undertaking readjustment of territorial constituencies in the newly created
States.
2.4       With regard to rotation of constituencies, the Committee was of the view that the Government should be clear in its mind as
to whether it would like to introduce the scheme of rotation at a later stage and if so, the same should be specifically mentioned in
the terms of reference of the Delimitation Commission.  The Committee, accordingly, decided that this aspect may be suitably
incorporated in the Report.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
Provisos to articles 82 and 170 (3) of the Constitution provide that no fresh readjustment of constituencies can be undertaken until
the figures of the first census taken after the year 2000 are published. These provisos were inserted by the Constitution (Forty-second
Amendment) Act, 1976 as a measure to boost family planning norms. Since the first census to be taken after the year 2000 has already
begun, the constitutional embargo on undertaking fresh delimitation will lapse as soon as the figures of this census are published.
2. There have been consistent demands, both for and against undertaking the exercise of fresh delimitation. Keeping in view the
progress of family planning programmes in different parts of the country, the Government, as part of the National Population Policy
strategy, recently decided to extend the current freeze on undertaking fresh delimitation up to the year 2026 as a motivational measure to
enable the State Governments to pursue the agenda for population stabilisation.
3. Government has also decided to undertake readjustment and rationalisation of territorial constituencies in the States, without
altering the number of seats allotted to each State in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies of the States, including the
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes constituencies, on the basis of the population ascertained at the census for the year 1991, so as
to remove the imbalance caused due to uneven growth of population/electorate in different constituencies.
4. It is also proposed to refix the number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the House of the
People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States on the basis of the population ascertained at the census for the year 1991.
5. The Bill seeks to achieve the aforesaid objects.

OFFICE MEMORANDUM
 
Sub:            Freezing  of seats in Lok Sabha on the basis of 1971  Census.
 
      The undersigned  is directed to refer Legislative Department O.M.No.7(4)/98-Leg.II dated 12 th May, 1998, and to convey that  the
Department of  Family Welfare  recommends the freezing  of the  present 1971  Census based inter-State allocation of seats in Lok
Sabha upto the year 2026 A.D.   The rationale for this recommendation is that the weakness of any State in achievement  of population
stabilisation should not lead to the increase in the entitlement of that  State to seats in Lok Sabha.  Allowing such States to increase their
entitlement to Lok Sabha seats would encourage  other States to go slow on population stabilisation.
 
      The above recommendation has the approval of Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare (Independent Charge).
 
            The year 2026 A.D. is the year in which the replacement  level of fertility is expected to be achieved at national level.  A Statement
showing the likely year of achievement of the replacement level of fertility in respect of India and major States  is attached.  Another
Statement showing the State-wise population at 5 year intervals  from 1991 to 2016, upto  which year State wise projections are available, is
also attached.

A meeting of leaders of various political parties was held in the main Committee Room, Parliament House Annexe on 22 nd May,

Justice and Company Affairs and the Minister for Parliamentary Affairs were also present.    The list of participants of the meeting is at

2.         In the meeting, out of the 24 additional proposals on electoral reforms identified  by the Government  for discussion with political
parties, the first 17 proposals alongwith the proposal for readjustment of parliamentary and assembly  constituencies were discussed.
3.1        After welcome address of the Minister for Parliamentary Affairs, the Home Minister initiated  the discussion.  He pointed out that
in the last meeting of political parties there was consensus on readjustment of the extent of parliamentary and assembly constituencies
without altering their numbers and he requested the participants to express their views  on the  proposal  that while undertaking
readjustment of parliamentary and assembly constituencies, the number of seats should be increased by 10 per cent on pro rata basis.

the extent of constituencies would change their community composition and may disturb the basis on which seats were reserved.  They

of the first  census taken after the year 2000, no useful purpose would be achieved by undertaking the exercise at this point of time.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            The Members in both the Houses had been raising from time to time, a demand for the delimitation of
constituencies.  The Government have also been receiving representations and suggestions for such delimitation from
various other quarters.  Hence, the matter was referred to the Committee appointed by the Central Government to go deep
into the matter of Electoral Reforms.  The  Committee has examined the question of increasing the total number of seats in
the House of the People and the legislative Assemblies of the States, the rotation of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes
and Scheduled Tribes and delimitation of constituencies.  After a careful study and discussion, they have recommended that
a fresh delimitation, on the basis of 1981 census may be undertaken, but such delimitation should not affect the total
number of seats allotted to various States on the basis of 1971 census.  They have also recommended that seats reserved for
Scheduled Castes may also be rotated on the basis of their population in the constituencies.  These recommendations
required amendments to the Constitution as at present there is a Constitutional bar not only in regard to the increase in the
total number of seats but also with regard to delimitation of constituencies.  The Government having accepted the
recommendation of the Committee now propose to amend the relevant articles of the Constitution.
           
Hence this Bill.

Clauses 2,3 & 4
 
14.       The Committee considered the matters relating to (i) Composition of the House of the People; (ii) Readjustment of
constituencies after each Census; (iii) Composition of the Legislative Assemblies; and (iv) Power of Parliament to make provisions
with respect to elections to Legislatures.
 
15.       The Committee note that the population of the country has increased enormously after the 1971 Census.  As per the 1981
Census population figures, the average population in each Parliamentary Constituency in major States is about 12 lacs as against
8.9 lacs on the basis of 1961 Census figures and 10.5 lacs as per 1971 Census figures.  The average is estimated to be around 14
lacs after the decennial Census of 1991 which means roughly as hundred per cent increase of average over the 1951 Census figures
per constituency.  The growth of population has not been uniform in all areas and, therefore, the size of electorate differs widely
from constituency to constituency.
 
16.       The Committee further note the following problems pointed out by the Election Commission:-
 
(a)
                Existence of certain villages  geographically found as enclaves have been included in certain Assembly
constituencies due to inadvertence at the time of last delimitation.
(b)               Exclusion or inclusion of certain areas without any rationale in or from certain Assembly constituencies causing
hardship to the local people.
(c)                The total number of electors overtaking in many cases the total population on the basis of which constituencies
were carved out thus disturbing the earlier co-relation between population and electors in a constituency or in a
State.
(d)               Large scale migration of population from one area to another on various grounds especially in the metropolitan
cities and industrial belts creating disparity in the number of electors among the various constituencies.
(e)                Certain Scheduled Tribes notified as such in earlier Census not found at subsequent census in the same area but
still the necessity of allocating seats as per their figures in the earlier Census.

(f)                 Many of the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes in particular have been continuing as such for the last 13 to 20
years causing feelings of frustration not only among the general public in that constituency but also the Scheduled
Castes of other constituencies whose claim for reservation has not been met.
 
17.       The Constitution also lays down that the number of seats as allocated and the territorial extent of constituencies as
determined on the basis of 1971 Census are unalterable until the publication of population figures of the census following the year
2000.  Thus, after 1971 and till 2000 as things stand at present, there can be no fresh delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly
constituencies in the State and Union Territories.
 
The Committee after examination of all these issues are of the opinion that there is a great need for fresh delimitation of
constituencies on the basis of 1991 Census.  They also feel the  avowed object of the existing constitutional embargo could be fully
achieved if the embargo is put only   on the total number of Lok Sabha seats allocated to each State and the total number of seats in
various State Legislative Assemblies and readjustment of territorial extent of Parliamentary and Assembly constituencies having
regard to the fixed number of the seats be allowed and as such delimitation of constituencies may be done on priority basis.
 
18.       The Committee, therefore, feel that Clauses 2,3 and 4 need not be amended.
 
Clause 5
 
19.       Closely related to the delimitation of constituencies is the important question of rotation of seats reserved for the Scheduled
Castes.  The Committee on Electoral Reforms appointed by the Government have also recommended that seats reserved for the
Scheduled Castes may also be rotated on the basis of their population in the constituencies.  The Committee are of the view that
even under the existing provisions of the Constitution, Parliament has legislative competence to make law for allocation of
reserved seats among the various constituencies within a State/Union Territory and as such there is no need to insert specifically
such provisions in the Constitution Amendment Bill.
 
20.       The Ministry of  Law, Justice and Company Affairs who were asked to tender their opinion in writing, in a written note,
however, communicated as follows:-
 
Constitutional provisions requiring reservation of seats in favour of Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes in the
House of the People and the Legislative Assembly of every State are contained in Articles 330 and 332.  The number of
seats to be reserved in any State or Union Territory is determined in accordance with the norms laid down in Clause (2) of
Article 330 and Clause (3) of Article 332.  The Constitution does not contain any explicit provision regulating the
allocation of reserved seats among the Parliamentary and Assembly constituencies within a State.  However, by virtue of
the provisions of Articles 330 and 332 read with Article 246(1) and Entry 72 of List - I Union List of the Seventh Schedule
to the Constitution, Parliament has legislative competence to make law for allocation of reserved seats among the various
constituencies within a State/Union Territory.
           
Section 9 of the Delimitation Act, 1972, inter alia,
  provides that constituencies in which seats are reserved for
Scheduled Castes shall be distributed and located, as far as practicable, in areas where the proportion of their population to
the total population is comparatively large.  Similarly, the constituencies in which  the seats are to be reserved for
Scheduled Tribes shall be located, as far as practicable, in areas where the proportion of their population to the total
population is the largest.
           
 
It would thus be seen that, as at present, the allocation of reserved seats is made on the basis of larger or largest
population as the case may be, under the Parliamentary law.  However, in view of the provisions of Article 330 (1) and
332(1) read with Article 246(1) and Entry 72 of the Union List, Parliament would have power to provide for allocation of
reserved seats by way of rotation.
           
However, since there is no explicit constitutional provision enabling Parliament to provide for reservation of seats
by way of rotation, schemes of Articles 330 and 332 envisage rotation of reserved seats, and also having regard to the
provisions in the Constitution (Seventy-second Amendment) Bill, and the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Bill
relating to rotation of reserved seats/Chairpersons in Panchayats and Municipalities, it would be advisable to retain Clause
(5) of the Bill and nothing should be left to any doubt.
 
21.       The Committee, as mentioned in Paragraph 19 above, are of the view that Clause 5  should be omitted since the opinion of
the Ministry  of Law is that even without amendment of Article 327, Parliament has powers to enact a law to provide for allocation
of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes by way of rotation, under the existing provisions of the Constitution.  However, the Law
Ministry have also mentioned that since there is not explicit constitutional provision enabling Parliament to provide for reservation
of seats by way of rotation, it would be advisable to retain Clause 5 of the Bill and nothing should be left to any doubt.  The
Committee, therefore, leave it to the wisdom of Parliament to decide whether Article 327 needs to be amended as per Clause 5 of
the Bill.

2.         It is my considered view that the Select Committee has lost a valuable opportunity to examine in depth and clarify the
principles of composition of Lok Sabha and the State legislatures, of delimitation of constituencies and of reservation in
favour of SCs and STs and place them on a sound constitutional and legal foundation.
 
3.         It goes without saying that the strength of the Lok Sabha itself has no logical rationale and that growing population makes a
mockery of the principle of democratic representation.  It is also admitted that there is a wide variation in the
population/electorate among the Lok Sabha constituencies from one part of the country to another and some times within
the same part.  This disparity has risen primarily because of the conceptually questionable practices of relating the Lok
Sabha constituencies to States/Union Territories and its natural consequences.  This is also partly due to inadequate
directive in the Constitution on the principle of delimitation so as to ensure equality among the people in respect of
representation in the legislatures.  One may argue that these questions are outside the scope of the Bill before the
Committee.  But these questions which are inter-related and provide the framework within which the scheme of
representation, reservation and rotation must function, can not be brushed aside.
 
4.         It is my view that the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha should be revised every 20 years keeping in view the principle
of effective representation, and the constituencies should be delimited on the basis of the latest the total number of Seats to
be reserved in Census that favour of the SC or ST should also be decided every 10 years on the basis of the latest Census
and that the constituencies selected for reservation should be decided on the basis of the principle of equity and fairness so
as to ensure, as far as possible, that the largest possible segment of SC/ST population enjoys the benefit of reserved
constituencies. One such principle could be that all constituencies in which the percentage of Scheduled Caste or Scheduled
Tribe population exceeds the average national percentage must be reserved in order of concentration and, for the balance, if
necessary the constituencies in which the percentage of Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe population falls short of the
national average by 1/3 should be rotated in alphabetical order. I admit that there could be other formulations, but the
objective must be the same as stated above.
 
5.         Secondly, I generally endorse the view of the Ministry of Law & Justice that Clause 5 should be retained so that nothing is
left to doubt.  However, I dare say that the language of Clause 5 is susceptible of improvement.  For example, it is
imprecise to speak in terms of "rotation of constituencies reserved for the SC"; it would be more precise to speak of
"rotation of reservation among the constituencies with a high concentration of the Scheduled Caste".
 
6.         It would also be fair and equitable to exclude such constituencies from the scheme of rotational reservation which have
high concentration of a religious minority.  In the existing circumstances, generally speaking, a member of a religious
minority (which does not enjoy either reservation or separate electorate) has a reasonable choice to win only from such a
constituency which has  a demographic concentration of, say, above 25 per cent.  The fact remains that the largest minority
in the country has been consistently under-represented in the Lok Sabha and in most State Assemblies.
 
I would request that this Minute of Dissent  may kindly be placed on record and included in the report of the Committee.
 
NEW
DELHI;                                                                                              
26 November 1992.
SYED SHAHABUDDIN

            The Members of both the Houses had been raising, from time to time, a demand for the delimitation of constituencies.  The
issue of fresh delimitation of constituencies was gone into by the Committee on Electoral Reforms, which had recommended fresh
delimitation without affecting the total number of constituencies allocated to various States on the basis of 1971 census.   The
Government has decided that fresh delimitation  should be undertaken on the basis of 1991 census without affecting the existing 
number  of seats allocated to various States on the basis of 1971 census.  This requires amendment to the Constitution, as at present

NEW DELHI;
May 28, 2001
PRANAB MUKHERJEE
Chairman
            Committee on Home Affairs                    
                                                                        
 
REPORT
 
A Study Group of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs headed by its
Chairman, Shri Pranab Mukherjee visited Srinagar, Kargil and Jammu from 6 to 9 July, 2000 to have a first hand assessment
of the problems of cross-border terrorism and insurgency in Jammu and Kashmir as part of its larger  study of internal
security scenario in the country. 
 
1.1       The details of the Study Group’s interaction with the Governor, the Chief Minister, the State Government officials,
the officials of the Central Para-military Forces and the Army authorities, representatives of political parties, several other
associations and representatives of public, are given in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
 
SRINAGAR (6 July 2000)
 
Meeting with the Officials of the 
State Government
 
2.         The Study Group held discussions with the Chief Secretary, Director-General of Police and other senior officials of
the State in Srinagar on 6 July 2000.
 
3.         The Chief Secretary made a detailed presentation before the Study Group on the current situation obtaining in
Jammu and Kashmir.  Giving a brief historical background of the cross-border terrorism and insurgency, he stated that
Pakistan had always considered the partition of India incomplete as per its concept of two nation theory, with Jammu and
Kashmir being the main focus.  It was precisely for this reason that it made repeated attempts to annex the State.  Three wars
and an impudent intrusion in Kargil were examples of Pakistan’s desperate attempts in that direction.  The failure of
Pakistan in its repeated attempts to annex the State led it to resort to the proxy war.  It all began by misguiding disgruntled
youth in the State by exploiting their sentiments.  It resulted into large-scale exfiltration to Pakistan from the valley in 1989-
90.  Pakistan trained those local youth in subversive activities, equipped them with sophisticated weapons and infiltrated
them back to foment trouble in the valley.  However, with the disenchantment of  their misadventure and fading away of the
initial local support,  Pakistan started pushing in foreign and Pakistani mercenaries into the State.  He stated that Jammu and
Kashmir was not faced with insurgency or indigenous militancy but a clandestine war that could be gauged from the fact that

75th report on Department-related parliamentary standing
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/75threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:52]
since 1990 to May, 2000, over 33,763 weapons of various calibres,  3 million rounds of ammunition, 1,22,332 explosive
devices and huge volumes of other war materials had been seized.  During  the same period, over 10,000 civilians had been
killed and an equal number injured.  This apart, 2217 security personnel were killed and 6474 injured.  Similarly, the
security forces killed 11,299 militants.
 
4.         Referring to the post-Kargil security scenario, the Chief Secretary stated that the situation up to the beginning of
May, 1999 was fully under control and was, in fact, improving steadily.  Security forces were able to gain an upper hand
over the militants.  As a result, there was a massive inflow of tourists into the valley.  Kargil war not only put an end to
tourism and hopes of the people of renewed economic activities but it also led to deterioration in the overall security
situation.  The major reasons which led to the deterioration in the security situation were as under:
 
(i)
                  Internal security grid was weakened to a large extent with the withdrawal of 58 Army battalions;
(ii)                Para military forces mainly CRPF were quantitatively and qualitatively inadequate;
(iii)               As a result of weakened security grid, a large number of hardcore militants infiltrated into the valley from May,
1999 onwards;
(iv)              The pre-occupation of the central para-military forces and the State police with the making of arrangements for
Darbar move, Independence Day celebrations, Amar Nath Yatra and Lok Sabha elections adversely affected the
operations against the militants and insurgents;
(v)                Increased pressure from Human Rights Organisations on the Special Operation Group of the State police led to the
loss of initiative;
(vi)              Flow of actionable intelligence remained sluggish;
(vii)             Army coup in Pakistan in October, 1999 led to emboldenment and better coordination and mutual support among
the main militant groups;
(viii)           Induction of Fidayeen (suicide) squads of militants led to high profile publicity oriented actions against security
forces which led to the rise in militant morale and fear psychosis among the people; and
(ix)              The release of three hardcore militants in the wake of hijacking of the Indian Airlines plane  in December, 1999 also
led to euphoria and high morale among the militant ranks.
 
5.         Apprising the Study Group of the present situation, the Chief Secretary told that barring a few high profile militant
attacks on civilians and headquarters of security forces, there was a perceptible trend indicating improvement in the
situation. Of late,  however, there had been an increase in the violent activities especially after the induction of a large
number of suicide squads.  Security forces were the main targets of the attacks.  Besides, political workers were also being
targeted.  In a nutshell, the situation could be characterised by the following points:
 
(i)
                  Unabated infiltration of militants from Pakistan/Pakistan Occupied Kashmir (PoK) both from the Kupwara-
Baramulla Sector and Rajouri-Poonch Sector;
(ii)                Increase in the component of foreign militants (they constituted 60-70% of the fresh infiltrators and were better
trained and motivated);
(iii)               Passing into the hands of foreign mercenaries the leadership of the militant organisations who now controlled the
cadres, arms/ammunition, finances etc, and using of the local militants mainly as guides and for logistic support;
(iv)              As a matter of policy, militants were targeting personnel of the State Police with the twin objectives of demoralising
them and disrupting the flow of actionable intelligence through them;
(v)                Targeting political workers, especially leaders of the National Conference, informers, Special Police Officers
(SPOs) and members of the Village Defence Committees (VDCs);
(vi)              Concentrating terrorist actions on Srinagar city such as the high profile attacks on Badami Bagh Cantonment and
the Special Operation Group (SOG) Hqrs, grenade attacks on the Civil Secretariat, resorting to killings of a large
number of policemen deployed on duty in Srinagar city with the objective of creating a fear psychosis in the city and
destabilising normal life;
(vii)     Up-gradation in the quality of arms of militants with heavy caliber weapons coming in, although they were not being
used extensively (perhaps being kept in reserve for some future contingencies);
(viii)      Making attempts to engineer communal disturbances;
(ix)       Making attempts to induct more and more local youth in militancy so as to give it a local colour once again and
project it to the world as an uprising of the Kashmiri people;
(x)
                Sizeable infiltration in Jammu region through the International Border (IB) viz. Samba-Hiranagar and Akhnoor
sectors (Earlier the IB was used for purposes of smuggling, limited to that of gold, drugs etc., but of late, the ISI had
been infiltrating militants and arms & ammunitions and explosives through this border); and
(xi)              The objective of infiltrating militants across the International Border in Jammu seemed to be:-

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
64.       On the basis of the Study Tour Note prepared by the Study Group which visited Jammu & Kashmir to assess the
problems of cross-border terrorism and insurgency, the Committee has formulated its
observations/conclusions/recommendations which are given in the following paragraphs :
65.       The Committee notes the fact that a proxy war is being waged in Jammu & Kashmir at the behest of a neighbouring
country.  Foreign mercenaries are being pushed into the valley to engineer large-scale terrorist activities.  Recovery of huge
cache of arms and ammunition, killings of hundreds of innocent people and high rate of causalities of the security forces 
and detention of foreign mercenaries are proofs enough to substantiate the fact that it is, more than anything else, a proxy
war being waged on the Indian soil by Pakistan.  Pakistan is not only aiding, abetting and financing terrorist activities in
Jammu & Kashmir but is also pushing in well equipped and trained mercenaries for the cause of so-called Jehad against
India.   The misadventure of Pakistan in Kargil is the clear manifestation of its nefarious designs on Jammu & Kashmir. 
65.1     The Committee, therefore, has come to the conclusion that a more concerted, well thought out and well planned
strategy should be chalked out to counter the ill designs of Pakistan aimed at destabilising and disintegrating India.
66.       One such attempt to destablise India was made in the form of large scale armed intrusion from across the Line of
Control (LoC) in Kargil during 1999.  The intrusion in Kargil led to the weakening of internal security grid of the security
forces in the entire State of Jammu & Kashmir as forces had to be withdrawn and deployed along the border to repulse
Pakistani attack.  The weakening of security grid  resulted into the terrorists and mercenaries managing to get foothold once
again.  The recent step-up in the strikes by the militants on security installations and innocent people were largely due to the
loosened grip of the security forces.  However, the Committee was given to understand that security forces were trying hard
to restore the grid.
66.1     The Committee notes the efforts being made to restore the security grid and feels that no stone should be left
unturned to strengthen the grip of the security forces on the militants.  The restoration and improvement  of the security grid
in the quickest possible time will deal a deathblow to the ever-rearing head of militancy in the State.
67.       Massive intrusion in Kargil in particular and the unabated growth of militancy in general have proved that
management of Indian border along LoC is not adequate enough to  check unstopped exfiltration and infiltration.  The
porosity of India’s international border with Pakistan and Line of Control is providing safe passage to the militants.  Large
scale exfiltration of Kashmiri youth for undergoing training at the terrorist training camps located across the border and
infiltration of trained and armed militants into Jammu and Kashmir was taking place.  Huge quantity of arms and
ammunition is dumped near the LoC and international border for the use of militants and mercenaries.  All this calls for
better border management on the LoC and the international border.  However, due to extensive deployment of paramilitary
forces especially Border Security Force for internal security duties, it  has  not been possible to spare adequate forces to man
LoC and international border.
67.1     The Committee is of the view that effective border management is key to the curbing of exfiltration and infiltration
across LoC and international border with Pakistan.  For that to happen, adequate force level is needed to be maintained to
plug the exfiltration and infiltration routes along the border.  The Committee understands the necessity for deploying
security forces extensively for maintenance of internal security in Jammu & Kashmir.  But at the same time, it is of the
considered view that unless exfiltration and infiltration is effectively checked, the problems of cross border terrorism and
proxy war cannot be overcome.  Moreover, so long as country’s borders remain porous, there cannot be a foolproof internal
security.  It is, therefore, essential to relieve as many BSF battalions as possible of their internal security duties so that they
are pressed into their primary responsibility i.e. guarding of country’s borders.  Army detachments are also guarding the
highway from  Srinagar to Laddakh.  They need  to be  relieved  of such duties.  The task of guarding the highway and the
