file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/75threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:52]
bridges   located along it  should be  entrusted  to the para military forces.
67.2     Apart from effective border management, strengthening of intelligence network in and around border areas is also
the need of the hour.  Since borders play a crucial role in exfiltration and infiltration of militants and dumping of arms and
ammunition near them, it is imperative to strengthen the intelligence network in border areas.  Vital intelligence inputs could
go a long way in helping security forces to check militant activities.  It  could also  go a long way in checking the Kargil
type infiltration.
68.       In the post-Kargil era, there has been increase in the number of attacks on security forces and their installations. 
Induction of ‘Fidayeen’ i.e. suicide squads into militant organisations had also led to the increase in the frequency of such
attacks.  The ratio of casualties of security personnel against the militants killed had also increased.  Such a trend has a direct
bearing on the morale of the forces especially when militants are resorting to frontal attacks on the camps and convoys of
security forces.  A slight fluctuation in the morale of the forces helps the militants and mercenaries to gain an upper hand
over them.
68.1     Keeping this in view, the Committee feels that there is need for further tightening of security cover for the camps of
security forces.  Effective deterrents are needed to see that attacks on camps of security forces are minimised. Basic
facilities  like lighting etc. and other infrastructure  should be provided to such camps.
69.       The decade long militancy in Jammu & Kashmir led to the weakening of police system.  However, in the recent past,
there has been revival of police system in the State.  Still, there is scope for improvement and further strengthening.  The
police of the State needs to be equipped with sophisticated arms and equipment as it was yet to achieve desirable level of
manpower, transport, firearms and communication requirements.  The Committee is made to understand that a broad
perspective plan for strengthening and modernisation of Jammu & Kashmir police including the revamp of intelligence
gathering machinery has been sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs by the State Government.
69.1     The Committee recommends that Ministry of Home Affairs should extend all possible assistance to the Government
of Jammu & Kashmir in its efforts to prop up an effective, reliable and efficient police system in the State.
70.         The Committee has been given to understand by the State Government authorities  that after the lapse of Terrorist
and Disruptive Activities Act (TADA), law enforcement agencies are finding it extremely difficult to cope with the
challenges being thrown up by the terrorists.  The absence of an anti-terrorist law is proving to be a major handicap for the
police.  In spite of committing  heinous crimes, terrorists go scot free as the existing laws fall short of leading to their
conviction.
70.1     Keeping this in view, the Committee is of the view that in order to enable the police to curb the activities of
terrorists, a suitable law needs to be enacted with adequate in-built safeguards to prevent misuse as had happended in the
past in case of TADA.  
71.       The role of Village Defence Committees (VDCs) and Special Police Officers (SPOs) has also drawn the attention of
the Committee.  During the visit of the Study Group to Jammu and Kashmir, it was given to understand that both VDCs and 
SPOs were playing an important role in combating terrorism especially in the Jammu division.  People living in remote
villages have shown keen interest in setting up such committees.  However, the lack of funds is hampering the efforts of the
State Government to further strengthen VDCs.  It was also impressed upon the Study Group that by providing better
weapons and communication equipment, VDCs could be made even more effective.
71.1     The Committee, having been apprised of the role being played by Village Defence Committees (VDCs),
recommends that more funds should be earmarked for the strengthening of VDCs.  It further recommends that efforts should
be made to set up such committees in the Kashmir division also.
72.       Recent massacres of local Sikhs and migrant labourers from other parts of the   country   have   exposed   the 
vulnerability    of  minorities  living in the State.  These massacres have also proved the fact that they were part of a well-
planned strategy to attack ‘soft targets’ in order to create fear psychosis among minorities.  It also reveals the contours of a
sinister game plan on the part of terrorists to engineer  mass exodus of minorities from the State.
72.1     In this regard, the Committee notes the steps taken by the State Government to tighten the security grid around the
villages  inhabited by the minorities especially Sikhs.  It, however, feels that a comprehensive exercise should be undertaken
to identify hitherto unattacked and potential soft targets so that preemptive measures could be taken to deter any attack on
them by the militants.  Efforts should also be made to set up Village Defence Committees (VDCs) in such villages.
73.       In a situation like the one obtaining in Jammu & Kashmir where innocent people are caught between the terrorists on
the one end and the security forces on the other, the violations of human rights  can take place.  However, any violation of
such rights by security forces is hyped and over-publicized which  leads to the widening of  the gulf between the people and
the State.  It is so, primarily because of the fact that State which is meant for the welfare of the people, is perceived  to be

75th report on Department-related parliamentary standing
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/75threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:52]
working against its very own people.  And, in the process, a common man feels isolated and alienated from the mainstream. 
In sharp contrast to this, the human rights’ abuses by the militants get overlooked for different reasons.  The net result of all
this is that the State is perceived as an enemy of the people.  It becomes all the more glaring when it receives open support of
the propaganda machinery of a hostile neighbour.
73.1     The Committee notes the efforts being made to set the human rights record straight by the Government.  It, however,
feels that security forces should win the confidence of the people by exercising utmost restraint while launching search and
combing operations to nab the militants.  Security forces should remember that in their battle against militants, they will not
be able to have the last laugh until they enjoy the support of the local people.
73.2     At the same time, the human rights violations committed by the militants and the mercenaries should also not be
allowed to get overlooked.   People in general  and   international community   should  be kept abreast of such violations
through print and electronic media.  The very fact that acts of violations by militants do not receive due attention of human
rights bodies has a very demoralising impact on the psyche of the security personnel.  Human rights bodies, national as well
as international, must realise the fact that in a situation like this, human rights of the security forces as well as of the people
being killed and harassed by the militants are also at stake.  As a matter of fact, it is not the loss of any particular individual
or group or community rather it is a loss of everyone.  In other words, the entire nation is at a loss.
74.       The Committee is given to understand that there are three types of migrants in Jammu & Kashmir.
(i)         One is the group of migrants who had come in the wake of armed attack in 1948;
(ii)        The second group is the Kashmiri Pandits who have been given some help in Jammu region; and
(iii)       The third group is the border migrants who had to flee the borders because of constant firing by the Pakistan
rangers and Pakistan Army on international border running along Jammu Division.
74.1     There is growing discontent among these three groups of migrants  who continue  to reel under the unabated spate of
terrorism.  These people have been rendered  homeless as well as jobless due to the ongoing violence in the State.  Their
agony is further compounded  by the fact that the Government, on the one hand, is rehabilitating the surrendered  militants
by giving them Government jobs  while on the other nothing has been done to provide them employment. This has forced
them to believe  that it is better to be a militant for a while and then surrender so that they can also get Government jobs. 
Some of these unemployed migrants are also falling into the ISI’s trap and are now on the pay rolls of it.
74.2     The ten year long strife in Jammu & Kashmir has taken a very heavy toll on the people of the State.  Thousands have
lost their lives and lakhs have been displaced due to the ongoing bloodshed.  The agony of those who have been uprooted
from their native places is insurmountable.  Uncertainty dogs these people who were forced to flee their homes leaving
behind everything they had inherited from their ancestors.  Today, their ordeal continues with no end in sight.  These
displaced people better  known as ‘Kashmiri migrants’ are having to live in miserable conditions in different parts of the
country.  They are refugees not only in their own State but in their own country as well.
74.3     The Committee expresses its deepest sense of sorrow on the seemingly unending plight of displaced Kashmiris.  It is
told that an action plan has been sent by the State Government to the Union Government for the return of displaced
Kashmiris  to the valley.  The Committee is of the view that sincere efforts should be made to facilitate smooth and safe
return of displaced people to their native places.  However, this could be possible only when an atmosphere of peace and
security is created in the valley and displaced people are convinced of their safe return.  Meanwhile, all possible help should
be extended to them to ensure a respectable and dignified standard of living for them.  Special care needs to be given to the
educational requirements of the children and youth so that they are not left behind in pursuit of their chosen careers.  It
should also be ensured that wards of displaced people have no difficulties in getting admission into the educational
institutions located in different parts of the country.
75.       Besides the people displaced from the valley, the plight of thousands of people displaced from the border areas of
Jammu division situated along the international border also deserves to be taken care of.  These people living in the villages
located near the international border have had to bear the brunt of Pakistani  shelling.  They have also gone through the
devastation caused during three Indo-Pak wars.  During the Kargil conflict, they came under direct attack of Pakistani guns
which led to the loss of livestock and human lives and damage to standing crops and property.  Constant threat to their lives
and property forced them to migrate to safer places where they are put up in make shift tented accommodation.
75.1     The Committee sympathises with the people displaced from the border villages of Jammu division and hopes that
solution to their problems will soon be found by the State Government.  It recommends that Government should come
forward with a long term rehabilitation programme to put an end to the miseries of the affected people.  The programme
should inter alia address  their various problems such as alternative accommodation, adequate compensation for the loss of
crop and livestock, enhanced ration, creation of employment opportunities, etc.
76.       Another human suffering which needs attention is the misery of Sikhs who migrated from Pakistan Occupied

75th report on Department-related parliamentary standing
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/75threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:52]
Kashmir (PoK) to Jammu & Kashmir.  The irony of their fate is that the Government does not consider them refugees.  The
Government’s stand is based on the premise that since PoK is a part of Jammu & Kashmir,  people living there are also
residents of Jammu & Kashmir and hence cannot be accorded the status of refugee within their own State.  This stand of the
Government deprives these migrant Sikhs of the benefits which accrue to the people who have migrated from the valley to
Jammu division.
76.1     The Committee is of the considered view that these migrant Sikhs should not be left to fend for themselves.  They
crossed over  to  the Indian  side of LoC with  high hopes and a sense of belonging.  It is, therefore, incumbent upon the
Government to extend a  helping  hand   to   them in their hour of crisis.  Moreover, when a set of benefits are accruing to
the people displaced from Kashmir, it defies the logic of comprehension as to why they should not be extended to the people
displaced from PoK.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Government should favourably consider the case of
Sikhs who have migrated from PoK and extend all the benefits to them which are available to the displaced Kashmiris.
77.       As a result of the ongoing violence, the people of the State have lost their traditional means of livelihood.  A large
number of uneducated and unemployed youth are falling prey to the militancy.  The dearth  of adequate educational and 
vocational institutions  in the State is one of the causes for growing number of uneducated youth.  The current situation calls
for opening up of sufficient number of educational and vocational institutions so that human resource of the State could be
nurtured.
77.1     The  Committee is, therefore, of the view that special attention should be paid to the setting up of adequate  number
of educational and vocational institutions.  Such a step will  help  the State not only to overcome the scourge of illiteracy but
will also enable the youth to be proficient in various self-employment  trades.  Besides, the Government should also make
efforts to generate employment opportunities by setting up small and medium industrial establishments and also by reviving
cottage industries in the State.
 78.      It has been over ten years ever since Jammu & Kashmir is in the grip of a turmoil.  The resources meant for
developmental activities had to be diverted to tackle militancy.  It goes without saying that developmental activities have
taken a backseat.  But with the rise in the scale of militancy, the funds earmarked for security related heads are also proving
to be inadequate.  As things stand today, there is lack of funds on both  fronts.  Though, Union Government has been
meeting the funds requirements of the State Government for both development as well as security related activities, there is
always a crunch situation as State’s own sources of income generation have suffered badly due to ongoing strife.  The
State’s expenditure for maintenance of law and order is met from the funds provided by the Union Government as “Security
Related Expenditure” (SRE).  In view of the special circumstances being faced by Jammu & Kashmir, the State Government
has been demanding that the facility of advance payment under this head should be extended to it so that it does not have to
run on overdrafts which accrue high rate of interest.  In regard to the plan allocation, the delay in approval was a major
stumbling block.  This delay in release of funds causes many difficulties for the State.  Because of a very short work season,
the delayed arrival of funds means that a large chunk of it remains unutilised.
78.1     The Committee understands the kind of difficulties being faced by Jammu & Kashmir and feels that keeping in view
its special circumstances, an out of the way mechanism should be found to ensure timely allocation and speedy release of
requisite funds so that the very purpose behind the desired funds does not get defeated. 
 79.      Central para-military forces   are  playing a crucial role in the fight against   militancy.  Indo-Tibetan   Border  Police
(ITBP) is one of these forces.  It has been assigned the task of guarding Banihal tunnel on Jammu-Srinagar national
highway.  This tunnel is a vital link between Jammu and Srinagar and has been in the eye of militants for long.  ITBP has
been doing commendable work by keeping round the clock vigil on the tunnel.  In order to maintain foolproof security of the
tunnel, ITBP requires sophisticated surveillance equipment for keeping watch on the movement of traffic passing through it.
79.1     The Committee appreciates the role being played by ITBP in guarding the Banihal tunnel and recommends that its
requirement for installation of State-of-the-art surveillance equipment in the tunnel should be accorded highest priority by
the Government .
80.       Kargil has borne the brunt of Pakistan’s misadventure of altering the Line of Control (LoC).  The exchange of
gunfire between Pakistani and Indian army, left the houses shattered, livestock dead and people homeless.  In the post-
conflict period, the wounds of the affected people seem to have not been assuaged by the Government.  The compensation
for the loss of livestock amounting to Rs.505 lakh has not yet been paid by the Central Government.  This apart, the state of
telecommunication and electricity services is in total disarray.
80.1     The Committee recommends that monetary compensation due to the people of Kargil for their losses during the
conflict with Pakistan, should be released without any further delay.  Besides, the electricity and telecommunication
requirements of the region should be looked after by the Government.  The operationalisation of the airport being built in
Kargil should be expedited so as to bring the region on the tourism map of the country.  The development of the region as a

REPORT
 
            The Repealing and Amending Bill, 1999 (Annexure-1) seeks to repeal altogether 357 amending Acts either wholly or partially.   The
Bill also seeks to rectify the patent error and inadvertent mistakes in Indian Succession Act, 1925 and the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973, respectively, by way of making amendments to those Acts.
 
2.0       All those 357 Acts to be repealed either wholly or partially are from the period spanning from 1985 to 1998 and are listed in the First
Schedule to the Bill.
 
2.1       Out of the listed 357 Acts, those amending Acts, which stand incorporated in the parent legislation would be repealed wholly as
those are no longer required on the Statute Book.  But some of the provisions of certain amending Acts have got independent existence and
retention thereof are necessary, and are, thus, to be repealed partially.  Thus, the basic purpose of the Bill is to    cleanse the Statute Book.
 
3.0       As mentioned in the Statement of Objects and Reasons, the Bill is one of those periodical measures by which enactments which
have ceased to be in force or have become obsolete or the retention whereof as separate Acts is unnecessary are repealed or by which the
formal defects detected in enactments are corrected.
 
3.1       It is, thus, in the nature of routine exercise by which Parliament weeds out ‘unnecessary’ enactments which clutter the Statute Book
and is often described as ‘legislative scavenging’ for it neither enacts any new law nor cancels any existing law.
 
3.2       In England, a provision called “Statute Law Revision Acts” which is akin to the Repealing and Amending Act in India exist there to
take care of legislative scavenging.
 
4.0       The Legislative Department being responsible for drafting of the laws and also keep reviewing the amendment Acts and other Acts
enacted by Parliament from time to time.
 
4.1       The Legislative Department has stated that since the Repealing and Amending Bill is a routine exercise, no prior approval of Cabinet
is taken before it is introduced in Parliament which has been followed as a practice since 1952.  The Bill also does not attract any provision
of the Constitution which requires prior recommendation of the President before introducing the  same in either House of Parliament. 
However, before proposing any repeal/amendment, the Legislative Department of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs
consults the concerned administrative Ministries/Departments in consultation with the Department of Legal Affairs and obtains the approval
of the Law Minister.
 
4.2       The Committee is not clear as to whether prior approval of the Cabinet for the Repealing and Amending  Bill before it is introduced
in Parliament is required or not.  The Department in their interim reply has stated that since this is a routine exercise, no prior approval of
Cabinet is taken before it is introduced in Parliament which has been followed as practice since 1952.  However, in their written submission
to the Committee, it is seen that the Department of Legal Affairs to whom the Legislative Department had forwarded a copy of the draft
Repealing and Amending Bill, 1999, for their comments had inter-alia advised that they concur in the draft note for Cabinet.   Here again,

4.3       The present legislation is twelfth in number which aims at weeding out unnecessary laws cluttering the Statute Book.  The
Department has mentioned eleven Repealing and Amending Acts enacted in the past which are as below:-
 
(i)

(enacted by the Dominion Legislature);
(ii)                The Repealing and Amending Act, 1950 (35 of 1950);

(vi)              The British Statutes (Application to India) Repealing Act, 1960 (57 of 1960) (By this Act the British Statutes (in their
application to India) were repealed. This was the only Act vide which the Statutes were repealed on the recommendation of
the Law Commission);

(xi)              The Repealing and Amending Act, 1988 (19 of 1988).
 
5.0       The repealing would not affect the substantive provisions of the parent legislation   by virtue of  section 6A of the General Clauses
Act, 1897, which reads as under:
 
“Repeal of Act making textual amendment in Act or Regulation where any Central Act or Regulation made after the
commencement of this Act repeals any enactment by which the text of any Central Act or Regulation was amended by the
express omission, insertion, or substitution of any matter, then, unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not affect
the continuance of any such amendment made by the enactment so repealed and in operation at the time of such repeal.”
 
Besides the provision of the General Clauses Act, a saving clause has been provided in the Bill itself.   Hence, the repeal of the Act will not
affect the continuance of any such amendment made by the enactment so repealed.
 
6.0       The Secretary (Legislative) in his presentation has outlined three types of amendment Acts listed in First Schedule to the Bill which
are to be repealed completely by the proposed legislation.
 
(i)
                  Acts which got incorporated in the parent Act and its independent existence is not required i.e. the Foreign Contribution
(Regulation) Amendment Act, 1985;
(ii)                Acts which are temporary in nature, renewed from time to time and lapsed by now i.e. the Terrorist and Disruptive
Activities (Prevention) Act, 1985; and
(iii)               Acts which were enacted as a one time measure and has outlived its purposes i.e. the cancellation of General Elections in
Punjab Act, 1991.
 
The other category of amendment Acts enlisted contain some provisions which are otherwise of independent nature and cannot get
incorporated in the provisions of the principal Act, would be repealed partially to the extent mentioned in column 4 of the First Schedule to
the Bill shown against the particular amending Act. 
 
6.1.0    He has mentioned that the Second Schedule to the Bill   lists two Acts, namely, the Indian Succession  Act, 1925 and the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 for the purpose of making amendments so as to correct patent   errors and inadvertent   mistakes pointed out at a
subsequent  phase.
 
6.1.1    In the Indian Succession Act, 1925, certain amendments would be made in entry 6 in Part II of Second Schedule to replace the
words “grand parents’ children” by the words grandparents’ parents’ children” to rectify the printing error.  At the time of enactment of the
said Act the word “parents” got omitted.  The provision is relatable to section 55 of the Act, which deals with the division of property where
a Parsi dies intestate  and leaves neither  lineal descendants nor a widow or  widower nor a widow of any lineal descendant.
 
6.1.2    The Bill also  proposes to replace all entries ( extent of punishment, nature of offence and the trial court) against   section 377 of the
Indian Penal Code in the First Schedule to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.  The Secretary has explained that the error with respect to
section 377 of the Indian Penal Code occurred when the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was amended in 1983.  In the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 as it stood in 1974, section 377 is followed by section 376 which relates to rape, (a cognizable offence) and the punishment
and the Court for which is imprisonment for life or imprisonment for the ten years and fine, and the court of sessions, respectively is
mentioned.  Section 377 relates to unnatural offences and the punishment and nature of offence are the same as in the case of Section 376,
thus, the word ‘ditto’ was used under the above heading against Section 377.  But when the Criminal Procedure Code was amended in 1983
sections 376A,376B and 376C and 376D were inserted.  Punishment, nature of offence and trial courts mentioned against Section 376B is

same as in Section Nos. 376 C and 376D.  Since word ditto is used against Section Nos. 376C & 376D and 377 under the aforesaid heading,
it is interpreted that the punishment, nature of offence and trial courts mentioned against 376B is applicable to Section 377 but the actual
intention is not so.  The punishment, nature of offence and trial Courts as mentioned against Section 376 is applicable to Section 377 and is
to be mentioned categorically in the place of word ‘ditto’.
 
6.1.3    The Legislative Department has clarified that clubbing of repealing and amending of Acts together in the present legislation would
not create any problem as no change of substantive nature is carried out in the Law by the Bill.
 
6.1.4    While scrutinizing First Schedule to the Bill, the Committee felt that there was no indication about the reasons for repeal of
amending Acts and details of their enforcements in the Schedule.  The Committee, hence, directed the Legislative Department to mention
aforesaid details against each amending Acts by adding another two columns to the existing one in the First Schedule.  Accordingly, the
Ministry had submitted a statement explaining details of enforcement and reasons for repeal of each Act enlisted in the First Schedule,
which is placed as Annexure-II.
 
6.1.5    The Department in its written replies has not given any reply to the query made by Shri Sahu as to why some of the Acts amended
earlier which are now being proposed to be repealed were never implemented.  The Ministry’s representatives at the meeting held on May
28, 2001, stated that it was for the concerned administrative Ministry to clarify the position.
 
6.1.6    the Committee is not satisfied with this type of clarification.   The Committee feels that since the Legislative Department is the
Department piloting the Bill, it is for this Department to collect the necessary and requisite information/data in respect of the contents of the
Bill and clarifications sought by the Members of the Committee.  To that extent Department’s reply is not complete and satisfactory.   The
Committee hopes that the Ministry will take this point into account while taking up the Bill for consideration in the House.
 
7.0       It was pointed out in the meeting of the Committee that the Commission on Review of Administrative Laws under the Chairmanship
of Shri P.C. Jain inter-alia  had recommended for repeal of 315 amending Acts.   In that connection, the Committee sought clarifications
whether any of the Acts out of the 315 amending Acts have been included in the Bill.
 
7.1       The Legislative Department has replied that the aforesaid Commission has not recommended repeal of any Acts included in the Bill
and Acts included in the Bill were also not considered by the Commission.
 
7.2       The Committee is not convinced with the reply of the Legislative Department.   It, therefore, fails to understand as to why the Jain
Commission did not consider 357 amending Acts included in the First Schedule to the Bill.
 
8.0       The Committee took note of the fact that the last Repealing and Amending Act was enacted in the year 1988 and wanted to know the
reasons for not including the amendment Acts of the year 1985 in that Act, which are sought to be repealed by the present Bill.
 
8.1       The Legislative Department in its written reply has submitted that the procedure regarding repealing of Acts is a lengthy one as the
concerned Ministries/Departments have to be consulted before finalizing the Bill for introduction in Parliament.  Only those Acts are to be
included in the Bill which are cleared by the concerned Ministries/Departments for repealing.   Other Acts are included in the subsequent
legislation.
 
8.2       In the same context the Department has mentioned that the last Repealing Bill was initiated in the year 1985 and consultation
process took considerable time after which the Bill was introduced in the year 1986 and enacted in the year 1988.  The process of drafting
the present legislation was initiated in the year 1997 and the Bill was introduced in Parliament in  December, 1999 after consulting the
concerned Ministries/Departments.
 
9.0       The Committee pointed out why laws struck down by the Supreme Court had not been included in the Bill.
 
9.1       The Legislative Department had replied that the Bill in question did not include any provision which had been struck down by the
Supreme Court.  Such provisions remained on the Statute Book and did not stand automatically repealed.  Such provisions were not covered
by the General Clauses Act and fell in a different category.

11.1.0  The clause repeals 357 amendment Acts to the extent mentioned against the particular Act in the fourth column of the First Schedule
to the Bill.
 
11.1.1  The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause – 3
 
11.1.2  The clause amends two Acts to the extent and in the manner mentioned in the fourth column against the particular Act in the Second
Schedule to the Bill to rectify the patent error and inadvertent mistakes in those Acts.
 
11.1.3  The Ministry was asked to clarify as to why the Indian Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code were not being amended.   In
response to that the Ministry in their written reply has stated that the Department has not proposed amendment in Section 377 of the Indian
Penal Code on merits.  The Section is being modified with a view to rectifying a patent error.  Suggestions given by the Hon’ble Member
will be referred to the Ministry of Home Affairs for their consideration as they are administratively concerned with the Indian Penal Code
and Criminal Procedure Code after the Committee submits its report to Parliament.
 
11.1.4  The Committee expresses its deep anguish at the manner in which Ministry has chosen to respond to this patent error in the present
Act.  Section 377 provides for imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years and fine.  The existing provision under the Criminal
Procedure Code provides that this offence is to be tried by a Magistrate of the First Class.  This is against the Criminal Procedure Code
provisions as offences attracting punishment more than three years are to be tried by Court of Session.  Therefore, the Legislative
Department itself should have taken cognizance of this anomaly in the Criminal Procedure Code and taken corrective action.   On the
contrary, it has decided to take the line of least resistance and passed on this responsibility to the Ministry of Home Affairs which
administers the Indian Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code.  The Committee hopes that while taking up the Bill in the House,
necessary remedial action would be taken to correct the mistake in the Section 377 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
 
11.1.5  The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause – 4
 
11.1.6  The clause is a saving clause which states that the repeal of any amending Acts will not  affect  the parent Acts in which the repealed
enactment have been applied, incorporated or referred to.  The clause also provides saving of right, title, obligation, liability acquired,
accrued or incurred or any remedy in respect thereof, etc. and also provides that the Bill shall not affect the principle of rule of law and also
any enactment revived, restored, any jurisdiction, office, custom, title, exemption, usage, etc. which are not now existing or in force.
 
11.1.7  The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause – I, The Enacting Formula and Title
 
11.2     Clause I, Enacting Formula and Title were adopted with some changes which are of consequential nature, namely, ‘1999’ and
‘Fiftieth’ to be substituted by ‘2001’ and ‘Fifty-second’ respectively.
 
11.3     The Committee recommends that the Bill be passed in the present form.

4.         The Secretary, Legislative Department   gave a brief introduction of the Repealing and Amending Bill, 1999. He  stated that  the
Government  of India periodically undertook measures to repeal Acts which were no longer required on the statute book as they had already
been  incorporated in the parent legislation, such as, Sections 2,3 & 4 of the General Insurance Business Nationalisation (Amendment) Act,
1985 or the whole of Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Act, 1985, or Acts which were  of temporary nature such as the
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1985, and also legislations which were enacted as a one-time exercise such as the
Cancellation  of General Elections in Punjab Act, 1991 or the Gold (Control) Repeal Act, 1990 as contained in the First Schedule of the
present Bill.
5.         The Secretary  apprised the Members that the Second Schedule consisted of two provisions; the first being the Indian Succession
Act, 1925 and the second provision relating to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.  While justifying the Second Schedule of the Bill, he 
stated that with the insertion of 376A, 376B and 376C in the 1983 amendment of the Criminal Procedure Code, and 376D followed by
Section 377 which related to unnatural offences, the words “ditto” which was in the original amendment got incorporated which was not
intended, resulting in the alteration of the nature of imprisonment and also offence and, therefore, called for an amendment.

exercise and, therefore, no prior approval of the Cabinet was required as the Secretary had stated in his presentation.   Other Members 
desired to know what would be the effect on pending appeals on revisions before court in cases where the whole Act was repealed.

3.1       A Member expressed his disappointment at the replies of the Legislative Department to some queries and made a special mention of

3.2       The same Member referred to an annexure    to the reply of the Department on the issue whether the   approval of the Cabinet for

4.0       The representatives of the Ministry clarified that there was a factual error in the annexure and that Cabinet approval was not required
for the introduction of the Bill.
4.1       The Chairman took serious exception to the slip-shod response of the Ministry and desired that this point should be reflected in the
Report.  Members also expressed their desire that the casual attitude of the Department to the queries raised in the meeting should also be
reflected in the Report of the Committee.
5.0       The Committee then took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Repealing and Amending Bill, 1999.
Clause-2
5.1.0    The clause repeals 357 amendment Acts to the extent mentioned against the particular Act in the fourth column of the First Schedule
to the Bill.
5.1.1    The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause-3
5.2.0    The clause amends two Acts to the extent and in the manner mentioned in the fourth column against the particular Act in the Second
Schedule to the Bill to rectify the patent error and inadvertent mistakes in those Acts.
5.2.1    The Committee expressed its deep anguish at the manner in which the Legislative Department had responded to its previous query
regarding amendment to Section 377 of Code of Criminal Procedure and wanted that this should be reflected in the Report.
5.2.2    The Clause was, however, adopted without any change.
Clause-4
5.3       This is a saving clause, which states that the repeal of any amending Acts will not affect the parent Acts in which the repealed
enactment have been applied, incorporated or referred to.  The clause also provides saving of right, title, obligation, liability acquired,
accrued or incurred or any remedy in respect thereof, etc. and also provides that the Bill shall not affect the principle of rule of law and also
any enactment revived, restored, any jurisdiction, office, custom, title, exemption, usage, etc. which are not now existing or in force.
5.3.1    The clause was adopted without any change.
Clause-1, The Enacting Formula and Title
5.4       Clause-1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which are of consequential nature, namely, ‘1999’
and ‘Fiftieth’ to be substituted by ‘2001’ and ‘Fifty-second’ respectively.

Committee to make necessary additions/alterations in the report taking into account today’s discussions.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Seventy-seventh Report of the Committee on the Indian Divorce (Amendment) Bill, 2000*.
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred ** the Indian Divorce (Amendment) Bill, 2000, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on December 15, 2000 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
 
3.0       The Committee considered the Bill in four sittings held on 23 January, 9 February, 29 May and 13 June, 2001.
 
3.1       The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs in its sitting held on 23 January 2001.
 
3.2       In its sitting held on 9 February, 2001, the Committee heard Secretary General of Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India, Representatives of National Council of Churches in India and Director, Joint Women’s Programme on the various provisions of the Bill.
 
3.3       In its sitting held on 29 May 2001, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
 
3.4       The Committee considered the draft Report in its sitting held on 13 June, 2001 and adopted the same.  It also decided that the evidence tendered before the Committee may be laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament.
 
4.0       In course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill and took note of recommendations of various Law Commissions, various judicial pronouncements on the subject, replies to queries raised by the Members on the Bill in the meetings, submitted by the Legislative Department and suggestions/observations made by experts/Church leaders.
 
5.         For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

1.0       The Indian Divorce (Amendment) Bill, 2000 (Annexure-I) seeks to amend  mainly sections 10, 17 and 20 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869* (see Annexure II)  suitably so as to remove the gender inequality as contained in section 10 and to do away with the procedural delays in  obtaining divorce due to the provisions contained in sections 17 and 20 of the Act.  The Bill also amends other sections of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, which are consequential in nature.
 
1.1       It further proposes to repeal the following British Statutes relating to Christian Personal Law which have become obsolete but still in force, in pursuance of the recommendations of the Commission on Review of Administrative Laws set up under the Chairmanship of Shri P.C. Jain in 1998.
 
(i)
                  The Indian and Colonial Divorce Jurisdiction Act, 1926;
(ii)                The Indian and Colonial Divorce Jurisdiction Act, 1940; and
(iii)               The Indian Divorce Act, 1945.
 
2.0       Sections 10,17 and 20 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 are most contentious and have made the said Act evidently anachronistic, antiquated and discriminatory contrary to the provisions of the Constitution.
 
2.1.0    Section 10 of the Act provides for the grounds on which spouses belonging to Christian community can sue for dissolution of marriage.  In accordance with the provisions contained in the section, the male spouse is entitled to dissolution of marriage on the ground of adultery simpliciter   on the part  of female spouse but the female spouse  is not so entitled unless some other matrimonial fault is also found to be superadded to the adultery which are as below:-
 
(i)
                  incestuous  adultery;
(ii)                bigamy with  adultery;
(iii)               marriage with another women with adultery;
(iv)              adultery coupled with cruelty ; and
(v)                adultery coupled with desertion without reasonable excuse,  for two years or upwards.
 
Thus discrimination between the Christian female spouses   and Christian male spouses in seeking divorce is writ large as grounds available to female spouses are onerous and, thus, violative of constitutional provisions enshrined in Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution.
 
2.1.1    Leaving aside adultery simpliciter, cruelty and desertion without reasonable excuse, for two years or upwards are not also independent grounds of seeking divorce a vinculo matrimonii  (a total divorce  releasing both the party wholly dissolving the marriage by releasing from their  matrimonial  obligations) for the female spouses.  However, the female spouse is entitled to  divorce  a mensa et thoro  ( a partial qualified divorce by which the parties are separated and forbidden to live or  cohabit  together without affecting the marriage itself)  under section 22 of the parent Act.  In other words, the grounds of adultery simpliciter, cruelty and desertion entails a Christian female spouse under the Act only judicial separation (i.e. separation from bed and board) not divorce proper.
______________________________________________________________________________
*This Act governs the divorce procedure  for the Christian community.
2.1.2    But the female spouses governed under other Acts governing divorce in India are entitled to divorce proper on the basis of the grounds mentioned in the foregoing para.  There are a total of five other Acts governing divorce in India which are as follows:-
 
(i)
                  The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955;
(ii)                The Dissolution of Muslim Marriage Act, 1939;
(iii)               The Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936;
(iv)              The Special Marriage Act, 1954; and
(v)                The Foreign Marriage Act, 1959.
 
2.1.3    It is relevant to note that Christian spouses can obtain divorce on the grounds specified  in para 2.1.1 supra  provided  that the marriage took place abroad in which case they are governed by the Foreign Marriage Act, 1959 (This Act applies to the Indian Citizen whose marriage has been solemnized in a foreign country).  Further, Christian couple married under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 are also entitled to get divorce on the grounds mentioned above.  Thus, the provision contained in section 22 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 discriminates Christian female spouses married in church vis-à-vis female spouses of other religions and Christian female spouse married under the Special Marriage Act and the Foreign Marriage Act and thus violative of Article 15 of the Constitution.
 
3.0       Sections 17 and 20 of the parent Act set out the confirmation procedure of decree of nullity of marriage of a District Court/High Court by a special bench of High Court which is conspicuous  by its absence in analogous Acts.  The special bench of High Court means bench consisting of three judges except where the total number of judges is two.  Parties who have obtained a decree nisi of dissolution of marriage from the District Court/High Court have to wait interminably till a special bench of three judges of High Court is constituted.  Thus, the requirement of compulsory confirmation of decree nisi of the District Court/High Court by the same High Court makes litigation protracted, prolonged and strenuous.  At present, the above sections are devoid of procedural   reasonableness
available to spouses belonging to other communities.
 
4.0       The provisions of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 are the exact copies of the English Matrimonial Causes Act, 1857.  The latter Act was enacted when the matrimonial jurisdiction was transferred from the Ecclesiastical Courts (Church Courts) to civil courts  (High Courts) and marriages were construed as dissoluble   contracts.  Limited grounds of dissolving marriages were provided under the Statute for the first time under English Law.  Prior to that, a divorce could only be obtained through an Act of Parliament.  The grounds mentioned in the English Act were incorporated under section 10 of the Indian Divorce Act , 1869 by the Britishers.
 
4.1       The English Matrimonial Causes Act, 1857 had been amended in England as early as 1923 by the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1923 putting the husband and the wife on equal footing by making adultery an independent ground of divorce for both the parties.  The Matrimonial Causes Act, 1937 added three new independent grounds of divorce i.e. desertion, cruelty and insanity and thereby became progressive.
 
4.2       The grounds provided in Matrimonial Causes Act, 1937 have been incorporated into analogous Acts governing divorce in India except Indian Divorce Act, 1869, Thus, the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 has not kept pace with the provisions of similar enactments relating to divorce in other communities which are far more progressive in character.  The Act even has not been alive to the amendments made in its parent Act i.e. Matrimonial Causes Act, 1857.  The Act appears to be antiquated and requires urgent amendment in order to make it progressive.
5.0       It is pertinent to note that Acts mentioned in paragraph 2.1.2 supra are unified legislations containing procedure relating to solemnization of marriage and divorce whereas Indian Divorce Act, 1869 contains provisions relating to divorce and matrimonial causes of persons professing Christian religion.  The procedures relating to the solemnization of marriage of persons of Christian community are governed by another legislation, namely, the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872 (see Annexure –III)
 
6.0       The Supreme Court and various High Courts especially Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bombay and Calcutta in their judicial pronouncements have held the view that the amendments to the sections 10, 17 and 20 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 are constitutionally   imperative.
 
6.1       The Law Commission of India in its Fifteenth, Twenty-second, Ninetieth and One Hundred and Sixty-fourth   Reports inter alia has held the similar view.
 
7.0       Marriage and divorce being in Concurrent List, the State of Uttar Pradesh has done away with the provisions in section 17 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 by a State Amendment, way back in 1957.
 
8.0       The Government of India realized the need for reforming the colonial laws relating to marriage and divorce of persons professing Christianity and, accordingly, took steps by making a reference to the Law Commission for revision of those laws in the year 1958.
 
8.1       The Commission prepared a unified legislation to repeal the existing Acts governing the subject of marriage and divorce amongst Christian community and circulated the same to State Governments and several churches and organizations of Christianity.  After taking into consideration the comments received and evidence taken by it, the Law Commission submitted its Fifteenth Report on “Laws relating to marriage and divorce amongst Christians in India” to Central Government in August, 1960, wherein a unified Bill, namely, the Christian Marriage and Matrimonial Causes Bill, 1961 was appended for introduction in Parliament.
 
8.2       The Government, however, at that time wanted the Law Commission to elicit public opinion on the Bill.  The Law Commission after eliciting public opinion submitted its Twenty-second Report in December 1961, wherein certain changes were made in the Bill referred to it.
 
8.3       Based on the recommendations contained in Twenty-second Report of the Law Commission,  the Christian Marriage and Matrimonial Causes Bill, 1962 was introduced in Lok Sabha, which was subsequently referred to a Joint Committee of both Houses.  Although the said Joint Committee had presented the Report to Parliament in 1963, the Bill could not come up  for discussion in Lok Sabha and lapsed on the dissolution of Third Lok Sabha.  The Government did not reintroduce the Bill due to strong  opposition from certain quarters of Christian community.
 
8.4       However,  in 1989, Shri Thampan Thomas, the then  Member of Parliament made an effort to bring in the legislation by introducing the Christian Marriage and Matrimonial Causes Bill, 1989 (Bill No.10 of 1989) in Lok Sabha on 10 March, 1989 as a Private Member’s Bill, but it could not come up for consideration.
 
8.5       The Law Commission headed by Mr. Justice K.K. Mathew suo motto took up the issue and in its Ninetieth Report on “Grounds of Divorce amongst Christians in India: section 10 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869”, submitted in May, 1983, had pointed out that section 10 of the Act is violative of Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution and held the view that amendment to section 10 was a constitutional imperative.
 
8.6.0    The Law Commission again in its One Hundred and Sixty-fourth Report  on “The Indian Divorce Act, 1869”, presented in November, 1998, had reiterated  its stand taken in the Reports referred to  in foregoing paras.
 
8.6.1    It had inter alia recommended that Parliament may enact a comprehensive law governing marriage, divorce and other allied aspects of the Christians.  The Commission, while relying upon observations/judgments of various High Courts, had also urged the Government to take immediate measures to amend sections 10,17 and 20 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869.
 
8.7       The Committee on Status of Women in India in its Report submitted in 1974 had also suggested to amend the Act on the lines suggested by the Law Commission.
 
8.8       However, the Government did not find a congenial atmosphere in view of the situation that arose in view of the judgement in Supreme Court in Shah Banu’s case and in view of its avowed policy not to interfere in the personal laws of the minority community unless the necessary initiative for the changes came from the communities concerned.  However, the Government took up the cudgel when the Joint Women’s Programme (JWP), a voluntary women’s   social organization submitted the following Bills to the Government   and also claimed that the Bills had the support of various churches including Catholic Bishop’s Conference of India (CBCI):
 
(i)
                  The Christian Marriage  Bill, 1994;
(ii)                The Indian Sucession (Amendment) Bill, 1994; and
(iii)               The Christian Adoption and Maintenance Bill, 1994.
 
The Bill at Sr. No. (i) was a unified legislation substantially conforming to the provisions of the Christian Marriage and Matrimonial Causes Bill, 1962 and the Special Marriage Act, 1954.
 
8.9
              The National Commission for Minorities also agreed with the proposed legislation.
 
8.10     As mentioned in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill under examination of the Committee, a draft-unified legislation called the Christian Marriage Bill, 2000 (see Annexure- IV) was prepared.  A meeting was convened between the Government and prominent church leaders and the Members of Parliament belonging to Christian Community in April, 2000 but no consensus was arrived at on some provisions of the Bill.  However, there was no opposition for    the amendments to sections 10, 17 and 20 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869.
 
8.11     In view of the above factors, the Government has shown urgency to bring in the Indian Divorce (Amendment) Bill, 2000.  But the process which started way back in 1958 which is yet to be completed as there is a need to have a unified legislation on Personal Law of Christian Community as in the case of communities professing other religions in India.

9.0       The Secretary, Legislative Department in his deposition before the Committee gave a brief outline of the salient features of the Bill.  He stated that the Bill hovered around amendments to sections 10, 17 and 20 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 and the rest of the amendments were consequential in nature.  He stressed that minimal charges were to be effected in the parent Act without disturbing the scheme of the Act in order to bring gender equality and to do away with procedural delay in confirmation of decree of divorce.
 
9.1       He mentioned that the four grounds i.e.  ‘adultery’,  ‘conversion’, ‘cruelty’ and ‘desertion’ contained in section 10 of the Act, would now be available for divorce to both the sexes.  In addition, wife can also obtain divorce on the grounds of ‘rape’ and ‘sodomy’ on the part of husband.
 
9.2       He informed the Committee about the urgency of introducing the Bill in view of several judicial pronouncements and lack of consensus amongst Christian community on draft comprehensiveLegislation  prepared by the Government on marriage and divorce of Christian community.
 
10.0     The Committee, is of the view that the Bill is a half-baked measure and in that context, urges upon the Government to bring in a comprehensive legislation on  Personal Law of Christian community in consultation with that community at the earliest.                            
 
11.0     The Commission on Review of Administrative Laws constituted under the Chairmanship of Shri P.C.Jain had inter alia    stated that there were a number of personal laws applicable to some religions and communities and that some of these may not be relevant now.  The perception of the concerned religion of the community would be relevant for their updating/codification/ repeal.  The Commission had, inter alia identified Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872 and the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 for the purpose.
 
12.0     Christians in India broadly belongs to three different traditions i.e. (i) Roman Catholic (ii) Protestants, who are followers of Church of South India (CSI) and Church of North India (CNI) and (iii) Syrian Christian, who are followers of Greek orthodox churches.  Christians amongst various tribes particularly in North-East Region are granted protection under the Constitution in respect of culture, traditions and customs.
 
12.1     Among the three traditions, the Roman Catholic Church considers marriage to be a sacrament and subscribes to the doctrine of indissolubility of marriage.  The other two Churches do not have doctrinaire objection to divorce.  However, in India the Christian community of different denominations do not have objection to divorce.  The Christian organizations, namely, Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India (CBCI) which represents nearly 50 per cent of Christian population and the National Council of Churches in India (NCCI) which is a conglomerate of 29 Protestant Churches representing 20-30 percent of Christian population have concurred with amendments in the Indian Divorce Act, 1869.  They have gone ahead in suggesting some additional amendments to the parent Act, which
was submitted to the Government on the day the Bill was presented to Parliament and the same has been placed as Annexure-V.
 
13.0.    The Committee also heard the representatives of Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India, National Council of Churches in India and Joint Women’s Programme collectively on the provisions of the Bill in its meeting held on 9 February, 2001.
 
 
13.1.0  The representatives of CBCI and NCCI stated that the teachings of the scriptures is ‘what God has united, let no man divide’ and, therefore, the Holy Scripture does not accept divorce.  However, in the larger interests of the community, and to free the parties from the civil bonds of marriage, they are accepting divorce and, therefore, appreciate the Bill as progressive. The witnesses felt that the provisions of section 10 of the Parent Act was inadequate and, therefore, in addition to what had already been provided in the Bill, the following other grounds, may be incorporated in the Bill;
 
(i)
                  incurability of an unsound mind for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition;
(ii)                has been suffering from a virulent and incurable form of leprosy; for a period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition;
(iii)               has been suffering from venereal  disease in a communicable form for a period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition;
(iv)              has not been heard of being alive for a period of seven years or more; and 
(v)                willful refusal to consummate the marriage, and the marriage not having been consummated. 
 
13.1.1  They had also suggested addition of section 10 A to include ‘divorce by mutual consent’ to bring the Act at par with the Special Marriage Act, 1954 and the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
 
13.2     The representatives of the CBCI also stated that, Churches have certain procedures for declaring marriages null and void.  Force, fraud in getting the consent for marriage, insanity,  gross immaturity, etc. are  the grounds on the basis of which church nullify the marriage. They wanted that   such a declaration of marriage as null and void by the decisions of ecclesiastical  authorities functioning under the Church should be recognized  and ratified by the Civil Courts.
 
13.3     In that context, the Committee drew attention of the witnesses to section 19 of the Act which reads as under:
 
“Nothing in the Section shall affect the jurisdiction of the High Court to make decrees of nullity of marriage on the ground that the consent of either party was obtained by force.”
 
The Committee wanted to know the procedure followed by the Church in declaring the marriage null and void and requested the witnesses to clarify the position in case the decision of church comes into conflicts with decree of the court.
 
13.4     The representatives clarified that the set procedure for dissolution of marriage which is  followed all over the world is based on universal common law.  The procedure is similar to the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code by hearing petitions, respondants and examining witnesses.  The Church may say whether the parties can remarry but unless they get civil divorce, they cannot get married again.  Therefore, they suggested that instead of undertaking the whole procedure of a detailed examination by the Court, the Court can pronounce  its judgment after  examining their files maintained by the Church authorities.  Thus, the trial will be speedy and inexpensive and reduce emotional trauma.
 
13.5     The Committee desires that the aforesaid suggestion of the Church leaders may be examined by the Government.
 
13.6     Since Judicial precedents in India are sufficient, the witnesses had suggested to deletion of  section 7 of the Act  wherein the Court is free to act on the principle of English Divorce Court.  They had suggested for addition of a new definition of District Court under section 3 of the Act.
 
13.7     Regarding the provision which deals with damages from the adulterer such as sections 34 and 35 of the parent Act, the witnesses have suggested that these sections should be deleted in order to empower women and remove gender bias.
 
13.8     With regard to section 36 of the Act, providing one-fifth of the property   to be given to the divorced woman as maintenance, the witnesses were of the opinion that it should be dependent  on the status and the needs of the wife and the status of the husband and vice-versa. The witnesses also felt that in order to ensure gender justice, section 39, about the wife’s property being given for the benefit of the husband  and the children, be deleted.  As for sections 37, 43 and 44 dealing with alimony and custody of children, the witnesses strongly felt  that the woman was  the most important factor.
 
14.0     Suggestions received from these organizations are mostly in nature of amendments to various sections of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 not covered by the Bill.  Some of the suggestions would also require amendments to clauses 4, 13, 17, 18 and 19 of the Bill.  The comments of the Legislative Department on each suggestion have been received and are put at Annexure-VI   
 
15.0     The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its sitting held on 29 May 2001, in the presence of representatives of Legislative Department and   Department of Legal Affairs.
Clause 2
 
15.1.0  This clause seeks to amend the short title of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 ( as contained in section 1 of the Act ) so as to omit the word “Indian” occurring therein.  This is in tune with the recent legislative practice of not  using the word “Indian” in the short titles of Parliamentary legislation.
 
15.1.1  The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 3
 
15.1.2  It is proposed to remove gender inequality in the matter of grounds of divorce as available to husband and wife under section 10 of the Act by substituting that section vide clause 4 of the Bill.  As the expressions “incestuous adultery” and “bigamy with adultery” as occurring in section 10 of the Act will no longer be in the said section, these expressions have become redundant.  This clause, therefore, seeks to omit the definitions of those expressions occurring at clauses  (6) and (7) of section 3 of the Act.
 
15.1.3  The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 4
 
15.1.4  This clause seeks to provide the grounds of dissolution of marriage.  Existing provisions of section 10 of the Act make a distinction between the husband and the wife in the matter of grounds on which they could obtain dissolution of marriage.  While adultery, without any other   ground, is a ground for seeking dissolution  of marriage  by the husband, in the case of the petition by the wife, there is in addition another  requirement that  it should be ‘incestuous adultery’ or ‘bigamy with adultery’ or ‘adultery coupled with cruelty or desertion for two years’.  Certain High Courts, including the High Court of Kerala have struck down the words “incestuous” and “adultery coupled with” in section 10 on the ground of gender inequality.  This clause seeks to substitute the said section 10 with a
new section providing same grounds for husband and wife for seeking dissolution of marriage.   In addition, a wife may also get divorce  on the ground that the husband has since the solemnization of marriage been guilty of rape, sodomy or bestiality.
 
15.1.5  Under the Act a petition for dissolution of marriage could be presented either to the District Court or to the High Court.  It is proposed that the petition may henceforth be presented to the District Court only.  Hence, the clause amends section 10 of the parent Act.
 
15.1.6
    The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 5
 
15.1.7  This clause seeks to substitute existing section 11 with the addition of the words “or adulteress”  to cover cases where the wife sues the husband for divorce on the ground of adultery.  Thus both adulterer or adulteress would be co-respondent in case of divorce petition. The amendment is consequential to the amendments made in the grounds of divorce under section 10.
 
15.1.8  The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 6
 
15.1.9  This clause seeks to amend section  13 of the Act so as to do away with the enabling provision for presenting a petition for dissolution of marriage to the High Court after such a petition has been dismissed by the District  Court.
 
15.1.10            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 7
 
15.1.11            This clause seeks  to amend section 14 of the principal Act by omitting certain  words therein.  The amendment is consequential to the amendments made in sections 16 and 17 of the Act.
 
15.1.12            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 8
 
15.1.13This clause seeks to amend section 15 of the Act.  The amendments are consequential to the changes made in the grounds  of divorce under section 10.
 
15.1.14            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 9
 
15.1.15            This clause  seeks to amend  section 16 of the Act.  The amendment is consequential to the amendments made in section 17 of the Act to do away with the requirement of confirmation  of decree of District Court by the High Court.
 
15.1.16            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 10
 
15.1.17            This clause seeks to substitute section 17 relating to confirmation of decree  for dissolution  of marriages made by  a District Judge by the High Court.  At present  every  decree  for a   dissolution of marriage made by a  District Judge is subject to confirmation by the High Court.  In order  to obviate the procedural delay and  consequential hardship to the estranged couples, this clause seeks  to do away with the requirement of confirmation by the High Court of such  decrees. 
 
15.1.18            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 11
 
15.1.19            This clause seeks to omit section 17A of the Act relating to appointment of officers to exercise duties of King’s Proctor as it has become obsolete.
 
15.1.20            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 12
 
15.1.21            The clause seeks to amend section 18 of the Act relating to petition for decree of nullity.  The omission of the words  “or to the High Court” as proposed in this clause in consequential to the amendment proposed in section 10.
 
15.1.22            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 13
 
15.1.23            This clause seeks to amend section 19 of the Act as consequential to the amendment made in section 10 as regards the court in which petition may be presented.  Thus, it substitute   the words “the jurisdiction of the High Court” with the words the “jurisdiction of the District Court” occurring with last paragraph of the section.
 
15.1.24            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 14
 
15.1.25            This clause seeks to omit section 20 of the Act relating to confirmation of decree of nullity  of marriage by a  District Judge.  At present, every decree of nullity of marriage made by a District Judge shall be subject to confirmation by the High Court.  In order to simplify the procedure and obviate delay and consequential hardship to estranged  couples, it is proposed to do away with the requirement  of confirmation.
 
15.1.26            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 15
 
15.1.27            This clause seeks to amend section 22 of the Act.  The amendment is consequential to the changes made in section 10.
 
15.1.28            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
 
 
 
Clause 16
 
15.1.29            This clause seeks to omit the words “or the High Court” occurring in sections 23, 27 and 32 of the Act as consequential to changes made in section 10 relating to the court in which petitions could be made.
 
15.1.30            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 17
 
15.1.31            This clause provides for damages from adulterer or adulteress.  While following the existing provisions of section 34 of the Act, it is proposed to allow the wife also to claim damages from the adulteress.  This is consequential to the changes made in section 10 of the Act.
 
15.1.32            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clause 18
 
15.1.33            This clause seeks to substitute section 35 of the Act so as to make provision for the adulterer as well as the adulteress to pay costs.  The changes  are consequential to the changes made in section 10.
 
15.1.34            The Clause was adopted without any change.
 
Clauses 19 to 23
 
15.1.35            The amendments suggested in these clauses are consequential to the changes made in sections 10 and 17 of the Act.

Clause 2
4.1.0    This clause seeks to amend the short title of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 ( as contained in section 1 of the Act ) so as to omit the word “Indian” occurring therein.  This is in tune with the recent legislative practice of not  using the word “Indian” in the short titles of Parliamentary legislation.
4.1.1    The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 3
4.1.2    It is proposed to remove gender inequality in the matter of grounds of divorce as available to husband and wife under section 10 of the Act by substituting that section vide clause   4 of   the  Bill.   As   the   expressions  “incestuous  adultery”  and  “bigamy  with
adultery” as occurring in section 10 of the Act will no longer be in the said section, these expressions have become redundant.  This clause, therefore, seeks to omit the definitions of those expressions occurring at clauses  (6) and (7) of section 3 of the Act.
4.1.3    The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 4
4.1.4    This clause seeks to provide the grounds of dissolution of marriage.  Existing provisions of section 10 of the Act make a distinction between the husband and the wife in the matter of grounds on which they could obtain dissolution of marriage.  While adultery, without any other   ground, is a ground for seeking dissolution  of marriage  by the husband, in the case of the petition by the wife, there is in addition another  requirement that  it should be ‘incestuous adultery’ or ‘bigamy with adultery’ or ‘adultery coupled with cruelty or desertion for two years’.  Certain High Courts, including the High Court of Kerala have struck down the words “incestuous” and “adultery coupled with” in section 10 on the ground of gender inequality.  This clause seeks to substitute the said section 10 with a
new section providing same grounds for husband and wife for seeking dissolution of marriage.   In addition, a wife may also get divorce  on the ground that the husband has since the solemnization of marriage been guilty of rape, sodomy or bestiality.
4.1.5    Under the Act a petition for dissolution of marriage could be presented either to the District Court or to the High Court.  It is proposed that the petition may henceforth be presented to the District Court only.  Hence, the clause amends section 10 of the parent Act.
4.1.6

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
 
            The Law Commission of India in its 164th Reports on “The Indian Divorce Act (IV of 1869)” presented to the Government in November, 1998 has, inter alia, recommended that Parliament may enact a comprehensive law governing marriage and divorce and other allied aspects of the Christians in India.  The Commission, relying on the judgments and observations of certain High Courts, has also urged the Central Governments to take immediate measures––
(i)                 to amend section 10 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 relating to grounds of dissolution of marriages so that the female spouses are not discriminated vis a vis male spouse in obtaining a decree of dissolution of marriage.
(ii)               To amend suitably section 17 and 20 of the Act to do away with the procedural requirement of obtaining confirmation from the High Court in respect of a decree of dissolution of marriage or decree of nullity of marriage as such a procedure is long-drawn and strenuous.
2.         With a view to ascertaining the views of the Christian community on proposal for a unified law on marriage and divorce, the Central Government convened a meeting of leaders of prominent Churches in India and the Members of Parliament belonging to the Christian community on the 28th April, 2000 buy there was no consensus for bringing in a comprehensive legislation on Christian marriage and matrimonial causes.  However, there is no opposition from any one to amend sections 10. 17 and 20 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 suitably to remove the gender inequality as contained in section 10 and to do away with the procedural delays in obtaining divorce due to the provisions contained in sections 17 and 20 of the Act.  The Government, therefore, proposes to make suitable changes
in the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 for removing hardship to all concerned.
3.         The Commission on Review of Administrative Laws which was set up by the Central Government on the 8th May, 1998 has, inter alia, recommended repeal of various enactment including three British Statutes relating to Christian Personal Law still in force.  It is proposed to repeal these enactments also they have become obsolete.
4.         This Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.
