34. (1) Every petition under section 14 shall be presented to the district court within the local limits of whose ordinary original civil jurisdiction the Minister discharges his functions or the office of the Marriage Registrar is situate, as the case may be.
      (2) Every petition under Chapters IV to VII shall be presented to the district court within the local limits of whose ordinary original civil jurisdiction ––
    (a) the respondent is residing at the lime of the presentation of the petition, or
    (b) the marriage was solemnised, or
    (c) the husband and wife last resided together, or
    (d) the petitioner is residing at the time of the presentation of the petition, provided that the respondent is, at that time, residing outside the territories to which this Act extends.
35.(1) Every petition presented under Chapters IV to VII shall state as distinctly as the nature of the case permits the facts on which the claim to relief is founded and shall also state that there is no collusion between the petitioner and the other party to the marriage.
    (2) The statements contained in every petition under Chapters IV to VII shall be verified by the petitioner or some other competent person in the manner required by law for the verification of plaints and may, at the hearing, be referred to as evidence.
36. Subject to the other provisions contained in this Act and to such rules as the High Court may make in this behalf, all proceedings under this Act shall be regulated, as far as may be, by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
37.    (1) In any proceeding under Chapters IV to VII, whether defended or not, if the court is satisfied that ––        
    (a) any of the grounds for granting relief exists and the petitioner is not in any way taking advantage of his or her own wrong or disability for the purpose of such relief, and
    (b) where the ground of the petition is adultery, the petitioner has not in any manner been accessory to or connived at or condoned the adultery, or where the ground of the petition is cruelty, the petitioner has not in any manner condoned the cruelty, and,
    (c) the petition is not presented or prosecuted in collusion with the respondent, and
   (d) there has not been any unnecessary or improper delay in instituting the proceeding, and
   (e) there is no other legal ground why relief should not be granted, then, and in such a case, but not otherwise. the court shall decree such relief accordingly.
    (2) Before proceeding to grant any relief under Chapters IV to VII, it sha11 be the duty of the court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible so to do consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to bring about a reconciliation between the parties.
   (3) For the purpose of aiding the court in bringing about such reconciliation, the court may, if the parties so desire or if it thinks it just and proper so to do, adjourn the proceeding and refer the matter to any person named by the parties in this behalf or to any person nominated by the court if the parties fail to name any person, with directions to report to the court as to whether a reconciliation can be, and has been, effected, and shall, in disposing of the proceeding have due regard to the report.
38.  (I) On a petition for divorce or judicial separation presented on the ground of adultery, the petitioner shall make the alleged adulterer or adulteress a co-respondent, unless the petitioner is excused by the court from so doing on any of the following grounds, namely:-
(a) that the respondent is leading the life of a prostitute, and that the petitioner
knows of no person with whom the adultery has been committed;
(b) that the name of the alleged adulterer or adulteress is unknown to the petitioner
although the petitioner has made due efforts to discover it;
(c) that the alleged adulterer or adulteress is dead;
(d) any other ground which the court may regard as sufficient in the circumstances of the case.
(2) The provisions of sub-section (I) shall, so far as may be, apply in relation to the answer of a respondent praying for divorce or judicial separation on the ground of adultery, as they apply in relation to a petition for divorce or judicial separation presented on that ground.
39. If, in any proceeding for divorce or judicial separation, the respondent opposes the relief sought on the ground of the petitioner's adultery, cruelty or desertion, the court may give the respondent the same relief to which he or she would have been entitled if he or she had presented a petition seeking such relief.
40.  (1) Every decree for divorce under section 26 shall, in the first instance, be a decree nisi, not to be made absolute until after the expiration of six months from the pronouncing thereof, unless the court fixes a shorter time.
   (2) After the pronouncing of the decree nisi and before the decree is made absolute, any person may, by an application made in accordance with such rules as may be made by the High Court in that behalf, show cause why the decree should not be made absolute by reason of the decree having been obtained by collusion or by reason of material facts not having been brought before the court, and in any such case the court may make the decree absolute, reverse the decree nisi, require further inquiry or otherwise deal with the case as the
court thinks fit.
    (3) Where a decree nisi has been obtained and no application for the decree to be made absolute has been made within six months from the pronouncement of the decree nisi by the party who obtained the decree, then, at any time within three months from the expiration of the said six months, the party against whom the decree nisi has been granted shall be at liberty to apply to the court and the court, on such application, may make the decree absolute, reverse the decree nisi, require further inquiry or otherwise deal with the case as the
court thinks fit.
41.  (1) A husband or wife may, on a petition for divorce or for judicial separation, claim damages from any person on the ground of adultery with the wife or husband of the petitioner.
     (2) The court may direct in what manner the damages recovered on any such petition are to be paid or applied, and may direct the whole or any part of the damages to be, settled for the benefit of the children, if any, of the marriage, or as a provision for the maintenance of the wife, or husband.
42.  Where in any proceeding under Chapters IV to VII it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum, as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, may seem to the court to be reasonable.
43.  (1) Any  court exercising jurisdiction under chapters IV to VII may, at the time of passing any decree or at any time subsequent thereto, on application made to it for the purpose by either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, order that the respondent shall, while the applicant remains unmarried, pay to the applicant for her or his maintenance and support such gross sum or such monthly or periodical sum for a term, not exceeding the life of the applicant as, having regard to the respondent's own income and other property, if
any, the income and other property of the applicant and the conduct of the parties, may seem to the court to be just, and any such payment may be secured, if necessary, by a charge on the immovable property of the respondent.
      (2) If the court is satisfied that there is a change in the circumstances of either party at any time after it has made an order under sub-section (1), it may, at the instance of either party, vary, modify or rescind any such order in such manner as the court may deem just.
     (3) If the court is satisfied that the party in whose favour an order has been made under this section has remarried, or, if such party is the wife, that she has not remained chaste, or, if such party is the husband, that he has had sexual intercourse with any woman outside wedlock, it shall rescind the order.
44. (1) In any proceeding under Chapter VI or Chapter VII, the court may make such provisions in the decree as it deems just and proper with respect to any property presented, at or about the time of the marriage, which may belong jointly to both the husband and the wife.
    (2) In any case in which the court pronounces a decree for divorce or nullity of marriage, the court may inquire into the existence of ante-nuptial or post nuptial settlements made on the parties whose marriage is the subject of the decree, and may make such orders, with reference to the application of the whole or any part of the property so settled (whether the settlement is for 
the benefit of the children of the marriage or of the parties to the marriage or both), as the court thinks fit.
     (3) The court shall not make any order under sub-section (2) for the benefit of the parents or either of them at the expense of the children.
45. In any proceeding under Chapters IV to VII, the court may, from time to time pass such interim orders and make such provisions in the decree as it may deem just and proper with respect to the custody maintenance and education of minor children consistently with their wishes, wherever possible, and may, after the decree, upon application by petition for the purpose, make, from time to time, all such orders and provisions with respect to the custody, maintenance and education of such children as might have been made by such
decree or interim orders in case the proceeding for obtaining such decree were still pending, and the court may also from time to time revoke, suspend or vary any such orders and provisions previously made.
46. A proceeding under this Act shall be conducted in camera if either party so desires or if the court so thinks fit to do, and it shall not be lawful for any person to and print or publish any matter in relation to such proceeding except with the previous permission of the court.
47. All decrees and orders made by the court in any proceeding under this Act shall be appealable as decrees of the court made in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction and such appeal shall lie to the court to which appeals ordinarily lie from the decisions of the court given in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction:
     Provided that there shall be no appeal on the subject of costs only.
48. All decrees and orders made by the court in any proceeding under this Act shall be enforced in the like manner as the decrees and orders of the court made in the exercise of its original civil jurisdiction for the time being are enforced.
CHAPTER IX
PENALTIES
49.  Every person whose marriage is solemnised whether before or after the commencement of this Act and who, during the lifetime of his or her wife or husband contracts any other marriage shall be subject to the penalties provided in section 495 and section 495 of the Indian Penal Code for the offence of marrying again during the lifetime of the husband or wife, and the marriage so contracted shall be void.
50.   Every person who procures a marriage of himself or herself to be solemnized under this Act in contravention of the conditions specified in clauses (ii) and (iv) of section 4 shall be punishable-
     (a) in the case of a contravention of the condition specified in clause (ii) of section 4, with simple imprisonment which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both, and
    (b) in the case of a contravention of the condition specified in clause (iv) of section 4, with simple imprisonment which may extend to fifteen days, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
51.   Whoever, for the purpose of procuring a marriage intentionally––
     (a) where an oath or declaration is required by this Act, or by any Church or group according to the rules of which a marriage is intended to be solemised, makes a false oath or declaration, or
    (b) where a notice or certificate is required by this Act, signs a false notice or certificate,
     shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
52. Whoever makes an objection to the issue, by a Minister or a Marriage Registrar, of a certificate, by falsely representing himself to be a person whose consent to the marriage is required by law, knowing or believing such representation to be false, or not having reason to believe it to be true, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence described in section 205 of the Indian Penal Code and shall be punishable accordingly.
53. Whoever, not being authorised by section 8 to solemnise marriages, solemnizes or professes to solemnise under this Act a marriage between persons who are Christians, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to two thousand rupees.
54.(1) Whoever, being a Minister or a Marriage Registrar, in contravention of the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 13, wilfully or without just cause takes more than thirty days from the date of any objection to an intended marriage for the purpose of inquiring into the matter of the objection and arriving at a decision, shall be punishable with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees.
    (2) Whoever, being a Minister or a Marriage Registrar, refuses, without just cause, to solemnise a marriage under this Act, shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.
55. Whoever, being authorised under this Act to solemnise a marriage, knowingly and willfully––
    (a) solemnizes such marriage––
        (i) without publishing a notice regarding such marriage as required by any provision of this Act, or
     (ii) in contravention of any other provision contained in this Act, or
        (b) issue any certificate in contravention of any provision contained in this Act,
     shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.
56.   Whoever, by himself or another, wilfully destroys or injures any Marriage Certificate Book, or any part thereof or any authenticated extract therefrom, or falsely makes or counterfeits any part of such book, or wilfully inserts any false entry in any such book or authenticated extract. shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to two thousand rupees.
57. Any person who prints or publishes any matter in contravention of the provisions contained in section 46 shall be punishable with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees.
58. No prosecution for any offence punishable under section 50, section 51, section 52, section 53, section 54, section 55, section 56 or section 57 shall be instituted after the expiry of two years from the date on which the offence is committed.
CHAPTER X
MISCELLANEOUS
59.   (1) Where any person makes an objection against the issue of any certificate of notice of marriage and the Marriage Registrar under section 13 or under section 14, declares that the objection is not reasonable and has not been made in good faith, the Marriage Register, may, after giving such person a reasonable opportunity of being heard, award. by way of compensation, costs, not exceeding one thousand rupees, to the parties to the intended marriage,
    (2) Any person aggrieved by an order of the Marriage Registrar under sub-section (1) may, within a period of thirty days from the date of the order, appeal to the district court.
    (3) Subject to any order passed on appeal under sub-section (2), the order of the Marriage Registrar under sub-section (1) shall be final.
   (4) Any order of costs made under sub-section (1) may be executed in the same manner as a decree passed by the district court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the office of the Marriage Registrar is situated.
60. Whenever any marriage has been solemnised between two Christians under this Act in accordance with the provisions of this Act, it shall not be void merely on account of any irregularity in respect of any of the following matters, namely:–
   (i) any statement made in regard to the dwelling-place of the persons married;
  (ii) the notice of the marriage;
  (iii) the certificate of the notice of the marriage of translation thereof;
   (iv) the registration of the marriage.
61.(1) Any person authorised to solemnise a marriage under this Act, who discovers any error in the form or substance of any entry in the Marriage Certificate Book may, within one month next after the discovery of such error, in the presence of the persons married, or, in case of their death or absence, in the presence of two other witnesses, correct the error by entry in the margin. without any alteration of the original entry and shall sign the marginal entry and add thereto the date of such correction.
   (2) Every correction made under this section shall be attested by the witnesses in whose presence it was made.
   (3) Where a copy of any entry has already been sent under sub-section (3) of section 19 to the Registrar-Gencra1, such person shall make and send in like manner a separate certificate of the original erroneous entry and of the marginal corrections therein made.
62.  Subject to the other provisions contained in this Act, a marriage under this Act 5 may be solemnized by a Minister-––
     (a) in a church building, or
    (b) in any other place agreed upon between the parties to the marriage, if solemnisation at such place is in accordance with the custom or usage applicable to the community to which the parties to the marriage belong.
63. Every Marriage Registrar shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.
64. The Marriage Notice Book shall be open for inspection at all reasonable times, without fee, by any person desirous of inspecting the same.
65.(1) The Marriage Certificate Book kept under this Act shall at all reasonable times be open for inspection and shall be admissible, as evidence of the statements therein contained.
    (2) Certified extracts from the Marriage Certificate Book shall, on application, be given by the person who solemnised the marriage or other person having the custody for the time being of the Marriage Certificate Book, to any person who applies for the same.
   (3) Inspection of the Marriage Certificate Book under sub-section (I) and the grant of certified extracts therefrom under sub-section (2) shall be–
      (a) without fee, if applied for by the parties to the marriage at or about the time of the marriage,
     (b) subject to the payment of the prescribed fees, in other cases.
66.  Every certified copy, purporting to be signed by the person entrusted under this Act with the custody of any Marriage Certificate Book, of an entry of a marriage in such Book, shall be received in evidence without production or proof of the original.
67.(I) Any notice to be given or declaration to be made by any person in respect of an intended marriage under this Act may be given or made in a language commonly in use in the State or the part of State in which the notice is given or declaration made; or in English.
   (2) Every person solemnising a marriage under this Act shall satisfy himself that the parties to the marriage have understood the contents of the notice given and the declaration made by each of them, and (where a certificate of notice of marriage is required to be issued under this Act) of the certificate of notice of marriage issued for the marriage.
68. No Minister shall be compelled to solemnise any marriage, the solemnisation of which would be contrary to the rules of the Church or group of which he is a Minister.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been
authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Seventy-eighth Report of the
Committee on the Freedom of Information Bill, 2000*.
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred ** the Freedom of Information Bill, 2000
(Annexure-I), as introduced in the Lok Sabha on July 25, 2000 and pending therein, to the Committee on 14 September
2000 for examination and report.
3.         The Committee considered the Bill in five sittings held on 23 October 2000, 24 January, 8 February, 25 June and
10 July 2001.
3.1       The Committee heard oral evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on
the Bill in its sitting held on 23 October 2000.
3.2       In its sitting held on 24 January and 8 February 2001, the Committee heard prominent organizations and eminent
experts connected with the issue (Annexure-II) on the various provisions of the Bill.
3.3       In its sitting held on 25 June 2001, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
3.4       The Committee considered the draft Report in its sitting held on 10 July 2001 and adopted the same. It also
decided that the evidence tendered before the Committee may be laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament.
4.         In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill received from
the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, similar legislations of various States of India and foreign
countries, papers received from organizations/experts mentioned in Annexure-I, replies of the Ministry, organizations
and experts to the queries raised by the Members on the Bill in the meetings, comments of the Ministry (Annexure-III )
on the suggestions/observations made by organizations/experts connected with the Freedom of Information Bill, 2000.
5.         For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been
printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
6.         On behalf of the Committee, I would like to acknowledge with thanks the contributions made by
experts/organizations who deposed before the Committee and submitted their valuable suggestions on the subject matter
of the Bill.  A special word of thanks is due to Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative who rendered valuable
assistance to the Committee and its Secretariat in the course of examination of the Bill.

REPORT
 
            The Freedom of Information Bill, 2000 seeks to provide for freedom to every citizen to secure access to
information under the control of public authorities, consistent with public interest, in order to promote openness,
transparency and accountability in administration and in relation to matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
2.         Article 19 of the Constitution ensures to the citizens a wide range of freedoms.  The Supreme Court has held that
the right to know and be informed would make the right to free speech and expression complete.  Besides, freedom to

78th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/78threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:46:01]
obtain access to information that has a bearing on the sustenance of life would functionalise the right to life and
livelihood.
2.1       There is a world-wide trend in democratic countries to have a legislation, for assuring to the citizens the right of
access to information of the public authorities, as part of the effort to promote openness, transparency and accountability
in the administration and to ensure greater participation of the people in decision making.
2.2       Legislation on Freedom of Information in democratic countries like the USA has been enacted way back in
1966.  Other countries like Japan, Ireland, the Netherlands, Australia, Canada, France, the United Kingdom, New
Zealand and South Africa have also enacted similar legislations to enforce a measure of accountability and transparency
on the agencies of the State.
2.3       In India also, at the State level, Tamil Nadu and Goa passed their own Acts on the right to information in 1997. 
In Rajasthan, the Bill is awaiting Cabinet approval.  The State of Maharashtra also brought forth its ‘Maharashtra Right
to Information Act, 2000’ in August 2000.  The State of Karnataka has also promulgated the Karnataka Information
Ordinance, 2000, before the Centre came up with a Bill to ensure public access to information.
3.         At the Central level, on 2 January, 1997, the Government set up a Working Group on Right to Information and
Transparency under the Chairmanship of Shri H.D. Shourie to examine the feasibility and the need for either a full-
fledged Right to Information Act or its introduction in a phased manner to meet the needs of open and responsive
governance and also to examine the framework of rules with reference to the Civil Services (Conduct) Rules and the
Manual of Office Procedure. 
3.1       The Working Group submitted its report on 21 May 1997 with a proposed Bill titled ‘The Freedom of
Information Bill, 1997’.   The report of the Working Group was forwarded to all ministries of the Government of India
as also to all States/Union Territories for their comments.  In the meanwhile, the statutory scheme prepared on the basis
of the deliberations in the Working Group was circulated for discussion during the Chief Ministers’ Conference on
“Effective and Responsive Government” held on 24 May 1997 at New Delhi.  The statutory scheme received the broad
approval of the Conference which recognized the need for enactment of such a law.
3.2       The report of the Working Group along with responses of the Union Ministries and State/Union Territory
Governments thereon, was placed before the Committee of Secretaries.  The Committee broadly endorsed the Freedom
of Information Bill, 1997 recommended by the Working Group subject to certain modifications.  The draft Freedom of
Information Bill, 1997, given by the Working Group, was accordingly revised with the help of the Legislative
Department and placed before the Cabinet for approval.  The Cabinet, however, decided to refer the Bill to a Group of
Ministers.  Accordingly, it was placed before the Group of Ministers constituted by three successive Governments
which considered it in eight meetings held between October 28, 1997 and February 2, 2000.  The Group of Ministers
approved the Bill subject to a few changes.  In the light of the changes suggested by the Group of Ministers, the draft
Freedom of Information Bill, 1997 was further revised and was placed before the Cabinet for approval as the Freedom
of Information Bill, 2000.  The Cabinet, in its meeting held on 13 May 2000, approved the Bill.
3.3       After its approval by the Cabinet, the Freedom of Information Bill, 2000 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 25
July 2000.  It was referred to this Committee by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 14 September 2000 for examination and
report.
4.         Here, it would be pertinent to mention that the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, in its 38
th Report on the Demands for Grants (1997-1998) of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions had observed that Right to Information Act for promotion of open and transparent Government was a long
overdue measure and in the view of the Committee was quite consistent with the democratic ideals. Accordingly, the
Committee felt that there should be a full-fledged Right to Information Act, as it would go a long way in firmly
establishing the culture of accountability.   In this backdrop, the Committee recommended    as follows:
“ The Committee emphatically recommends that the refusal of a request must be appealable to an authority
whose ruling should be final and binding.  Further, as the subject ‘Right to Information’ is not specifically
provided for in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the Union through the residuary clause (97) of List I,
has the right to legislate on the subject.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry take up this matter
urgently to facilitate early enactment of the ‘Right to Information Act”. *
5.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill states that in our present democratic frame work, free flow of

information for the citizens and non-government institutions suffers from several bottlenecks including the existing
legal frame work, lack of infrastructure at the grass root levels and an attitude of secrecy within the civil service as a
result of the old frame work of rules.  The government proposes to deal with all these aspects in a phased manner so that
the Freedom of Information Act becomes a reality consistent with the objective of having a stable, honest, transparent
and efficient government.  Moreover, the proposed Bill will enable the citizens to have an access to information on a
statutory basis.  With a view to further this objective, Clause 3 of the proposed Bill specifies that subject to the
provisions of this Act, every citizen shall have right to freedom of information.  Obligation is cast upon every public
authority   under Clause 4 to provide information and to maintain all records consistent with its operational requirements
duly catalogued, indexed and published at such intervals as may be prescribed by the appropriate Government or the
competent authority.
6.         The Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions in his deposition before the Committee on
23 October 2000, traced the genesis of the Bill and gave a brief   outline of its salient features. He stated that the basic
feature of the Bill lay in Clause 3 which guaranteed that all citizens should have freedom of information subject to the
provisions of this Act.  It cast an obligation on every public authority to provide information and to make all records,
consistent with its operational requirements, duly catalogued and published at such intervals as may be prescribed by the
appropriate government or the competent authority.  He stated that the ambit of the Bill covered the two Houses of
Parliament, the State legislatures, the Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts including their
administrative offices, constitutional authorities like the Election Commission, Comptroller and Auditor General of
India and the Union Public Service Commission.

below:
(i)

(iii)               The Bill should provide for a specific date from which the Act will come into effect;
(iv)              The Bill should apply to all including organizations/associations/ parties/trusts/unions/societies private
or non-Governmental in addition to Governmental bodies and agencies;
(v)                The Bill should say that all citizens have the freedom of information instead of saying “shall have” as
this freedom is already there in the Constitution;
(vi)              The Bill should provide for the delegation of the authority of the Public Information Officer;
(vii)             The ultimate responsibility to ensure adherence to the provisions of the Bill should be vested with the
head of each public authority;
(viii)           Since the intent of the Bill is to put in place an effective procedure for enforcing the right to

(xiv)           Section 8(2) provides for a period of 25 years for releasing information which  is unconscionably  long.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
           
            The need to enact a law on right to information was recognized unanimously by the Chief Ministers Conference
on “Effective and Responsive government” held on 24
th May, 1997 at New Delhi. In its 38 th Report relating to
Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pension, the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Home Affairs recommended that the Government should take measures  for enactment of such a
legislation.
           
2. In order to make the Government more transparent and accountable to the public, the Government of India
appointed a Working Group on Right to Information and Promotion of Open and Transparent Government under the
Chairmanship of Shri H.D. Shourie. The Working Group was asked to examine the feasibility and need for either full-
fledged Right to Information Act or its introduction in a phased manner to meet the needs of open and responsive
governance and also to examine the frame work of rules with reference to the Civil Service (Conduct) Rules and manual
of Office Procedure.  The said working Group submitted its report in May, 1997 along with a draft Freedom of
Information Bill to the Government.  The Working Group also recommended suitable amendments to the Civil Service
(Conduct) Rules and the Manual of Departmental Security instructions with a view to bring them in harmony with the
proposed Bill.
           
3. The draft Bill submitted by the Working Group was subsequently deliberated by the Group of Ministers
constituted by the Central Government to ensure that free flow of information was available to the public, while, inter
alia, protecting the national interest, sovereignty and integrity of India, and friendly relations with foreign states.
           
4. The proposed Bill is in accord with both article 19 of the Constitution as well as article 19 of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights.
           
5. In our present democratic frame work, free flow of information for the citizens and non-Government
institutions suffers from several bottlenecks including the existing legal framework, lack of infrastructure at the grass
root levels and an attitude of secrecy within the Civil Service as a result of the old framework of rules.  The Government
proposes to deal with all these aspects in a phased manner so that the Freedom of Information Act became a reality

consistent with the objective of having a stable, honest, transparent and efficient Government.
 
6.  The proposed Bill will enable the citizens to have an access to information on a statutory basis. With a view
to further this objective, clause 3 of the proposed Bill specifies that subject to the provisions of this Act, every citizen
shall have right to freedom of information.  Obligation is cast upon every public authority under clause 4 to provide
information and to maintain all records consistent with its operational requirements duly catalogued, indexed and
published at such intervals as may be prescribed by the appropriate Government or the competent authority.

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM
 
1. Sub-clause 1 of clause 5 of the Bill provides for appointment of one or more officers as Public Information
Officers to deal with requests for information.  It is expected that the various agencies would be appointing some of
their existing officers as the Public Information Officers for the purpose of this Act or redesignating the publicity or
information officers as Public Information Officers.  Only in a few cases, it might be necessary to create additional posts
for this purpose.  Thus, the manpower requirement in this regard arising from the legislation is expected to be met from
within the existing sanctioned strength of the various agencies at the Central and State level, all within the existing
budget.
2. At this stage, it is not possible to give precise details of the expenditure to be incurred on material resources in
terms of computers and other office equipment required for supply of information.  However, the requirement of these
items is likely to be met by the ongoing programmes for computerization of operations in various agencies and any
additional expenditure might be offset by recovery of fees for supply of information.
3. After the proposed Bill becomes an Act, a nodal Cell for finalization of rules and instructions, guiding the
States and reporting progress to Government shall have to be set up in the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions under the Central Government.  This Cell shall consist of one Joint Secretary , two Deputy Secretaries, two
Senior Analysts and two conventional sections.  In addition, the personal staff of the above officers will also be
appointed.  An estimated recurring expenditure of Rs. 28 lakhs is likely to be incurred on the salaries of the officers and
staff in the Cell.
4. The Bill does not involve any other recurring or non-recurring expenditure.

period of two years from the commencement of this Act.  Every such order shall be laid before both Houses of
Parliament.

of India.

PART 2: OTHER IMPORTANT ISSUES THAT ARE NOT COVERED BY THE BILL
 
1.

that Right to Know is an integral part of
Right to Life and Liberty and Right to
Equality. Since the Right to Life and Liberty
and Right to Equality are available to all
persons and not restricted to only citizens,
the Right to Information should be available
to all persons.
 
 
 
Some of the advanced democracies such as Australia,
New Zealand, the U.K. etc. have already considered it fit
to make available the information not only to their citizens
but to other persons as well, such as persons residing in
that country, bodies doing business in that country etc. 
The Canadian Act, under which information was initially
available only to its citizens and permanent residents, was
amended in 1989 to include all persons who are living in
Canada.  Therefore, there may not be any objection to
grant access to information not only to Indian citizens but
to all individuals who are present in India but are not
Indian citizens.

REPORT

The Registration and Other Related Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2000, (See Annexure-I)
purports to introduce the following features in the process of public registration of documents
relating to transfer of properties:

(i) Discontinuance of the registration of documents relating to any land
situated in any part of India in a Registry of a Presidency town’ or at
Delhi’;

(ii) Compulsory affixing of photographs and finger-prints of the executants
on the documents at the time of registration;

(iii) Compulsory registration of documents in respect of transfer of
immovable properties on the basis of “agreement to sell”, “power-of-
attorney”, etc. in accordance with Power-of-Attorney Instruments; and

(iv) Computerisation of registration records.

2.0 To put the aforesaid objectives into effect, the Bill proposes amendments/deletions of
certain provisions enumerated in the following Acts:

(i) The Registration Act, 1908; (Section 16,17,30,32,49,67 and 69)
(ii) The Transfer of Property Act, 1882; (Section 53) and
(iii) The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 (Schedule-I)

मन The Bill would entail substantive changes in the Registration Act, 1908; changes in other
two legislations mentioned above are relatable to changes effected in the Registration Act and are
consequential in nature.

2.2 The genesis of proposed changes in the Registration Act emanates from the proposals of
State Governments/Union Territory Administrations for discontinudnce of registration of
documents pertaining to immovable property in any part of India in the Registry of a Presidency
town or Delhi as registration of property belonging to a State, elsewhere causes loss of revenue
(Stamp duty)’ to that particular State. Furthermore, they have expressed the view that the
afotesaid provisions have been grossly misused for illegal transfer of property (benami
transaction)

23 In view of above, most of the State Governments have suggested deletion of sub-section
(2) of Section 30 of the Registration Act, 1908, which empowers the Registrar of a Presidency
town or Delhi to receive and register any document relating to the transfer of an immovable
property situated in any part of India. So far ten States’ and three Union Territories’ have
endorsed the proposal to delete the foregoing sub-section of the Registration Act, 1908.

24 Even some States i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and
Rajasthan have gone a step further in forwarding their respective State Bills so as to do away

to the questionnaire has stated that those States and West Bengal have since omitted the said sub-
section of Section 30 of the Registration Act, 1908 with the concurrence of Union Government.

documents relating to immovable property suggests insertion of a new section i.e. 32 A in the
Registration Act, 1908.

2.5.1 The new provision i.e. 32 A as envisaged under clause 5 of the Bill also owes its genesis
to the suggestions of State Governments/Union Territories stating the misuse of immovable
property through benami transaction for hire and purchase thereof by terrorist outfits operating
from Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab and North-East. These unscrupulous elements launders money
in purchase and hire of immovable property under the cover for furthering terrorist activities or
for providing financial security to themselves and their families. The problem is acute in
Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore, Ahmedabad as well as in Punjab and Terai areas of Uttar Pradesh.

there was no uniformity in the size of photographs required to be affixed on the document of

3.0 The Committee appreciates the rationale underlying the mandatory provision of
affixing of photographs and finger-prints on registration documents. The Com mittee
understands that the requirement of finger-prints is in addition to signature/thumb
impression’. The Committee also understands that registration of documents relating to
immovable property takes place either at Registrar Office’ or at sub-Registrar Office”
under whose jurisdiction the property or any portion thereof is actually situated. The
Registrar Office is located at District Headquarters and sub-Registrar Office mostly at sub-
Division of the State. The Committee notes that it may happen that photographing facility
is not available at the village, where the property is situated but the same is available at the
place of registration i.e. sub-Divisions or District Head-quarters ofa State. Therefore, the
Committee is of the view that the difficulties to the compulsory photograph expressed by a
State are not convincing and recommends to the Union Government to go ahead with the
implementation of said provisions of the Bill after its enactment.

3.1 The Committee while taking cognizance of the suggestion of Orissa Government for
taking photographs and finger-prints of both vendor (seller) and yendee (buyer) on the
registration documents, enquired about existence of any legislation/practice in any
State/Union Territory. The Secretary, Legislative Department had cited the instance of
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi for affixing of photographs (not finger-
prints) of both seller and buyer on the registration documents and informed the practice is
in vegue in some States/ Union Territories. The Committee points out that clause 5 of the
Bill which intends to insert Section 32 A in the Registration Act, 1908, does not specifically
mention about the requirement of affixing of photographs and finger-prints of both buyer
and seller.

3.2 The Committee appreciates the compatibility of requirements of both photographs
and finger-prints on the registration documents with the specific purpose to deter the
misuse of immovable property by unscrupulous elements including terrorist outfits. To
achieve that objective in an effective manner, the Committee recommends to the
Government to examine the feasibility of making compulsory for both seller and buyer to
affix their photographs and finger-prints on the documents of registration relating to
immovable property.

4.0 The compulsory registration of documents containing contract to transfer any immovable
property deserves attention of the Government in view of the fact that property transferred under
contracts other than sale deed are not registered as a result of which evasion of payment of stamp
duty on the property takes place, which results in gross loss of revenue to the Government. This
apart, transfer of property without their proper registration also create confusion as to the claim
of title thereby creating legal hassles to the vendee (buyer). In view thereof, some States i.e.

Gujarat, Rajasthan have since amended section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 to make
registration of contract in nature of part performance compulsory.

4.1.0 It may be mentioned that property worth one hundred rupees or more are required to be
registered after which mutation takes Place but section 17 (2) (v) of the Registration Act, 1908
allows certain documents (which does not create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right,
title or interest of the value of Tupees one hundred or more in the immovable Property) to transfer
property without registration. The document of ‘agreement to sale’, in accordance with section
53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1988 fall under the section 17 (2) (v). Thus, the same is not
required to be registered.

4.1.1 Transfer of property usually takes place under “power-of-attorney”. Power-of-Attorney
is of two types 1.6. General Power-of-Attorney (GPA) and Special Power-of-Attorney (SPA).
Power of Attorney, which is otherwise known as “Letter-of-Attorney” is an instrument
authorizing another to act as one’s agent or attorney. The person in whose favour Power-of-
Attorney is executed and the person who gives the same under it are both known and indicated in
the instrument of Power-of-Attorney.

4.1.2 Though Power of Attorney empowers the attorney to sell immovable property on behalf
of the Principal (Owner) in accordance the Powers-of. ~Attomey Act, 1882 but sections 32 and 33
of the Registration Act, 1908 allow the attorney to present documents on behalf of the Principal
for registration at the registration office. Registration of property transferred under Power of
Attorney is not mandatory in view of the provisions laid down in section 53 A of the Transfer of
Property Act, 1882 (popularly known as Power of Attorney deals). Thus, Power-of-Attorney
does not transfer any title to the ‘Property to any other person nor is it compulsory to registerthe
same. But even without registration, the same is a valid document.

4.1.3 Section 53 A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 speaks about “part-performance of
contract”. In accordance with part-performance of contracts property sold through the instrument
of contracts may not be registered but receive legal protection in accordance ‘with “Part-II-
Specific Performance of Contracts” of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

4.2.0 Sale and purchase under part-performance of contracts had started way back in 1972,
when the Delhi Land (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972 came into effect. The epicenter of
transfer of property under the Part-performance of contracts was the National Capital Territory of.
Delhi itself. The Delhi Land (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972, came into force with effect
from 14 June 1972 as a sequel to Delhi Development Act, 1957 for the development of Delhi in
accordance with Master Plan prepared therefor, In accordance with the Delhi Development Act,
1957, large scaie acquisition of lands was made under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for
planned development of Delhi, which put certain restrictions on private colonization activity but
could not stop registration of sales of private lands as that was legally permissible at that time.
The Delhi Land (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972 put restriction on transfer of land which
have been acquired by the Central Government or in respect of which acquisition proceedings
have been initiated by the Government. Thus, it became legally not permissible to enter into
regular deeds of sale which could be got registered. In other words, registration of property, other
than developed by the Government, in Delhi, ceased to exist,

4.2.1 In the aftermath of enactment of the Delhi Land (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972,
Properties were transferred through the deeds in nature of agreement to sell which has protection
of section 53 A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Thus, began the phase of the transfer of
property without registration.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE

The Committee appreciates the rationale underlying the mandatory provision of
affixing of photographs and finger-prints on registration documents. The
Committee understands that the requirement of finger-prints is in addition to
signature/thumb impression. The Committee also understands that registration of
documents relating to immovable property takes place either at Registrar Office or
at sub-Registrar Office under whose jurisdiction the property or any portion
thereof is actually situated. The Registrar Office is located at District Headquarters
and sub-Registrar Office mostly at sub-Division of the State. The Committee notes
that it may happen that photographing facility is not available at the village, where
the property is situated but the same is available at the place of registration i.e. sub-
Divisions or District Head-quarters of a State. Therefore, the Committee is of the
view that the difficulties to the compulsory photograph expressed by a State are not
convincing and recommends to the Union Government to go ahead with the
implementation of said provisions of the Bill after its enactment.

Clause 2

3.0 The clause intended to insert new Section 16A after section 16 in the Registration Act,
1908 for keeping the. books for maintaining documents of registration as provided in sub-section
(1) of Section 16 of the said Act, in computer floppies or diskettes or in any other electronic form
in the manner and subject to the safeguards prescribed by the Inspector General of Registration
in the State.

3.1 The Committee appreciated the idea of keeping registration records in electronic form, in
addition to the traditional methods. But the Committee was unhappy with the sorry state of
affairs in most of the registries located at Sub-Divisional levels and felt that there was an utmost
need for their proper up-keeping.

3.2 The Committee was given to understand that the life of floopy, diskette should be taken
into account and necessary care should be taken to transfer the records to other floopy, diskette
well in advance so as to check loss of data therefrom.

3.3. The Committee was further given to understand that State Governments provided fire-proof

boxes to the office of every Registrar for safe custody of the registration records and the State
Government ensured safe custody of the records in sub-Districts in accordance with sub-section
(3) of Section 16 of the Registration Act, 1908. In that context, the Committee was also aware of
the fact that the transfer of the entries in indexes Nos. I, II and III by the sub-Registrar to
Registrar was no more in existence.

3.4 The Committee expressed apprehension about the safety of registry records at the sub-
Registrar Office and recommended that provisions may be made in the Act to make it mandatory
for the States to supply fireproof boxes to each registration offices in sub-Districts in that State

Clause §

5.0 The clause made it compulsory for every person presenting any documents relating to
transfer of property at the Registration Office to affix his/her passport size photograph and finger-
prints to the documents of registration.

5.1 The Committee appreciated the rationale underlying the mandatory provision of affixing
of photographs and finger-prints on registration documents. The Committee was given to
understand that the requirement of finger-prints was in addition to signature/thumb impression.
The Committee also understood that registration of documents relating to immovable property
took place either at Registrar Office or at sub-Registrar Office under whose jurisdiction the
property or any portion thereof was actually situated. The Registrar Office was located at District
Headquarters and sub-Registrar Office mostly at sub-Division of the State. The Committee noted
that it may happen that photographing facility was not available at the village, where the property
was situated but the same was available at the place of registration i.e. sub-Divisions or District
Head-quarters of a State. Therefore, the Committee was of the view that the difficulties to the
compulsory photograph expressed by a State were not convincing and recommended to the
Union Government to go ahead with the implementation of said provisions of the Bill after its
enactment.

5.2 The Committee while taking cognizance of the suggestion of Orissa Government for
taking photographs and finger-prints of both vendor (seller) and vendee (buyer) on the
registration documents, enquired about existence of any legislation/practice in any State/Union
Territory. The Secretary, Legislative Department had cited the instance of Government of
National Capital Territory of Delhi for affixing of photographs (not finger-prints) of both seller
and buyer on the registration documents and informed the practice was in vogue in some States/
Union Territories. The Committee pointed out that clause 5 of the Bill which intended to insert
Section 32A in the Registration Act, 1908, did not specifically mention about the requirement of
affixing of photographs and finger-prints of both buyer and seller.

53 The Committee appreciated the compatibility of requirements of both photographs and
finger-prints on the registration documents with the specific purpose to deter the misuse of
immovable property by unscrupulous elements including terrorist outfits. To achieve that
objective in an effective manner, the Committee recommended to the Government to examine
the feasibility of making compulsory for both seller and buyer to affix their photographs and
finger-prints on the documents of registration relating to immovable property.

5.4 The Committee adopted the clause subject to the observations/recommendations above.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS

The Registration Act, 1908 was enacted to consolidate the law relating to the regis-
tration of documents. The Conference of Chief Ministers and Finance Ministers of States and
Union territories convened by the Union Finance Minister held on the 14th September, 1998 at
New Delhi, inter alia, arrived at the following conclusions, namely:-

(i) sub-section (2) of section 30 of the Registration Act, 1908 should be repealed;
(ii) registration of general power of attorney which is in the nature of a contract to sell
immovable property be made compulsory and consequential amendments be made in the

Registration Act, 1908, the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899:

(iii) to make affixing of the photograph and finger prints of the executants compulsory at
the time of registration of documents;

(iv) to make an enabling provision for computerisation of registration records.
2. Based on the above conclusions arrived at the said Conference, it is proposed-

(i) to insert a new sub-section (1A) in section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 for
making registration of the documents containing contracts to transfer for consideration
any immovable property compulsory for the purpose of section 53A of the Transfer of
Property Act, 1882 and for consequential amendments in section 56 of the said Act,
section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Schedule I to the Stamp Act, 1899;

(ii) to omit sub-section (2) of section 30 and section 67 of the Registration Act, 1908;

(iii) to insert new section 16A in the Registration Act, 1908 to enable the State
Governments to computerise registration records;

(iv) to insert new section 32A to make affixing of the photographs and finger-prints on
the documents compulsory at the time of registration

3. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

MINUTES OF THE CONFERENCE OF
THE CHIEF MINISTERS/FINANCE MINISTERS OF STATES AND UTs
HELD ON 14.09.1998 AT VIGYAN BHAWAN

The Conference of the Chief Minister/Finance Ministers of States and Union Territories
convened by the Union Finance Minister was held on 14th September, 1998 at New Delhi. Chief
Ministers of West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Haryana, Orissa, Meghalaya, Manipur and
Nagaland, Deputy Chief Ministers of Rajasthan and Karnataka and Finance Ministers of other
States and UTs attended. The conference was also attended by Minister of State for Finance Shri
K.M.R. Janarthanan, Prof. Raja J. Chelliah and senior officers of the Union Government, States
and Union Territories.

2 Minister of State for Finance delivered his welcome address to the delegates Finance
Minister of India delivered his inaugural address. Subseqeuntly, the Special Secretary (Banking)
introduced the subject of NBFCs and Secretary (Revenue) introduced the agenda items relating to
the revenue department.

PHASING OUT OF CST AND STAGE OF INTRODUCTION OF VAT BY STATE
GOVERNMENT.

| State Governments expressed varying points of view on introduction of VAT. While
most of the States favoured the introduction VAT simultaneously, some states wanted a cautious
approach. Chief Minister of Orissa suggested that a clear view and an in-depth examination of
all pros and cons of introduction of VAT in the whole country needs to be deliberated. He
pointed out that any hasty introduction of VAT may lead to regressive taxation and loss of
revenue to the States. Dy. Chief Minister of Rajasthan requested Union Govt. to assure the states
that the Union Government will step-in, in case of any loss of revenue to the States.in the event of
introduction of VAT. Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh and Finance Ministers of Karnataka and
Rajasthan suggested that preliminary steps to create an atmosphere conducive to introduction of
VAT must be taken by all the State Govts. Rationalization of tax structure and reduction in input
tax is a pre-requisite. It was generally agreed that phased introduction of VAT should be
simultaneous in all the States at least in a zone.

4. There was total agreement that there was a need for training, dissemination of
information on VAT to officials, traders, dealers and the public at large. Methods and procedures
of VAT and strategies for preventing tax evasion should be part of the training. Computerization
of tax departments and modernization of information system in tax administration is very
important. Union Finance Minister agreed to the views expressed by the States and assured that
the Centre would do its bit in supporting the states in their training programme. A method to
compensate the States in case of loss of revenue during the transition period will also be worked

out.
PHASED REDUCTION IN CST
Sy A large number of States were agreeable to the reduction of rates of CST in a phased

manner However, Chief Minister of Orissa, Haryana and West Bengal expressed their

47


reservations as reduction in CST would lead to loss of revenue. A method must be found for
compensating the States if CST has to be reduced and subsequently abolished,

FIXING OF UNIFORM FLOOR RATES

6 Many State Governments suggested that the Union Govt. may fix uniform floor rates for
all the commodities similar to the tax rates fixed for “declared goods”. Chief Minister of West
Bengal suggested that the States in the North Zone at least may take the lead by agreeing to floor
Fates on major items. While Finance Ministers of Assam and Karnataka informed that they had
taken steps to rationalize the tax structure in their States, the neighboring States must also take
initiatives for harmonization and rationalization of taxes. It was generally agreed that the band of
rates suggested by the Committee of State Finance Ministers on Sales Tax reforms should be
accepted

7 All the State Governments recognized the danger to trade and commerce as a result of the
rate wars between States. Chief Minister of West Bengal pointed out that there is an urgent need
that sales tax rates in all the states should gravitate towards these floor rates for a stable economic
environment.

TAX INCENTITIVES

8 Most of the Chief Ministers and Finance Ministers of the States agreed with the views
expressed that competition between States to offer tax incentives to industries has led to 2
shrinking in the revenue base of the States. It is also leading to lopsided industrial development
in the country, revenue leakages and industrial indiscipline. A consensus emerged that the States
should gradually reduce these incentives so that additional resources generated may be invested
in development of infrastructure. Chief Minister of Haryana informed the House that the State
was taking a lead in reduction of ad hoc incentives to industry. Chief Minister of West Benga!
appealed for ending this unproductive and self defeating competition amongst the States and
wanted that all the States may discontinue these schemes at least from 1.4.99. However, Chief
Minister of Nagaland was of the view that for promoting industrial development, some incentives
are required in the North-Eastern States. Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh was also of the view
that since the State is land locked, some incentives have to be offered to attract industry. Chief
Minister of Orissa and Finance Minister of Gujarat were in favour of a nationally accepted tax
policy on industrial incentives.

ABORGATION OF TAX RENTAL ARRANGEMENT FOR SUGAR, TOBBACCO AND
TEXTILE.

9. Most of the States desired that additional excise duty on these three items must be
scrapped. West Bengal, Assam, Kerala and Karnataka emphasized that these three items should
be removed from the list of declared goods and the States must be allowed to tax them to
augment their revenue base. They also suggested’ that once floor rates are agreed between the
States, the restriction imposed by Section 15 of the CST Act should be removed and States
allowed to tax the declared goods. They also suggested that the definition of dealer should also
include works contract, lessors and transaction under hire purchase scheme. The Finance
Minister of Gujarat suggested that high sea sales should be allowed to be taxed by the State
Govts. Section 8(5) included in the CST Act, 1956 should be deleted as it is leading to trade
diversion. Finance Minister of Kerala complained about bogus booking of goods by Railways
leading to tax evasion and requested the Union Govt. to take steps to limit such bogus booking of
goods by Railways. There was a general consensus that the Centre should set up a fund to

48



counter any possible revenue loss to the States owing to reduction in CST rates, introduction of
floor rates and introduction of VAT. They also suggested that unregistered dealers should also be
taxed in inter-State sales to augment resources of the States. They also wanted the simplification
of Tax Laws to facilitate the State Governments in taxing selected services. This would offset
any revenue loss that the State may incur due to tax rationalization.

10. There was a general demand from the States for introduction of consignment tax.
However, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, J & K and some North Eastern States were of the
view that the introduction of the consignment tax will benefit only the developed States at the
cost of the developing States. Since there was no general agreement regarding consignment tax,
discussion was p9ostponed for the next conference.

ll. All the State Govts. Agreed that computerization of sales tax administration should be the
national goal and it is absolutely essential to prescribe standard in the areas of data definition,
allotment of identification numbers to the dealers and establishment of a system for exchange of
data between the States.

STAMP DUTY REFORMS

2s Chief Ministers/Finance Ministers of States and UTs, in general welcomed the
recommendation contained in the report of the Committee of State Finance Ministers on Stamp
Duty Reforms. Many State Governments informed that a number of recommendations of the
Committee have already been implemented in their respective States. The Chief Minster of
Haryana was, however, not in favour of reduction in Stamp Duty rates as it would adversely
affect the resource mobilization of States. He informed that in Haryana, nearly 90 per cent of the
revenue comes from Stamp Duty on conveyance instruments. The Finance Minister of Bihar was
also not in favour of uniform rates although he agreed that the rate of Stamp duty should be more
on larger property and there should be a slab system of Stamp Duty rates.

13; Most of the State Governments agreed to the widening of definition of “conveyance” to
cover transfer on power of attorney and agreement of sale which was leading to evasion of Stamp
Duty. They requested to widening of the definition of Power of Attorney to cover transfer of
property under the garb of GPA and/or an agreement sale. The Chief Minister, Haryana
suggested prescribing a validity period of two years on Power of Attorney. Finance Minister of
Gujarat said that lakhs of property are transferred on Power of Attorney or on the basis of a
collusive court decree, which again causes loss of revenue to the states. Chief Minister of
Haryana said that people get collusive consent decrees from civil courts .elating to transfer of
immovable property for evading Stamp Duty and Registration Fee. He said that it is, therefore,
necessary to make registration of such collusive decrees compulsory.

14. Regarding procedural simplification in implementation of Indian Stamp Act, 1899, State
Governments agreed with the initiative taken so far. It was suggested that Rules should be
simplified and the requirement of taking NOC from a number of Departments for Registration
should be done away with. The states of Himachal Pradesh and Karnataka said that non-
availability of stamp papers of small denomination has been a problem and, therefore, franking
machines are being used in Karnataka, other States may also introduce it. Himachal Pradesh
suggested that the Stamp Act can be amended to make it possible to execute documents on simple

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Eightieth Report of the Committee on the Code of Civil Procedure(Amendment) Bill, 2000*.
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred ** the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on December 22, 2000 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.0       The Committee considered the Bill in five sittings held on 11 June, 11 & 12 July, 17 October and 2 November, 2001.
3.1       The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs in its sitting held on 11 June 2001.
3.2       In its sittings held on 11 & 12 July, 2001, the Committee heard  Chairman and Members of Bar Council of India, President of Supreme Court  Bar Association and Former Judge of  High Court of Delhi , respectively,  on the various provisions of the Bill.
3.3       In its sitting held on 17 October 2001, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
3.4       The Committee considered the draft Report in its sitting held on 2 November 2001 and adopted the same.  It also decided that the evidence tendered before the Committee may be laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament.
4.0       In course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill and took note of the recommendations of various Law Commissions,  replies to queries raised by the Members on the Bill in the meetings, submitted by the Legislative Department and suggestions/observations tendered by  the witnesses.
5.                  For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.     
 
NEW DELHI;
 November 2, 2001
PRANAB MUKHERJEE
 Chairman
               Committee on Home Affairs
 
* Bill Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II, Section-2, dated 22 December, 2000.
** Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, No.38599 dated 4 January 2001.
 
 
REPORT
 
            The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000 (See Annexure-I) seeks to amend Code of the Civil Procedure, 1908 (hereinafter referred as Code) and the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.
2.0       The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 which came into force w.e.f. 1 January, 1909 contains Laws relating to the procedure in suit and civil proceeding in India except in the case of State of Jammu and Kashmir, Nagaland, Tribal areas of Assam and certain other areas.12.1.0    The code is mainly divided into two parts :-
(i)         Sections – (158 Sections divided under 21 Parts)
(ii)
                Orders & Rules -  (51 Orders under the First Schedule of the Code)
 
2.1.1    Sections contain main principles while the detailed procedures with regard to matters dealt with by the Sections are specified in Orders and Rules.
2.2.0    The Code of Civil Procedure, being in List-III-Concurrent List2 in Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, is amenable    to amendments by the Acts of both Union and State Legislatures3.  Furthermore, the High Courts are also empowered to amend, by rule, the Code. It may be highlighted that the Union/State Legislatures can amend both Sections and Orders of the Code whereas the High Courts can bring in amendments to the Orders only.4
2.2.1    The Code has been amended innumerable times by the Acts of Union/State Legislatures. So far the Code has been amended sixty-six times approximately by Parliament.
2.3.0    The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 (See Annexure-II) was enacted by Parliament and assented to by the President on 30 December, 19995
 but was not brought into force due to strong opposition to the same from various quarters.
2.3.1    The aforesaid Act was enacted on the basis of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997  which was introduced as an official Bill in the Rajya Sabha on 14 August, 1997.
2.3.2    The Bill was introduced to bring in comprehensive changes in the Code to expedite the disposal of civil suits and proceedings so as to ensure that justice was not delayed.
2.3.3    The CPC (Amendment) Bill, 1997 was referred to this Committee on 19 August, 1997 for examination and report. The Committee, in turn, had presented its Forty-ninth Report on the Bill to Parliament on 17 December, 1998.
2.3.4    The Committee had considered the thirty six clauses contained in the Bill and recommended changes in six clauses (clause Nos.1,9, 26, 29, 33 and 34) and recommended no changes in twenty eight clauses (clause Nos. 2 to 8, 10 to 25, 27, 28, 32 and 35) and recommended for dropping of two clauses (clause Nos. 31 and 36).
2.3.5    Almost all the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Report referred above were accepted by the Government and was, accordingly, reflected in the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999.  In effect, the CPC (Amendment) Act had thirty four Sections after dropping two clauses from the CPC (Amendment) Bill, 1997.
2.4.0    The amendments to the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 have been necessitated due to numerous representations from Members of Parliament, members of the Bar, Bar Councils, individuals and other quarters like Law Commission of India.
2.4.1    The Law Commission of India under the Chairmanship of  Shri  Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy presented its One Hundred Sixty-third Report  on 13 November 1998 wherein it had suggested in great detail a re-look  at some of  the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill 1997 (Clause Nos 2,7, 10 to 20, 23, 24, 26 to 28 and 30 to 32).  The Ministry has admitted that the recommendations of Law Commission on the aforesaid Bill could not be taken  into account while enacting the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.
 2.4.2   The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000 contains seventeen clauses out of which there are four altogether new clauses in addition to commencement clauses i.e. clause 1, clause 16 which makes consequential amendments and clause 17 which is repeal and saving clause.  The remaining ten clauses of the said Bill intents to either substitute or amend the provisions of the 1999 Act.
2.4.3
        The proposals contained  in the Bill, 2000 can  be classified broadly into two groups:-
(a)    Amendment to the Code of Civil Procedure ,  1908
(b)   Amendment to the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999
 
2.4.4    Clauses of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000 and the relevant provisions of the Act, 1999 and Code which are intended to be amended by the Bill are presented in the accompanying table.

(A) NEW AMENDMENTS IN THE CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE, 1908
2.5.0    Amongst the seven proposed new amendments in the Code as contained in the Bill, three are based on the recommendations contained in the Law Commission’s Reports which are as below:-
(i)
                  Clause 2 based on One Hundred Forty-fourth Report;
(ii)                Clause 3 based on Fifty-fourth Report; and
(iii)               Clause 14 based on One Hundred Thirty-ninth Report.
 
The remaining Clauses are 1, 13, 16 and 17 of the Bill.
2.5.1    In addition to the above seven new amendments, one is partially new as it seeks to amend both the Code and the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 i.e. clause 12 of the Bill:-
Sub clause (a) of the clause amends rule 2 of Order XVIII of the Code, and the sub-clause  (b) of the clause of the Bill amends Section 27 of the 1999 Act i.e. rule 4 of Order XVIII of the Code.
The clause has been analysed in great detail in para No. 2.22.0 of the Report.
 2.6.0.  Clause 2 intends to incorporate a clarification under Section 39  - “Transfer of decree” - of the Code which says that the court cannot execute a decree against a person or property outside the local limits of its jurisdiction. 
2.7.0    Clause 3 proposes to insert a new sub-section to Section 64 - “ Private alienation  of Property after attachment to be void” - of the Code.  This would, in effect, resolve the conflict of decisions with a view to clarifying that a transfer or delivery of property, etc. in pursuance of any contract entered into and registered before the attachment shall not become void.
