2.8.0    Clause 13 amends sub-rule (1) of rule 1 of Order XX to fix time limit for pronouncement of a judgement as it is felt that reserved judgements should be delivered within a reasonable time.  It is therefore proposed that the courts shall make an endeavour to pronounce a judgement within thirty days from the date on which the hearing of the case is concluded.  Where it is not practicable to do so on the ground of exceptional and extraordinary circumstances of the case, the court shall pronounce the judgement ordinarily within sixty days from the date on which hearing was concluded.
2.9.0    Clause 14 has two parts – The first part of the clause inserts an explanation to sub-rule  (5)  of rule 32 of Order XXI with a view to removing doubts as to whether  the expression  The act required to be done  covers only mandatory injunction or prohibitory injunction or both.
2.9.1    It is pertinent to explain that rule 32  of  Order XXI  provides  for punishment  for disobedience to an injunction  issued by the Court.  Sub-rule  (5) of rule 32 provides that where a decree for specific performance of a contract or for an injunction has not been obeyed, the Court may direct that the act required to be done may be done  by the  decree  holder or some other person appointed by the Court at the cost of judgment debtor.
2.9.2    Now the explanation  to be inserted in the aforesaid rule would   imply that the act required to be done would cover both prohibitory as well as mandatory injunction.
2.9.3    The second part of  Clause 14 seeks to amend rule 92 of Order XXI  to bring congruity between  article 127 of Limitation Act, 1963 and  sub-rule (2) of rule 92 of Order XXI. 
2.9.4    It may be mentioned that initially an application   to set aside   an execution sale  (which is required   to be accompanied by deposit of requisite amount in the Court, to the decree holder by the judgment debtor) was thirty days.  The period of thirty days is insufficient to enable the judgment debtor to arrange for requisite fund having regard to the fact that Banks usually take more than thirty days to sanction loans and advances. Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963 was amended in 1976 and time for making application stood increased to sixty days from thirty days.
2.9.5    The Law Commission in its One Hundred Thirty-ninth Report (1991) [Chapter II Para 3.2)] has pointed out that while preparing the Bill for amendment of Limitation Act, 1963, amendment to corresponding provision in the CPC i.e. sub-rule (2) of rule 92 of Order XXI escaped the notice of draftsmen inadvertently.  The net position is that while time for making application is sixty days whereas the time for making deposit (supposed to accompany the application) remains unaltered as thirty days. Now the amendment in the CPC through the said clause would increase the period for making deposit to sixty days so as to establish congruity between Limitation Act and the CPC.
B. AMENDMENT TO THE CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE (AMENDMENT)   ACT, 1999
2.10.0  Letters Patent Appeal (LPA):  Clause 4 of the Bill amends Section 100 A of Code as substituted by Section 10 of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 which is relating to Letters Patent Appeal (LPA).
2.10.1  Certain High Courts including chartered High Courts have been empowered to entertain appeals against decree or order of its single Judge to Division Bench under Letters Patent Appeal (LPA).  Under the scheme of LPA, appeal can be preferred against the decree or order of a single Judge in two cases:
(i)                  original jurisdiction (Section 96 of the Code); and
(ii)                Extra-ordinary jurisdiction (Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution).
2.10.2  To check appeal against the decree pronounced in the exercise of original power of the High Court as permissible under Section 96 of the Code, the CPC wasamended way back in February 1976 by inserting a new Section (100A) under the heading of “Appeals from appellate decree”.
2.10.3  By the Act of 46 of 1999, Section 100A was substituted again in order to prohibit second appeal from its original decree along with extra-ordinary decree to Division Bench.
2.10.4  The above provision in the Act is same as clause 10 of the CPC (Amendment) Bill, 1997 and introduced in order to implement the recommendations of Justice V.S. Malimath Committee.  The Committee in its Forty-ninth Report had also adopted the clause.
2.10.5  By virtue of 1999 Amendment Act, the Letters Patent Appeal against the judgement and decree of a single Judge made in the appeal preferred under Section 96 of the Code as well as the Letters Patent Appeal preferred against the judgement and order of a single judge in an application made under Articles  226 and 227 of the Constitution was sought to be done away with altogether.
2.10.6  The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report (vide para 2.6.1) has observed that there is strong and uniform opposition from the members of the Bench and the Bar that abolition of Letters Patent Appeal against the judgement of a single judge made on an application under Article 226 would add enormously to the burden of the Supreme Court because the only remedy would then be available to approach the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.
2.10.7  The Law Commission has pointed out that appeal lie straight against the original decree of Single Judge of Allahabad High Court to the Supreme Court under Article 226 since 19626 and has burdened the Supreme Court.
2.10.8  As regards Article 227 of the Constitution, the practice is not uniform.  In some States appeal under Article 227 is treated at par with an application under Article 226, thereby has the scope of second appeal.
2.10.9  The Law Commission in the said Report (para 2.8.3) had recommended strongly against the abolition of LPA against the judgement pronounced by single judge on an application made under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution.
2.10.10  As regards the abolition of LPA against the judgement of a single Judge made in an appeal against decree (under Section 96 of the Code) which was taken away in 1976, the Commission observed that it should be exercised in the following restricted manner:
(i)                  appeal should be against final  decree/judgement not interlocutory/interim order; and
(ii)                the appeal in the suit should involve substantial question of law on the lines of Section 100 of the Code.
 
2.10.11   The Government has introduced the CPC (Amendment) Bill, 2000 to restore Section 100 A to its pre-1999 position not pre-1976 position.
2.10.12     The Bar Council of India (BCI) has suggested to restore LPA to its pre-1976 position (decree pronounced in exercise of both original as well as extra-ordinary jurisdiction)
2.10.13     The Legislative Department has commented that it would be a retrogative step and thus is not acceptable.
2.10.14      The Committee agrees with the comments of the Legislative Department.
2.10.15     Appeal and Revision: Clause 5 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 11 of the  Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 so as to bring some desirable  changes in Section 102 of the Code.
2.10.16    Section 102 of the Code, before 1999 amendments, prohibits second appeal in certain cases which satisfies the following two conditions:-
(i)
                  the suit is of a nature cognizable by a court of small cause; and
(ii)                the value of the subject matter of the suit does not exceed three thousand rupees.
 
The 1999 Act eliminated the requirement at (i) supra and increased the valuation of subject matter of the suit mentioned at (ii) supra from rupees three thousand to twenty-five thousand  (in view of depreciation in the value of money).  The net position of Section 102 after   1999 amendment  is  that no second appeal in all cases where the value  of subject matter of the suit does not exceed rupees twenty five thousand. 
2.10.17     The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third  Report  has suggested that restriction as to the nature and character of the suit be dropped as it felt that the Section 102 might entail grave injustice to suit for mere permanent injunctions which are valued at low figures unrelated to the subject-matter of the suit.
2.10.18    Thus clause 5 of the Bill intends to substitute Section 102 of the Code  in a way to confine its application to money suit only, the reason being that money suits are comparatively simple suits and Order XXXVII of the Code provides its summary procedure.
2.11     There was no opposition from any quarter to the aforesaid provision of the Bill.
2.12.0  Issue and Service of Summons :        Clause 6 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 which is related to the provision relating to issue and service of summons laid down inorder V of the Code.  The Clause has two parts and amend clause 15(i) and  (ii) which substitute rules 1 and 9 of Order V, respectively.
2.12.1  Rule 1 of Order V of the Code as stood amended by 1999 Amendment Act empowers  the Court to issue to the defendant  summons to appear and answer the claim on a day to be specified therein, after the institutions of suit.  The following are the main features of the said rule:-
(a)
    The date of appearance of defendant to answer the claim is within thirty  days from the day of the institution of suit;
(b)   Both the appearance and filing of written statement by the defendant are on the same day; and
(c)    In case of failure on the part of defendant to file written statement on the date specified, he shall be allowed by the court to file the same on later day which shall not be beyond thirty days from the date of service of summons on the defendant.
 
The net position is that the date fixed for appearance shall never be beyond thirty days from the institution of suit and the date for filing written defence can never be beyond thirty days from the date of service of summons.
2.13.    The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report has observed that it is necessary to take into account the practical  problem and the realities  of the situation  while  fixing mandatory time limits.  Some of the suits are complicated in nature which call for good amount of preparation by the defendant before filing his defence.  Further, where Government is a defendant, it is not as prompt as a private party in filing the written statement due to the requirement of coordination and internal correspondence  between one Department and the other.  Members of the Bar, who participated  in the conference arranged by Law Commission on the issue, opposed any sort of time limits whereas the members  of the Bench supported the time limits.  However, the members of the Bench felt that the time
limit set by the amendment was unrealistic and might result in failure of justice in some cases.  However, there was consensus that the time limit for thirty days from the date of institution of suit  to be substituted by sixty days from the institution of suit.  In case of failure to file written statement  within thirty days from the date of summons on defendant, the period may be extended to ninety days from the date on which the period of 60 days expires, which has also been recommended by Law Commission.
2.14     Now clause 6 (i) intends to make a provision that the defendant would be required to file written statement in his defence within  thirty days from the date of service of summons  but this period could be extended upto ninety days from the date  summons by the court for reasons to be recorded.
2.15     Here the Law Commission’s recommendation has not been accepted in toto by the Government.  Law Commission recommended to increase the time limit from appearance of defendant from thirty days to sixty days from the date of institution of suit, whereas period of thirty days provided by 1999 Act remains unaltered in the present Bill.  Further-more, the maximum period for submitting written statement recommended by  the Law Commission was 150 days from the date of institution of suit whereas the Bill makes provision  of 90 days from the date of summons.
2.16     There is no opposition to reasonableness of time limit envisaged by the Bill by any of the witnesses and thus appears to appropriate.
2.17.0  Service of Summons :Clause 6 (ii) substitutes the scheme for service of summons envisaged in Section 15 (ii) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 which, is turn,  had amended  rule 9 of Order V.
2.17.1  The Code as stood amended by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999  envisages the following scheme to serve summons on the defendant:
(a)
    The Court  shall hand over the summons to the plaintiff or his agent, who shall arrange  to serve it  within  two days  from the delivery of summons in the manner provided in (b) below.
(b)   The plaintiff or his agent has to serve the summons on the defendant by
 
(i)                  registered post acknowledgement due; or
(ii)                speed post; or
(iii)               approved courier service; or
(iv)              fax message; or
(v)                Electronic mail service; or
(vi)              other means prescribed by the High Court by rules.
 
The actual mode to be adopted out of (i) to (vi) above, has to be specified by the court. [Vide sub-rule (1) of Rule 9)]
(c)    In addition, the court may also direct service of summon through the proper officer of the court (process server ) (vide rule 9A of order V).
Thus sub-rule (1) of Rule 9 of Order V places the duty of serving summons upon the plaintiff within two days.
2.17.2  The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report has pointed out that supplementary means of serving summons specified in sub-rule (1) of rule of 9 of Order V was treated as welcome step but there was uniform opposition both from the members of the Bar and the Bench to the proposal for serving summon by the plaintiff or his agent on defendant.  It was submitted that summons should be sent in any of the modes specified in sub-rule (1) of rule  of 9, by the court itself, though at the expense of the plaintiff since the present scheme may give room to mischief and fraud.
2.17.3  The Law Commission therein had suggested to make it mandatory or obligatory on the court to service summons through normal mode of delivery of summons i.e. process server and registered post acknowledgement due, in addition to mordern means of transmission at the expense of plaintiff.  Further, the service of summons through plaintiff may be in addition to above method.
2.17.4  The Bill as envisaged under clause 6(ii) contains the following features:
(i)   summons shall be delivered by the process server or such other means approved by the registry of court, itself at the expense of plaintiff.  In addition, summons can also given to the plaintiff for service on defendant
(ii)  no time limit for servicing summon by the court/plaintiff is prescribed (in 1999 Act the period was 2 days for plaintiff).
(iii) panel of courier agencies can be prepared by High Courts or the District Judge
(in 1999 Act it was High Court only).
2.17.5  The Bar Council of India has no objection to the modern means of transmission of summons.  But the President of Supreme Court Bar Association had expressed apprehension about the reliability of fax message and was against privatisation of judicial service by sending summons through courier who are private agencies and may lead to corruption.  He suggested that mode of transmission of summons should be conjuctive not disjunctive.  There must be at least two/three modes of sending summons. If one fails the other would succeed. 
2.17.6  The Committee was of the view that the system of sending summons through process server in lower courts particularly Munsiff Court has been unsatisfactory and felt the need for introduction modern means of transmission for sending summons.  It also  felt that the there should be at least two additional fast means of sending summons to ensure its service on defendant.
2.17.7  As regards courier agencies, the Committee wanted to know how the private parties could be prevented from doing any mischief with the service of summons. The Secretary, Legislative Department  had informed the Committee that the courier agencies were accountable to the court; if they serve wrong document or give wrong statement with regard to failure to deliver the summons, they would be punishable under the Indian Penal Code.
2.17.8  The Department has further informed the Committee that in the State of Tamil Nadu plaintiff can serve summons on defendant, by a way of State amendment to Section 19 A of Order V. The Department do not find merit in the suggestion for introduction of conjunctive mode of serving summons.
2.18.0  Amendment of Pleading:  Clause 7 of the Bill, 2000 seeks to amend Section 16(iii) of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 in order to restore rules 17 & 18 of Order VI in a new form.
2.18.1  Rules 17 & 18 of Order VI stood omitted with the enactment of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 to get expeditious trial of cases.
2.18.2  The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report has recommended to restrict the amendment to plaint to the direction of court to the effect that the amendment is necessitated (i) by change in law subsequent to the framing of the issues (ii) on account of any fact coming to the knowledge of applicant after framing of the issue which could not have been discovered by him with due diligence before framing the issue, once the trial commences.  It has been pointed out that it has the support of members of the Bench.
2.18.3  The provision contained in clause 7 of the Bill intends to implement the above recommendation in toto.  The Bar Council of India has suggested to restore rule 17 along with relatable rule 18.  Bar Council of India has averred that there is utmost necessity to restore the same for the following reasons:
(i)
                  plaint is mostly drafted in hurry
(ii)                the poor and illiterate litigants are mostly incapable of giving factual position at the time of filing case
 
Thus the clause should be restored with a proviso:
“that no application for amendment shall be allowed after trial has commenced unless the court comes to the conclusion that inspite of due diligence the party could not have raised the same matter”.
2.18.4  The Chairman of Bar Council of India has informed the Committee that there is no single dissenting voice in the Bar for the same.
 2.18.5The other witnesses, Shri A.B. Rohtagi, Ex-Judge, Delhi High Court and  Shri Kapil Sibal, President, Supreme Court Bar Association has appealed to the Committee for restoration of rules 17 & 18 of Order VI.  The President of Supreme Court Bar Association in addition to his above suggestion, also suggested that application for amendment under rule 17 of order VI must be decided within thirty days.
2.18.6  The suggestion of witnesses was unacceptable to the Legislative Department as that would give too much liberty and discretion to the courts thereby delay the trial.
2.18.7  The Committee agreed to the proviso suggested by Bar Council of India (BCI) to rule 17 of Order VI.
2.19.0  Procedure for admitting plaints:Clause 8 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 17 of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 which in turn, has amended rules 9, 11, 14 and 18 of Order VII.
2.19.1  The relevant rules as modified by 1999 Act vis-a-vis amendments thereto by 2000 Bill are as below:
(a)
                                                    Requirement two days’ time for plaintiff to present copies of plaint alongwith requisite fees for service of summons on the defendants [sub-rule (3) of rule 9]. 
The two days period in the aforesaid rule is proposed to be substituted by seven days [Clause 8(i) of the Bill].
(b)                                                   Sub-rule (f) of rule 11 of Order VII is being amended to bring congruity with the amendment suggested in clause 6 of the Bill.
(c)                                                    Sub-rule (3) of rule 14 of Order VII as modified by the 1999 amendment says that where a document or a copy thereof is not available with the plaint, it shall not be received in evidence on behalf of the plaintiff at the hearing of the suit.  A plaintiff is obliged to produce a document or a copy thereof on the basis of which he files suit. 
Now as per the provision of the Bill, a document which was not attached to the plaint at time of filing of suit can be produced in support of evidence with the leave of the court.
2.19.2  In the pursuance of Law Commission’s recommendation (183rd Report) sub-rule (3) of rule 14 is proposed to be modified with a view to allowing a plaintiff to file documents with the leave of the Court [Clause 8(iii)].
2.19.3  The Chairman of BCI had suggested to substitute the words hearing of the suit by the trial of the suit as the term “hearing” is not defined in the code.  Shri A.B. Rohtagi, Ex-Judge has requested to delete clause 8 (ii) as it is a very harsh provision, rejecting a plaint for not completing filing process within seven days. 
2.19.4  The Legislative Department did not find any merit in the first suggestion and as to latter suggestion, the time can be extended upto a period of thirty day by the court under Section 148 of the Code.
2.19.5  The Committee accepted the aforesaid suggestion of Bar Council of India.
2.20.0  Clause 9(i) of the Bill intends to amend Section 18 of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 which in turn amends rule 1 of Order VIII so as to bring conformity with amendments proposed in Clause 6 of the Bill.  Thus the filing of written statement would be increased from thirty days to ninety days with the permission of court.
2.20.1  Clause 9(ii) modifies sub-rule (3) of rule 1A of Order VIII so as to enable the  plaintiff to produce any document as evidence at the hearing of the suit with the permission of the Court.  This is a consequential change to the  amendments proposed in sub-rule (3) of rule 14 of Order VII by clause 8 (ii) of the Bill.
2.20.2  Clause 9 (iii) intends to restore rules 9 and 10 which were omitted by CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 so as to allow filing of additional written statement subsequent to  written statement filed at the institution of suit with  a little modification.
2.20.3  Various legal experts had suggested to restore Rule 9 to its  pre 1999 position.
2.20.4  The clause now proposes that the Court may fix a time of not more than thirty days for filing written statement or additional written statements by a defendant.
2.20.5  Simultaneously rule 10 which empowers the Court to pronounce a judgement on failure of the defendant to file his written statement within time permitted or fixed by the Court is also being restored as it is felt that this rule does not contribute in any manner to delay in disposal of suits.
2.20.6  The BCI has suggested to substitute the words “hearing of the suit” by the “trial of the suit”  as the word hearing is not defined in the CPC.  But the Ministry did not find merit in the suggestion. 
2.20.7  The Committee accepted the suggestion of Bar Council of India.
2.21.0  Clause 10  intends to substitute rule (2) of Order IX by amending Section 19 (i) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.
2.21.1  Rule (2) of Order IX as stood amended by 1999 Act says  that the Court makes an order for dismissal of suit where summons are not served by the plaintiff or his agent or in consequences of failure to pay costs of summons.
2.21.2  The Bill proposes to make the provision of dismissal of suit  in consequences of  failure of plaintiff to pay  costs of the summons only.  This is consequential to proposed changes envisaged under clause 6 (ii) of the Bill.
2.21.3  None of the witnesses has objection to the clause. 
2.21.4  Clause 11 seeks to restore rule 5 of Order XIV so as to empower the court to amend and strike out issues before passing the decree by amending Section 24 (ii) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.  The clause has been introduced in pursuance to the recommendations of  Law Commission as contained in its  One Hundred Sixty-third Report.
2.21.5  The President of Supreme Court Bar Association has commented  that   99.99% of the judges have never exercised this power which have also been agreed to by the Legislative Department.  However,  one of the witnesses has objection to the restoration of rule 5 of Order XIV.
2.22.0  Clause 12(a) is a new amendment to the Code.  It proposes to insert some provision after sub-rule (3) of rule 2  of Order XVIII   with a view to providing the time limit for completion of oral argument.  The main features are:-
(i)
            Before the  oral argument, the party should submit, with the permission of  court,  concise written argument;
(ii)          That written argument would form part of the record and would be simultaneously furnished to the opposite party
(iii)         No adjournment to be granted for filing written arguments unless  court  direct after recording the reasons therefor;
(iv)        The Court shall fix time limit for oral argument
 
2.22.1  The Legislative Department had stated that the proposed amendment had been necessitated as it  was felt  that  prolix oral argument  not only increase the cost of litigation but also contribute to the accumulation of  arrears of cases.
2.22.2  The BCI had submitted that the party, within the period of 15  days of making oral  submission, should submit  concise written arguments in support of the case and further period of 15 days, for reasons to be recorded,  might be granted, for the purpose.
2.22.3  The Legislative Department had stated that the proposed provision was substantially on the lines of Section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and did not agree with this submission of the BCI.
2.22.4  Clause 12 (b) amends section 27 (ii) of the CPC (Amendment)  Act, 1999.  The latter has amended rule 4 of Order XVIII which provides for the manner of recording of evidence by Commissioner.  Features with regard to recording of evidence by Commissioner, in 1999 Act vis-a-vis  2000 Bill are presented  in the accompanying Table.

2.22.6  The Legislative Department had informed the Committee that they  did not find any substance in the objection raised by the witnesses. But one ex-Judge of Delhi High Court who appeared before the Committee as witness supported Clause  12(b)  and submitted that the Commissioner may be appointed from  retired district judges or senior  lawyers  and suggested the drafting  of sub rule (3) of rule 4 of Order XVIII as under
“The Court or the Commissioner, as the case may be, shall record evidence either in writing or  mechanically in the presence of  the Judge or of the Commissioner, as the case may be, and where such evidence is recorded by the Commissioner he shall return such evidence together with his report in writing signed by him to the Court appointing him and the evidence taken under it shall form part of the record of the suit”.
2.22.7    The Department has no  objection to the above formulation.
2.22.8  The BCI had also suggested the deletion of the provision  relating to the filing of affidavit in the case of examination-in-chief.  The evidence will be virtually an evidence given before an  advocate as the  advocate  who prepares  affidavit can put any words in the mouth of witness which he has not uttered. In order words, he  can include in the affidavit what he wants the witness to say.
2.22.9  The Legislative Department had stated that Order V, rule 19; Order XI, rules 8 to 20; Order XXXII, rule 3, Order XXXVIII, rules 1 to 5 and Order XXXIX, rules 1 to 7 are in the Code,  under which the court may decide  certain  matters  in affidavit.
2.22.10 The Committee did not support the idea of appointing Commissioner to cross -examine and re-examine the witness.  In the Committee’s considered view cross -examination and re-examination should be done in the presence of Judge,  who can observe demeanor  of the witness(s).
2.23.0  Clause 15 seeks to amend section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 which would in turn omit sub-rule (2) of rule 2 of  Order XXXIX and insert sub-rule 2A under  rule 1 to make provision for requirement of security as a pre-condition for grant of temporary injunction.  This is proposed to bring uniformity in depositing  security in temporary injunction on any  matter (be it breach of contract  or property dispute).  The BCI has submitted that the requirement of  security as pre-condition or for the grant of temporary injunction would adversely affect interest of an indigent and poor litigant.
2.23.1  The Legislative Department did not find much substance in the said objection.
2.23.2  The Committee, however, agreed to recommend deletion of deposit of security from the provision of the Bill.

Giving  the historical background, the Secretary informed that after independence, a number of Committees had been constituted to deal with the problems of arrears of cases and other issues, namely, High Court Arrears Committees of 1949 and 1969.  Besides, the Law Commission had given more than half a dozen Reports (14th, 27th, 54th, 55th, 77th, 129th, 139th and 163rd) suggesting measures for reforms  in judicial administration.
3.1       The Secretary, further informed that on the lines of recommendations made by the Law Commission in its 27th, 54th  and 55th Reports, the Code of Civil Procedure was comprehensively amended by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976.  He also stated that the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997 was an attempt to give effect to the recommendations made by Justice Satish Chandra Committee and Justice V.S. Malimath Committee set up in pursuance of the recommendations of the Chief Justices’ Conferences in 1983 and 1989, respectively.  The Bill was examined  by this Committee and suggestions  of the Committee (49th Report on Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997) were also accepted by both the Houses and enacted on 30th December, 1999,  but, the
Act could not be notified in view of strong opposition by the lawyers to some of the provisions of the Act.

3.2.1    He mentioned that clause 4 of the Bill sought to restore section 100 A as it existed prior to the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999, thereby restoring the right to appeal against judgement, decision or order of a single judge of the High Court made in a petition under article 226 or 227 and  under Clause 5 of the  Bill, second appeal was proposed to be abolished only in money suits of the value of less than Rs.25,000. But it was not convinced how by increasing certain time provisions from 30 days to 60 days or 90 days, the Government was proposing to reduce the delay in disposal of the cases.

4.2       An objection was raised about recording of evidence by the Commissioner  and then hearing of the case  by Presiding Officer himself. Under the Indian Evidence Act, the cross-examination was to impeach or accept the credit of the witness. 2.1       The Chairman, then welcomed the representatives of Bar Council of India to make presentation on various provisions of the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Bill, 2000.
 
3.0       The Chairman of the Bar Council of India  referred to the provisions of Order VI, rule 17 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 relating to amendment of  the  plaint which was  removed from the Statute Book through the 1999 Amendment  Act and supported  its proposed reinstatement.  He mentioned that even the Law Commission had  recommended for its  retention.
 
3.1       Elaborating on the above provision the witness said that the litigants, especially poor ones in rural areas are not aware of the facts  of the case while filing a plaint and sometimes plaint was drafted in a hurry.  The provision to amend the plaint allowed the litigant as well as the lawyers to give all the facts at a later stage which may not be available at the filing stage.  He fully justified the reintroduction of the above Order and rule, by saying that if the amendment was used  to cause some delay or it was done with some ulterior motive, the Courts using their discretionary power could rule them out.

Clause 6
 
4.2.0    Clause 6 substitutes certain amendments made in 1999 by new amendments. The purpose of this clause is to provide for (i) modern means of transmission of summons and (ii) service of summons by the plaintiff as an additional mode of service.
 
4.2.1    Earlier, clause (1) of section 15 of the 1999 Act made provision of 30 days for a defendant to file his defence from the date of institution of suit and he was given a further period of 30 days if the Court thought fit.  Under the proposed clause 6 (i) the period for filing statement could be extended upto 90 days from the date  of service of summons on the defendant for reasons to be recorded in writing.
 
4.2.2    Some members of the Committee also raised objection to the proposal contained in clause 6 (ii) regarding service of summon through courier as it would allow private entities to enter the judicial process.  It was further added that service of summons is normally done by the Amins of the Court or postal authorities.  A member wanted to know the remedies, if the Summons served by courier agencies come back.  It was stated that under the General Clauses Act, there was a perception that if summons were sent by registered post and were returned, they could be taken as served and the Amins give certificate to that effect. but, no such thing had been contemplated as far as couriers were concerned.
 
4.2.3    The representatives of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs informed the Committee that couriers would have to be accountable to the Court, and would be punishable under the Indian Penal Code for any wrong deed.

The Committee’s attention was drawn to some of the rules of Order V relating to issue of or service of summons which provided persons to acknowledge, endorsement of time and manner of service, examination of serving officers. TATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            This Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as the Code contains the law relating to the procedure in suits and civil proceedings.  The Code has been amended from time to time by various Acts of Central and State Legislatures.  Recently, the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 was enacted by Parliament with a view to cutting short the delays at various levels.  After its enactment, a large number of representations were received both for and against its enforecement.  The Law Commission of India in its 163rd Report also dealt with the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997 which was enacted later on as the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.
 
            2. Before action could be initiated for enforcement of the said Act, the Bar Council of India and certain local Bar Associations asked the Government to relook into certain provisions which could cause hardship to the litigants.  Accordingly, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 and other proposals to reduce delay in the disposal of civil cases were discussed with legal luminaries.  The Government has further considered the matter in all its aspects after consulting the Bar Council of India and others concerned and based on the outcome of the deliberations, it is now proposed to further amend the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, consistent with the demands of fair play and justice.
           
            3. The proposed amendments inter alia seek to provide, that ––
(a)         plaintiff shall produce documents and pay requisite fee for service of summons on the defendants within seven days from the date of order by the Court for issue of summons;
(b)         the summons would be served on the defendant by the Court either by its process servers or through private courier agencies approved by the Court.  In addition to the service of summons by the Court, the plaintiff may also serve summons on the defendant;
(c)          a defendant is to file written statement within thirty days from the date of service of summons but such date can be extended up to ninety days by the Court for reasons to be recorded in writing;
(d)         the documents may be produced by the plaintiff or by the defendant, as the case may be, with the leave of the Court at the time of the hearing of the suit where such documents could not be filed by the plaintiff along with the plaint or by the defendant with this written statement.  Rule 14 of Order VII of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, (hereinafter referred to as the “Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act,”) and rule 1A of Order VIII after the amendments made in the year 1999 do not provide an opportunity to the plaintiff or the defendant, as the case may be, to produce documents at the hearing of the suit;
(e)          shall produce documents and pay requisite fee for service of summons on the defendants within seven days from the date of order by the Court for issue of summons;
(f)under rule 5 of Order XIV of the Code, amendment of issues or framing of additional issues may be allowed.  This rule was omitted by clause (ii) of section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act,  1999;
(g)         in place of insertion of sub-rule (2) 1 of XXXIX, a new rule 2B be added which would provide that the stipulation of furnishing security would apply under rule 1 as well as under rule 2 of Order XXXIX.  By section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999, a new sub-rule (2) was inserted in rule 1 of Order XXXIX so as to provide that a person seeking injunction will be required to furnish security by the Court.  This section is proposed to be omitted.
(h)         time-limit  for oral arguments by the parties may be fixed and with the leave of the Court, the parties may be required to submit written arguments before concluding the oral arguments in a case by insertion of a suitable provision in Order XVIII of the Code;
(i)the examination-in-chief of a witness shall be recorded on affidavit.  The cross-examination of a witness in the High Courts having original jurisdiction shall be recorded ordinarily by the Commissioner and in Courts subordinate to the High Court, such evidence shall be recorded either by the Court or by the Commissioner appointed by it.  The Commissioner shall also have the power to record the demeanor of a witness and any objection made in regard to such matter shall be decided by the Court at the time of arguments of the case.  A Commissioner is required to submit his report within six months from the date of issue of the commission.  Rule 4 of Order XVIII as amended in the year 1999 which provided for recording of evidence (cross-examination and re-examination) of the
witnesses by the Commissioners in all cases is proposed to be substituted in this regard.
(j)the judgments are to be pronounced within definite time-frame after a case has been heard.  The general rule proposed is that a judgment is to be pronounced at once and where it is not practicable to do so, the Court shall make an endeavour to pronounce judgment within thirty days from the date on which hearing of the case was concluded.  Where it is not practicable for the Court to pronounce judgment within thirty days because of exceptional and extraordinary circumstances of the case, the Court shall fix a day for  the pronouncement of judgment which shall not ordinarily be beyond sixty days from the date on which the case was heard;
(k)         appeals to division Bench of the High Courts in writs under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution shall be restored, Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 abolished appeals against judgments of a single Judge of the High Court in all cases;
(l)no second appeal shall lie in money suits where the value of the subject matter in the suit does not exceed rupees twenty-five thousand.  Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 abolished second appeal in all cases where value of the subject-matter in the suit did not exceed rupees twenty-five thousand;
(m)       section 39, section 64 and rules 32 and 92 of Order XXI of the Code, shall be amended on the basis of the 54th , 139th and 144th Reports of the Law Commission of India.  These amendments are clarificatory in nature.   
 
4.  The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

ISSUE OF SUMMONS

     32. (1) Where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction, has been passed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced in the case of a decree for restitution of conjungal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for an injunction by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property, or by both.
      (2) Where the party against whom a decree for specific performances or for an injunction has been passed is a corporation, the decree may be enforced by the attachment of the property of the corporation or, with the leave of the Court, by the detention in the civil prison of the directors or other principal officers thereof, or by both attachment and detention.
     (3)  Where any attachment under sub-rule (1) or sub-rule (2) has remained in force for six months if the judgment debtor has not obeyed the decree and the decree holder has applied to have the attached property sold, such property may be sold; and out of the proceeds the Court may award to the decree holder such compensations as it thinks fit, and shall pay the balance (if any) to the judgment debtor on his application. 
     (4) Where the judgment debtor has obeyed the decree and paid all cost of executing the same which he is bound to pay, or where, at the end of six months from the date of the attachment, no application to have the property sold has been made, or if made has been refused, the attachment shall cease.
     (5) Where a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction has not been obeyed, the Court may, in lieu of or in addition to all or any of the processes aforesaid, direct that the act required to be done may be done so far as practicable by the decree holder or some other person appointed by the Court, at the cost of the judgment debtor, and upon the act being done the expenses incurred may be ascertained in such manner as the Court may direct and may be recovered as if they were included in the decree.

SECTION 7:
 
Shri D. V. Subba Rao Chairman, Bar Council of India The Bar has no reservation to the resolution of disputes through the system of Lok Adalats. Wherever there is a clause for arbitration or conciliation or mediation, the law says that you refer the disputes to an arbitrator.  A court may not be in a position to say whether it
can be settled.  Again, arbitration, conciliation and mediation require trained personnel, people who have the capacity to bring the parties together, discuss with them and then bring about a settlement between them.
The Code of Civil Procedure,  1908 prior to its amendment in 1940 contained section 89 regarding the provisions relating to reference to arbitration by the courts.  On enactment of the Arbitration Act, 1940 the said section 89 was omitted.  However, by the Code of
Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 section 89 has been reintroduced with a view to empowering the courts to refer cases to arbitration, conciliation etc.  Where the parties to the suit have no objection to such reference.  This provision was introduced with a view to
implementing the Malimath Committee recommendation relating to compulsory conciliation and also to take out certain matters from the docket of the courts where the parties are agreeable to alternate dispute resolution mechanism.
     There is no compulsion requiring any dispute or pending cases to be referred to Lok Adalats for arbitration or conciliation.  At present, the institution of alternate dispute resolution mechanism does not exist on a permanent basis. With the enactment of section 89, it
would be possible to create parallel system of alternate dispute resolution at Taluka level, Tehsil level, District level and State level parallel to the system of courts. Such bodies may be established as permanent bodies either by the Bar or with the assistance of Chambers
of Commerce etc.  It may be provided that the filing of records shall be before courts so that such records may be preserved and copies of records could be provided to the functionaries of the alternate dispute resolution mechanism.
 
Shri Kapil Sibbal, President, Supreme Court Bar Association If you include the concept of consent in section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it will further expedite the process, and at the same time there would be no compulsion on the parties to go to arbitration merely because of the quality of the judge, I think section 89 is a
good provision.  But, it must be reformulated by incorporating the concept of consent.
There was already such a provision earlier as stated above.  Further, if the settlement indicated in section 89 materializes, the parties would be entitled to refund of the fee deposited in the court.  In Department’s view, the provision in section 89 is eminently desirable.   
Shri Anadi Charan Sahu Mediation and conciliation of civil disputes including property disputes by the Village Panchayats, Gram Panchayats and block level has stood the test of time as an established custom.  This will help in deciding the issues at local level instead of taking the matters to the
courts.
The statement seems to support section 89.  Hence, no comments are needed.

            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Eighty-first Report of the
Committee on the Lotteries (Prohibition) Bill, 1999. *
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred** the Lotteries (Prohibition) Bill, 1999, as introduced
in the Rajya Sabha on 23 December 1999 and pending therein, to the Committee on 14 February 2000 for examination
and report.
3.         The Committee considered   the    Bill    in six sittings held on 29 June, 24 October, 6 and
8 November 2000 and 26 June and 2 November 2001.
3.1       The Committee heard oral evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs on the Bill in its sitting held on
29 June 2000.
3.2       In its sitting held on 24 October 2000, the Committee heard the representatives of Governments of Meghalaya,
Punjab, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh.
3.3       In its sittings held on 6 and 8 November 2000, the Committee heard the oral evidence of representatives of
associations/organisations associated with lottery and allied trades (see Annexure-II).  In addition to this, representatives
of a voluntary organisation called Lok Abhiyan also presented their views on the subject of the Bill in their presentation
before the Committee in its sitting held on 8 November 2000.
3.4       The Committee considered the draft Report in its sitting held on 2 November 2001 and adopted the same.  It also
decided that the evidence tendered before the Committee may be laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament.
4.         In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill received from
the Ministry of Home Affairs, memoranda received   from various State Governments, memoranda/representations
received from MPs, associations/organisations mentioned in Annexure-II and general public, replies of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, State Governments and associations/organisations to the queries raised by the Members in the sittings of
the Committee.
5.
                  For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been
printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

            The Lotteries (Prohibition) Bill, 1999 (see Annexure-I) seeks to prohibit the Central Government, State
Governments and any organisation controlled by such Government from conducting, organising or promoting any
lottery.  It also seeks to repeal the Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998.
2.         Under the existing constitutional framework, Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to
matters enumerated in the Union List as contained in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.  As regards the items
enumerated in the State List, the legislature of any State has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part
thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated therein.
3.         As per the Constitutional provisions pertaining to the lotteries, there can be two following categories of lotteries:
(i)
                  Lotteries organised by the Government of India or the Government of State under Entry-40 of the Union
List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; and
(ii)                Lotteries organised under Entry-34 viz. ‘Betting and Gambling’ of the State List of the Seventh
Schedule.
3.1       As regards the first category, the Parliament is fully competent to legislate.  In contrast to this, lotteries organised
by private individuals, institutions, etc. are covered under the second category which a State Government is fully
competent to authorise.
4.         Here it may be noted that the Central Government does not organise any lottery.  It has also advised Union
Territories not to permit any private lotteries.  However, according to the Background Note supplied by the Ministry of
Home Affairs, 12 States namely, Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir,
Madhya Pradesh, Meghalaya, Orissa, Rajasthan, Tripura and Uttar Pradesh do not organise any lottery. Besides, no
Union Territory is at present organising any lottery.  In contrast, 13 States namely, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Haryana,
Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Punjab, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal are
organising their own lotteries.
5.         While tracing the genesis of the Lotteries (Prohibition) Bill, 1999, its Statement of Objects and Reasons states
that the malpractices in the conduct of lotteries and its impact on the poorer sections of the society had been under
scrutiny of the Government for quite some time.  The continued prevalence of the popularly known single digit and
instant lotteries and the temptation offered by them had proved to be the undoing of many families.  In spite of the
guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time as also the guidelines issued by the Supreme Court in the
matter, the evil could not be totally eliminated and it was felt that a Central legislation to regulate the conduct of lotteries
was necessary to protect the interests of the gullible poor.  To tackle this evil, the Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998 was
enacted by the Parliament.  This Act, besides imposing stipulations for conduct of lotteries in the country, banned single
digit and pre-announced number lotteries.
5.1       The Statement of Objects and Reasons inter alia  states that the matter was debated at length in Parliament when
the said Bill was taken up for consideration.  During the debate there was an overwhelming view in both Houses of
Parliament in favour of banning the lotteries.  The matter was also placed before the Conference of Chief Ministers held
on  27 November 1998 in New Delhi.  The general consensus in the Conference was that lotteries should be statutorily
banned.
5.2       In this backdrop, the Lotteries (Prohibition) Bill, 1999 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 23 December 1999. 
Subsequently, it was referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs on 14

(a)                There should be total prohibition on lotteries because this trade has ruined lakhs of poor families.
(b)               About half of the country is free from the menace of lotteries. Therefore, rest of the country should also be got

(c)                Though there is an outright ban on the operation of single digit lotteries, lottery operators have devised new

(d)               The number of persons employed in lottery trade is much less than being claimed by lottery lobby. As for those

Hence, a ban on lotteries will actually harm a small number of people who could be rehabilitated by the

(e)                The financial loss to the States as a result of the proposed prohibition can be compensated by the Central
Government by way of additional grants.
(f)                 The argument that prohibition on lotteries will encourage illegal gambling like Satta, etc. is also untenable

Why restrict it to Government companies only?  Why not private or public limited companies, trusts, societies,

I.          MPs both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
(a)                Ban on lotteries will lead to huge financial losses to the State Governments.
(b)               The problem of massive unemployment will further compound once the ban on lotteries is imposed. 
Lakhs of people will be rendered jobless.
(c)                Lottery trade consumes nearly 1,00,000 tonnes of paper and thus sustains paper industry.  Ban on

(d)               More than 50 security printing presses are entirely dependent on lottery trade.  Ban on lotteries will lead

(e)                Nearly 15 States are opposed to the proposed prohibition on lotteries.  Therefore, the Committee should

II.         Associations of Lottery Traders/Agencies/Agents
(a)                Prohibition on lotteries will lead to  lakhs of people being rendered jobless. Around 25 lakh people are
estimated to be affected due to the proposed prohibition.
(b)               Both Centre and State Governments will lose revenue worth crores of rupees due to prohibition on
lotteries.
(c)                To prevent cheating and other malpractices associated with lottery trade, private lottery should be banned

(d)               Ban on lotteries will lead to rise in gambling in various forms such as Satta, etc.
(e)                Since the menace of single digit and instant lottery has already been put to an end by the Lotteries

(f)                 There are several other practices which have more pernicious effect on the society such as consumption
of liquor, tobbaco, gutkha, etc. than lotteries.  Then why the lottery trade is being singled out?
(g)                There are several allied industries linked with the lottery trade such as paper, printing, transport and
other industries like courier service, electronic and print media.  With the ban on lotteries, they will also
have to bear the brunt.
(h)                Lotteries should not be prohibited but should be regulated instead.

(a)                Lottery trade is a means of livelihood for lakhs of people including aged persons, women and physically

(b)               There will be widespread unemployment in allied industries also.

(a)                Ban on lotteries will have an adverse impact on paper mills.  This impact will further spread to the allied

V.        Printers/Printers’ Associations
(a)                Prohibition on lotteries will mean closure of security printing presses which in turn will create large scale
unemployment.
(b)               The printers have acquired security-printing machinery after spending crores of rupees especially for
printing lottery tickets. Ban on lotteries will mean loss of crores of rupees to the presses.
(c)                Lottery trade should be regulated not prohibited.
 
VI.       Transporters
Transport companies are engaged in the movement of lottery tickets right from the procurement of raw material
such as printing paper etc. to the delivery of printed tickets to the distributors, stockists, agents, etc.  Ban on
lottery trade will result in large-scale unemployment and loss of business and livelihood to thousands of people in
the transport sector.
 
VII.      Social Institutions
Lottery trade has been quite generous in offering donations to several social institutions engaged in the welfare of
the masses, such as hospitals, healthcare research institutes, charitable trusts, etc.  Ban on lotteries will deprive
such institutions of one of their sources of donations.
 
VIII.     Other Individuals
Lotteries should be regulated  and this can be done by further amending the Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998. 
Some of the suggestions for further regulation are as follows:
(i)         The States should receive a minimum percentage of the gross value of the tickets approved by the
Government for sale proceeds of the authorised lotteries instead of fixed amounts payable to the
States by the distributors.  This could prevent the evil of unlimited printing of tickets and
irregularities in the sales.
(ii)        There should be a proper mechanism to ensure uniform accounting of the sale proceeds.
(iii)
               There should be a provision for the appointment of Auditors by the State Governments to audit
the sale proceeds.
(iv)              Unclaimed prizes/amounts should be spent on social welfare activities.
(v)        State Governments can even think of imposing a levy on the turnover of lotteries.
(vi)       There should be more intense supervision over the process of draws and publication of the results
authenticated by an independent agency such as a small tribunal in each State to ensure
transparency in the whole process.
(vii)      There should be restriction on number of draws held in a day by each State.
(viii)
           Lottery trade provides employment to lakhs of people and generates a huge amount of revenue
for both Union as well as State Governments.  Prohibition on lotteries will not be in anybody’s
interest.
(ix)       The country has not given up horse racing, casinos, forward trading, hedging, dealings in stocks
and shares all of which have a segment of gambling about their operation.  These activities have
not been    banned instead the effort is to refine them.   There is no reason at all why a similar
constructive approach should not be adopted in the case of lotteries as well.

Committee has received a large number of memoranda from different quarters opposing the proposed ban.  Likewise,
several witnesses in their presentations before the Committee have pleaded against the imposition of total ban on
lotteries.  The Chairman of the Committee has also been flooded with representations from 247 Members of Parliament
(LS Members-207; RS Members- 40) against the prohibition of lotteries. They have inter alia stated that there is need for
better and effective regulation of the lotteries. A ban on lotteries will lead to large-scale unemployment and loss of
revenue to State Governments. Therefore, they have urged that in view of the far-reaching socio-economic implications
of a ban on lotteries, the Lotteries (Prohibition) Bill, 1999 should not be enacted.
           
14.       The Committee, in its meeting held on 26 June 2001, held detailed discussion on the Bill.  During the discussion,
two divergent views emerged.  This divergence of views sharply divided the Committee in two sections with one
favouring the Bill and the other opposing it.  Due to this sharp division amongst its Members, the Committee could not
reach on a consensus either in favour or against the Bill.
 
14.1     One of the two sections is of the view that the real menace for the society was single digit lottery which stood
banned after the enactment of Lotteries (Regulation) Bill, 1998.  Therefore, keeping in view the fact that the society has
already been rid of the real menace, there is no need to impose an all out ban on the lotteries.  However, if certain
malpractices have been detected in the operation of lotteries, these can be removed by further regulation. An outright
prohibition will not only lead to large-scale unemployment and loss of revenue to the States but it will also encourage
certain illegal activities such as Matka, Satta, etc.  In view of this, a comprehensive prohibition of lotteries run by the
State Governments may not be the real need of the hour.  The real need of the hour is to put in place an effective
regulatory mechanism to keep a check on the covert and overt malpractices associated with the operation of lotteries.
 
14.2     The other section favours a complete ban on lotteries on the premise that it is an act of gambling which has a
direct bearing on the moral character of the society.  Lotteries encourage the desire to become rich overnight as a result
of which poor people tend to spend whatever little money they have on buying lotteries.  Since lotteries are based on
chance, thousands of poor people have lost their hard earned money as one gains at the expense of many.  The desire to
become rich overnight has ruined many a family.  This apart, lotteries are being run deceptively and fraudulently as a
result of which people who play lotteries are being duped of their hard earned money.  Another argument of this section
favouring the enactment of the Bill is that the present Bill owes its origin to the Forty-second Report of the Committee
on the Lotteries (Regulation) Bill, 1998, in which it had recommended to the Government to come forward with a
comprehensive Bill for a complete prohibition on lotteries.  Therefore, now there is no rationale in opposing the present
Bill.  As regards the argument that a ban on lotteries will lead to large-scale unemployment and loss of revenue to the
States, this section believes that this argument is a façade to prevent a ban on the lotteries.
           
15.       Notwithstanding the fact that the Committee is sharply divided on the issue of banning lotteries, there is,
however, a complete unanimity amongst its Members that Government should attempt to evolve a larger political
consensus with regard to the subject  matter of the Bill, in the light of the evidence recorded by the Committee,
memoranda received from different quarters and the views expressed by Committee Members both for and against the
Bill.
 
15.1     Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Government should take up this issue at the political level to
explore the   possibilities of   evolving a   larger consensus    in the matter.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            The malpractices in the conduct of lotteries and its impact on the poorer sections of the society had been under
scrutiny of the Government for quite some time.  The continued prevalence of the popularly known single digit and
instant lotteries and the temptation offered by them had proved to be the undoing of many families.  Inspite of the
guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time as also the guidelines issued by the Supreme Court of
India in the matter, the evil could not be totally eliminated and it was felt that a Central legislation to regulate the
conduct of lotteries was necessary to protect the interest of the gullible poor.  To tackle this evil, the Lotteries
(Regulation) Act, 1998 was enacted by Parliament.  This Act, besides imposing stipulations for conduct of lotteries in
the country, banned single digit and pre-announced number lotteries.
 
2.         The Lotteries (Regulation) Bill, 1998 was referred to the Department related Parliamentary Committee on Home
Affairs.  The said Committee, after considering the matter in all its aspects, had strongly recommended to the
Government to come forward with a comprehensive Bill, at the earliest, in consultation with all the State Governments
and the Union territory Administrations, imposing a complete ban on the lottery trade in the country.  The matter was
debated at length in Parliament when the said Bill was taken up for consideration.  During the debate,  there was an
overwhelming view in both Houses of Parliament in favour of banning the lotteries.
 
3.         The matter was also placed before the Conference of Chief Ministers held on the 27 November, 1998 in New
Delhi.  The general consensus in the Conference was that lotteries should be statutorily banned.
 
4.         Under the Constitutional frame-work, Parliament has legislative competence with regard to lotteries falling under
entry 40 of List I (Union List) of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.  Other types of lotteries fall under entry 34 of
List II (State List) of said Schedule which is within the legislative competence of the State Legislatures.  The Bill,
therefore, proposes to prohibit the Central Government, State Government and any organisation controlled by such
Government from conducting, organising or promoting any lottery.  It also seeks to repeal the Lotteries (Regulation) Act,
1998.
 
The Bill seeks to achieve the aforesaid object.

REPORT
 
            The North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill, 1998 (see Annexure-I) seeks to restructure the North-Eastern
Council so as to make it more effective. To achieve this objective, the proposed amendments inter alia seek to provide
for inclusion of Sikkim as one of the members of the Council; discontinuance of Governors as Members of the Council;
nomination of three members by the President; functioning of the Council as a regional planning body and conferring of
such powers as may be delegated to it by the Central Government; formulation of regional plans with priority to
schemes and projects benefiting two or more States; formulation and review of implementation of specific projects and
schemes for Sikkim; and setting up of a Screening Committee to examine projects/schemes to ensure that selected
projects/schemes have a regional character and reflect the needs of the member States of the Council.
 
2.         However, some of the above-mentioned proposals as contained in the North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill,
1998, have been reconsidered by the Government. Accordingly, the Government proposes to amend some of the
provisions of the Bill as per the amendments given notice of by the Home Minister (see Annexure-II). These
amendments inter alia seek to restore the membership of the Council to the Governors of the constituent States; provide
for the nomination of the Chairman of the Council by the President; do away with the provision for setting up of the
Screening Committee; and provide that the Council shall meet at least twice a year.
 
3.         As a result of the amendments given notice of by the Home Minister, the final shape of the Bill, in contrast to the
earlier Bill, seeks to maintain status quo ante by restoring the membership of the Council to the Governors of the
constituent States. In addition to this, it provides for nomination of the Chairman of the Council by the President and
holding of the meetings of the Council at least twice a year and does away with the provision of the Screening
Committee.
 
4.         Here it may be pertinent to have a peep into the profile of the North-Eastern Council. The North-Eastern Council
was set up in 1972 under the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971. The Council is an advisory body. It can discuss any
matter in which some or all the States represented in the Council, or the Union and one or more of the States represented
in the Council, have a common interest, and advise the Central Government and the Government of each State
concerned as to the action to be taken on any such matter. The Council’s objectives include, inter alia, balanced
development of the North-Eastern Region. The Council endeavours to achieve this objective by formulating for the
States represented in the Council a unified and coordinated regional plan in regard to matters of common importance.
The Council also reviews, from time to time, the implementation of the projects and schemes included in the regional
plans. In addition to this, the Council has been entrusted with the task of reviewing the measures taken by the States
represented in the Council for the maintenance of security and public order. The North Eastern Council presently
consists of the Governors as well as the Chief Ministers of the seven North-Eastern States. One of the members of the
Council is nominated by the President of India as its Chairman.
 
5.         So far as the genesis of the North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill, 1998 is concerned, it is relevant to refer to
the Background Note received from the Ministry of Home Affairs which states that the North-Eastern States have been
demanding restructuring of the Council so as to make it more effective. There has also been a demand from the
Government of Sikkim for inclusion of that State in the Council. After careful consideration of the matter, the
Government is also of the view that North-Eastern Council Act, 1971 needs to be amended for effective restructuring of
the Council. In this backdrop, the North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill, 1998 came into being. It was introduced in
the Rajya Sabha on 8 December, 1998.
 
6.         After its introduction in the Rajya Sabha and while pending therein it was referred to the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs on 9 August, 2001 for examination and report.
 
7.         Accordingly, the Committee first took up the consideration of the Bill in its meeting held on 13 September,
2001. It heard the oral evidence of the Special Secretary (NE), Ministry of Home Affairs in the same meeting.
 
7.1       The Special Secretary (NE), Ministry of Home Affairs made an audio-visual presentation on the Bill.  In his
presentation, he gave a brief account of the genesis and the mandate of the North-Eastern Council as provided for in the
North-Eastern Council Act, 1971.  While tracing the genesis of the North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Bill, 1998, the

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/82ndreport.htm[30-06-2016 17:47:07]
special Secretary stated that the proposed amendments emerged from the meeting of the Prime Minister with the Chief
Ministers of seven North-Eastern States and Sikkim held on 8 May 1998 at Shillong.  In that meeting, it was decided
that the Council would be reconstituted with the Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission as its Chairman and Chief
Ministers of North-Eastern States and Sikkim as its members.  It was also decided to include Sikkim as a member of the
Council.
 
7.2       While touching upon the salient features of the Bill, the Special Secretary stated that the Bill inter alia provided
for (i) inclusion of Sikkim as a member State; (ii) cessation of Governors as members of the Council; (iii) nomination of
three members on the Council by the President; (iv) setting up of a Screening Committee; and (v) identification of the
Council as a regional planning body.
 
7.3       After underlining the salient features of the Bill, the Special Secretary stated that due to efflux of time it was felt
that Governors might be retained as Members of the Council keeping in view the special role envisaged for them in the
Sixth Schedule to the Constitution.  Similarly, the provision for having a Screening Committee was also dropped as it
might lead to delays in the approval of the Council’s schemes/projects. On the other hand, it was considered necessary
to provide for having at least two meetings of the Council in a year.  It was also specifically mentioned that the
Chairman of the Council shall be nominated by the President.
 
7.4       Accordingly, the Special Secretary informed, the amendments were given notice of by the Home Minister and
the Statement of Objects and Reasons was revised (see Annexure-III).
 
8.         While considering the Bill in its meeting held on 13 September 2001, the Committee proposed to invite
Secretary, North-Eastern Council, Secretary, Planning Commission, Chief Secretaries of North-Eastern States and
Sikkim, and MPs of North-Eastern States to hear their views on the Bill.
9.         In its meeting held on 4 October 2001, the Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary, North-Eastern
Council, Principal Advisor and Secretary, Planning Commission and Chief Secretaries of Meghalaya, Mizoram,
Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura, on the Bill.
9.1       The Secretary, North-Eastern Council, in his presentation before the Committee, gave a brief account of the
various aspects and functions of the Council.  He stated that North-Eastern States were administratively and
economically weak which is why the Council was seen as a source of supplementary funding agency to prop up them. 
He informed the Committee that ninety per cent of North Eastern Council schemes were implemented by agencies of
the constituent States and the Central Government.  As such North-Eastern Council had no role to play in the actual
execution of its schemes.  He opined that since no security role had been assigned to the Council till date, it need not be
part of its mandate.  The Council, as a matter of fact, should confine itself to development activities with a focus on
planning.  He felt that in order to be more effective, the organisational structure of the Council needed a review.  He
suggested the opening up of the North-Eastern region for economic investment from outside.  With regard to
membership of Governors in North-Eastern Council, the Secretary stated that they should be retained as members as
their presence brought to bear a more balanced and objective outlook to the discussions in the Council. 
 
9.2       In her presentation before the Committee, the Secretary, Planning Commission stated that originally three
distinct roles were envisaged for the North-Eastern Council. First as a regional planning body; second as a zonal council
for North-East; and third as a coordinating agency for security matters.  However, the focus of the Council had been on
development and planning only.  While elaborating the Council’s role, the Secretary stated that it was required to
formulate regional plans in order to secure a balanced development of the region; prioritise the projects/schemes; and
thereafter make recommendations to the Central Government for consideration of those projects/schemes.  She briefed
the Committee about the financing pattern for the projects/schemes of the Council and stated that the Planning
Commission provided funds for the annual plans of the Council out of the available Central assistance to State plans. 
The allocated funds were then placed at the disposal of the administrative Ministry i.e. Ministry of Home Affairs.  The
draft annual plans were proposed by the Council to the Ministry of Home Affairs which, in turn, recommended the plans
for approval to the Planning Commission which formally accorded final approval to the plans.  The Secretary informed
that Ninth Plan period witnessed a slight shortfall in the expenditure of the Council.  She further informed that the
Government had taken a decision to reallocate the business relating to the Council from the Ministry of Home Affairs to
a newly created Department for Development of North-Eastern Region.  With the reallocation of business, the Tenth
