5.1.0    The Lokpal Bill, 2001 is modelled on the basis of reco mmendations/observations of the
Committee as contained in its Fiftieth Report on Lokpal Bill, 1998. 
5.1.1    The earlier Committee had suggested re-examina tion   of seven clauses out  of thirty two clauses
of the Lokpal Bill, 1998.  The basic issues raised in that Report hovered around the following points: -   
(i)                  Rationality of bringing Members of Parliame nt within the purview of the Lokpal, in
view of the Supreme Court j udgement in the case of Shri P.V. Narsimha Rao Vs. State,
wherein the court has held MPs and MLAs as  public servants who could be prosecuted
under the Prevention of Corruption (PC) Act, 1988; 
(ii)                Views and recommendations of the Committe e of Privileges of Lok Sabha regarding 
procedure to be followed by Lokpal in investigating cases of corruption against Members
of Parliament under the PC Act; and 
(iii)               Views of Ethics Committee of  the Rajya Sabha wherein it had not favoured the idea o f
subjecting the Members to the disciplinary authority of an agency outside the jurisdiction
of the House. 
5.1.2    The Secretary (Personnel) in his deposition before the Committee on 15 October 2001 had stated
that the Government while finali sing Lokpal Bill, 2001 on the lines of Lokpal Bill, 1998, constituted a
Group of Ministers (GOM) to consider certain issues i. e. implications of the inclusion of Prime Minister
within the purview of Lokpal and the question of bringing Members of Parliament within the ambit o f
the Lokpal.  The Government also took into consider ation the three basic issues mentioned in para 5.1.1
and decided that clause 18 of Lokpal Bill, 1998 relati ng to declaration of asse ts and liabilities by the
Members of Parliament should not be included in the 2001  Bill and other consequential  amendments
have also been reflected in Lokpal Bill, 2001. 
5.1.3    The Committee of Privileges (Eleventh Lok Sabha) (under the Chairmanship of Dr. Mallikarjun)
in its Report on “Ethics, Standard s in Public Life, Privileges, Faci lities to Members and Other Related 
Matters” (1997) was of the opinion that Lokpal may be empowered to deal with only those complaints
falling under the provisions of Pr evention of Corruption Act, 1988.  After investig ation on those
complaints, Lokpal may forward its Report to the Sp eaker, Lok Sabha, who may refer the same to the
Committees on Ethics and Privileg es for suggesting action.  The Com mittee in turn may report back to
the Speaker with its suggestion and actions in such matters.   The said report had not been adopted by
the Lok Sabha.

6.0       The Lokpal Bill, 2001 is the eight h attempt in a series by the Government 13  to establish the 
institution of Lokpal at the federa l level  during the last four deca des.  Upon a  perusal of all eight
Government  Bills, it appears to th e Committee that there is perceptible  shift in th e central focus of the
legislation from the issue of  redr essal of public grievances to  co rruption at high places.  This radical
departure can be observed from the Lokpal Bill, 1977 and Bills intr oduced thereafter  which have  no
provision for redressal of ci tizens’ grievances and thereby stripped off Lokpal its intrinsic  concept.  In
the first two Bills (Lokpal and L okayuktas Bill, 1968 and Lokpal and Lokayktas Bill, 1971) clause 2
contained definition of the term s ‘grievance’ and ‘maladministra tions’ which were conspicuously 
missing in the proposed legislations  introduced from 1977 onwards.  Rest of the Bills in their clause 2
had inter-alia the definition of the terms ‘complaint’ or  ‘corruption’ instea d of ‘grievance’ o r 
‘maladministration’. 
6.1       The Committee posed the query to know the reason for such shift in the subsequent proposed 
legislations, from the Ministry.  Th e Ministry in its reply has recoun ted the functions of three existing
grievances mechanisms i.e. (i) Internal Grievance Redressal Ma chinery within each
Ministry/Department (ii) External Grievance  Redressal Machinery in the Department of Administrative 
Reform and Public Grievances;  a nd (iii) Directorate of Public Grievances, Cabinet Secretariat, without
answering the query of the Committee.  
6.2.0    With the shift in focus from redressal of public grievances against injustice caused by
maladministration, Members of Parliament, Members of Legislative Assemblies of Union Territories, in
addition to Ministers of the Un ion, were brought within the ambi t of Lokpal  whilst Government
Servants were excluded from its purview, as   clearly envisaged in the 1977 Bill. 
6.2.1    It may be  highlighted that  the first two Bills (1968, 1971) had the provisions for keeping
Ministers of the Union and Govern ment Servants under the purview of   Lokpal and the term “public 
servant” was used to denote  them.  Bu t the 1977 Bill used the term ‘public man’ inter alia to denote 
Ministers, MPs and Ch ief Ministers.  In subseque nt Bills, the term “public  functionary” was used to 
denote Ministers, MPs and even th e Prime Minister.  Whether the pur view of Lokpal extends  to the
Prime Minister  and the Members of Parliament  has been  given in the accompanying table  Bill-wise:-

6.3.0    The Committee wishes to point out   that the Members of Parliament have been declared as 
public servants in the case P.V. Narasimha  Rao  versus State, JT 1998(3) S.C.318,  by the Supreme 
Court  although the definition laid down in Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code or in Section 2(c) of the 
Prevention of  Corruption  (PC) Act, 1988 implicitely mention about them.  The Committee wanted to 
know  the rationale  for using the term “public functionary” for the Members of Parliament, who have 
been    declared as public servant  by the Supreme Court and can be tried under the  P.C. Act, 1988, like 
other Government Servants,  by the ordinary Court of Law.  So, in the Committee’s view,  the Members 
of Parliament,  as a consequence, would be subjected to one more  enquiring  agency i.e. Lokpal,  in 
addition to   the Central Bureau of Investigation/Police, Ethics/Privileges Committee of respective  
Houses, whereas public servant committing offences  under P.C. Act, 1988 would be  subjected to only 
one investigating agency i.e. Police/CBI.  From that angle, the Committee wanted to know whether 
subjecting Members of Parliament  to multiplicity of authorities would not violate the principle  of 
equality before  law (Article 14)or whether  it would not run contrary to the spirit of Article 20 of the 
Constitution. 
6.3.1    The Ministry  in its written submission has stated that the term “public functionary” is used in 
the Bill to distinguish certain category of public servants from the rest of the public servants.  The term 
“public  functionary” is used  for limited purpose of conducting enquiries by Lokpal.  Further, Lokpal is 
not a  prosecuting  agency  rather it is a fact-finding body.  The appropriate action is to be taken as per 
the normal law of the land after  Lokpal submits its inquiry report to the competent authority as 
prescribed in the Bill.  Therefore, the inquiry by Lokpal into the allegations against Members of 
Parliament is not violative  of the principle of equality. 
6.3.2    Though the Committee understands that Members of  Parliament  are public servants  sui 
genesis , yet on the issue of keeping the Members of Parliament  within the ambit of the Lokpal, 
divergent views were expressed.  One strand of view was that the Members of  Parliament should not be 
brought within the ambit of Lokpal as 
(i)                  it would subject them to the authority of an agency, other than the House, which 
enjoyed broad autonomy  under the scheme of Constitution and may amount to 
encroachment  upon the authority, autonomy, privileges and dignity of Parliament; 
(ii)        it would make them subject to multiplicity  of authorities –Ethics/Privileges  
Committees  of the House, Police/CBI, Court of Law, Lokpal; 
(iii)       they may be made  to  appear before Second Class  Magistrate as the Supreme Court has 
power  to transfer cases  from the Lokpal to the Court of Sessions in accordance with 
clause 22 of  the Bill, which may impinge upon the dignity and privileges of Members 
and thereby of the House; and  
(iv)              the proposed legislation does not provide safeguards nor any safeguard exists to protect 
the Members of Parliament from simultaneous  investigation  by Police/ CBI and inquiry  
by Lokpal for the same offence.

6.4.0        The office of Prime Minister was brought within the ambit of Lokpal by the Government 
headed   by Shri V.P. Singh through the Lokpal Bill, 1989.  In the subsequent   legislations , the Prime 
Minister have been proposed to be placed under the purview of Lokpal. 
6.4.1    The Committee underscores the point that though the Prime Minister is primus inter pares (first 
amongst equals), virtually, he is more than that and enjoys the highest authority in Indian democratic 
system as long as he enjoys the confidence of the House of the People.  The Committee deliberated at 
length on the implications of bringing the institution of Prime Minister within the purview of Lokpal, 
which privy to so many secret  and sensitive issues of national importance/interest. 
6.4.2    One group of opinion was that the Prime Minister being privy to vital information should not be 
brought under the jurisdiction of Lokpal, as the constitutional process i.e. no confidence motion is 
available   in the Lok Sabha for removing  him.  They wondered  how the Prime Minister could 
function, when allegations were brought to the notice of Lokpal and that body initiates injury.  
Furthermore , situations may arise, where opposition may demand the resignation  of the Prime Minister 
pending inquiry by Lokpal.  That would bring instability to the democratic set up evolved during last 
fifty two years. 
6.4.3    The other strand of opinion was that no one is above the law of the land and the Prime Minister, 
thus, should be brought within the purview of Lokpal.  A view amongst this section was that the Prime 
Minister may be brought  within the ambit of Lokpal with some sort of checks and balances – providing 
concurrence of the President of India for initiating inquiry against him by Lokpal. 
6.5.0    The Committee also deliberated on the issue of extending the jurisdiction of Lokpal to the 
judiciary.  The Committee feels that the judiciary is not as clean and as respectable as it used to be in the 
past.  Their accountability has been insulated by the deterrence of the inherent  power of judiciary i.e. 
contempt of the Court.  The Supreme Court has evolved safeguards for the judges with the 
pronouncement of its judgment in K. Veeraswamy vs Union of India and others  (1999) , in terms  of 
which no FIR could be registered against a Judge of a High Court, Chief Justice of a High Court or 
Judge of the Supreme Court without the clearance of the Chief Jusitce of India and sanctions for 
launching prosecution against them could not be granted by the President of India without the 
concurrence of the Chief  Justice of India.  In the light thereof, the Committee is of the view that 
judiciary ought to be made accountable to the public for their conduct. 
6.5.1    While referring to one of the observations of the ARC that in the discretionary field, matters 
involving acts of justice or injustice, corruption or  favoritism were to be inquired into by the Lokpal, a 
view was expressed that  since the judiciary had been at times passing orders in a discretionary manner, 
it should be brought under the Lokpal.  One section of opinion was that the ambit of Lokpal should be 
broadbased enough to cover Judges including Chief Justice of India.   It was also felt that the Chief 
Justice of India may be brought within the ambit of Lokpal with some checks and balances i.e. by 
making the President of India as sanctioning authority for granting permission for initiation of inquiry

6.5.2    The other section of opinion desires that since in the scheme of the present Bill, Judges would 
not fit in, another piece of legislation may be brought to make the Judges accountable. 
6.5.3    The Committee was, however, of the unanimous view that a separate legislation may be brought

7          Be that as it may, the Committee regards the Bill as an half -baked measure and which contains 
the following serious anomalies and inconsistencies which needed to be addressed before enacting the 
law on Lokpal:- 
(i)         Connotations of the two terms i.e. ‘Public functionary’ and ‘complaint’ detailed   in 
clause 2 of the Bill are incoherent with the scheme of Bill to the extent that complaint 
against the offences under the PC Act, 1988 have to be investigated not inquired.  Further 
inquisitioning of the said offences committed by public functionaries  (who have been 
declared  as public  servant by the Supreme Court) by the Lokpal put the public 
functionaries in  double jeopardy vis-a-vis public servant  (bureaucrats ), and is therefore, 
against the   principle of equality before the law. 
(ii)        The term “public functionary” in the Bill included those who have been declared as 
‘public servant’ by the Supreme Court and has not been explained, rationale of using the 
term ‘public functionary’ in the place of ‘public servant’. 
(iii)               The term ‘inquiry’ had not been defined in the Bill whereas the inquiry as defined by 
Cr.P.C. meant inquiry by a Magistrate. 
(iv)              Inquiry into the complaint under the PC Act, 1988 by Lokpal as envisaged under clause 
10 of the Bill may create a situation where two parallel authorities would be inquiring 
and investigating into the same offence as the Magistrate and Police were not duty bound 
to keep the complaint pending till the matter was finalised by the Lokpal and the 
provisions of Chapters XII and XV of the Cr. P.C. could not be kept in abeyance during 
that period. 
(v)                Provisions in the Bill particularly in Clauses 10 to 17 were a queer mixture of provisions 
of Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 and Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.  It amounted to 
civil trial of corruption cases by an inquiry officer which ought to have been done by an 
investigating officer. 
(vi)              Taking evidence on oath at i nquiry stage by the Lokpal  (whi ch is usually done at the 
time of trial) amounts to putting the cart before the horse. 
(vii)             Further the Lokpal cannot compel  a person who is not willin g to appear before him but
is willing to give evidence before the Court of Law. 
(viii)      The Legislati on has dangerous port end by clubbing provisions  of Commissions o f
Inquiry Act with the provision of Code of Criminal Procedure. 
(ix)       The Lokpal has no nexus with Pa rliament as has been the Swedish Ombudsman and
Parliamentary Commissioner in U.K. 
(x)                The Legislation does not   a ddress public grievances; rath er focusses its attention on
bribery and corruption at high places, 
(xi)       Ranks of Officers to assist Lokpal in conducting inquiry are not specified in the Bill.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
  
•        The Committee was, however, of the unanimous vi ew that a separate legislation may be brought
forward to set up appropriate institutional mechanism to ensure accountability of Judges. 
(Para 6.5.3)
•        Be that as it may, the Committee regards the Bill as an half -baked measure and which contains 
the following serious anomalies and inconsiste ncies which needed to be addressed before
enacting the law on Lokpal:- 
  
(i)         Connotations of the two terms i.e.  ‘Public functionary’ and ‘complaint’ detailed   
in clause 2 of the Bi ll are incoherent with the sche me of Bill to the extent that
complaint against the offences under the PC Act, 1988 have to be investigated not
inquired.  Further inquisitioning of th e said offences committed by public
functionaries  (who have been declared  as public  servant by the Supreme Court)
by the Lokpal put the public functionaries in  double jeopardy vis-a-vis public 
servant  (bureaucrats ), and is therefore, against the   principle of equality before
the law. 
(ii)        The term “public functionary” in  the Bill included those who have been declared 
as ‘public servant’ by the Supreme Court and has not been explained, rationale o f
using the term ‘public functionary’ in the place of ‘public servant’. 
(iii)       The term ‘inquiry’ had not been  defined in the Bill whereas the inquiry as 
defined by Cr.P.C. meant inquiry by a Magistrate. 
(iv)       Inquiry into the complaint under the PC Act, 1988 by Lokpal as envisaged unde r
clause 10 of the Bill may cr eate a situation where two parallel authorities would
be inquiring and investigating into the same  offence as the Ma gistrate and Police
were not duty bound to keep the complain t pending till the ma tter was finalised
by the Lokpal and the provisions of Chapters XII and XV of the Cr. P.C. could
not be kept in abeyance during that period. 
(v)        Provisions in the Bill particul arly in Clauses 10 to 17 were a queer mixture o f
provisions of Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 and C ode of Civil Procedure,
1908.  It amounted to civil trial of corr uption cases by an inquiry officer which
ought to have been done by an investigating officer. 
(vi)       Taking evidence on oath at inquiry stage by the Lokpal  (which is usually done at
the time of trial) amounts to putting the cart before the horse. 
(vii)      Further the Lokpal cannot compel  a person who is not wi lling to appear before
him but is willing to give evidence before the Court of Law. 
(viii)      The Legislation has danger ous portend by clubbing pr ovisions of Commissions
of Inquiry Act with the provision of Code of Criminal Procedure. 
(ix)       The Lokpal has no nexus with Parliament as has been the Swedish Ombudsman
and Parliamentary Commissioner in U.K. 
(x)                The Legislation does not   address public grievances; rather focusses its attention
on bribery and corruption at high places, 
(xi)              Ranks of Officers to assist  Lokpal in conducting inquiry are not specified in the 
Bill.

2.0       The Chairman welcomed Members of the Committee along with Secret ary  (Personnel) and his
colleagues to the meeting of the Committee. 
2.1       Thereafter, he touched upon, in brief, diff erent phases of attempts at legislation on Lokpal which
spanned over more than four decades.  He apprised the Committee that the proposal on Lokpal had been
referred twice earlier to this Committee.  The pr edecessor Committee   had also articulated its view
thereon and subsequently had presented its Reports (Fortieth) and (Fiftieth) to Parliament. 
2.2       Thereafter, he requested the Secretary (Personnel) to make a brie f presentation on the proposed
legislation and requested Members to seek clarific ation from the Secretary after his presentation was
over.  He also indicated that the Committee would have another round of internal discussion   on the Bill
on 19 October 2001. 
3.0       The Secretary, before delineating the salient features of the Bill, apprised the Committee that the
proposed legislation had incorporat ed all the amendments suggested by this Comm ittee contained in its
Fiftieth Report which was presented to Parliament on 25 February 1999. 
3.1.0    Thereafter, he touched upon, in brief, the b ackground leading to setting up of the institution o f
Lokpal which were as follows: 
            The Administrative Reforms Commission had recommended setting   up of an institution
of Lokpal for Central Government and Lokayukta   for the State Government way back in
1966.  As a follow up action, the Central Government introduced legislation in the years -
1968, 1971, 1977, 1985,1989,  1996 and 1998.  Except  the 1985 Bill which was
withdrawn upon its introduction, all other Bills  lapsed on the dissolution  of concerned
Lok Sabhas. 
3.1.1    The Secretary then stated that the Lokpal  Bill, 1996 was referred  to the Standing Committee  on
Home Affairs chaired by Shri Sompal   which in turn   presented it s Report  to Parliament on  9 May 
1997.  The Lokpal Bill,  1998 was base d on Lokpal  Bill, 1996 and   was al so  referred to this Standing
Committee under the chairmanship  of present Chairman. 
3.1.2    Referring to Lokpal Bill , 1998 the Secretary mentioned that 23 clauses out of  32 clauses 
contained  in the Bill  were  adopted by this Committee without any change.  Recommendations in 
respect other eight clauses excluding clause 1 were duly considered by the Government.  The basic 
issues raised in the Fiftieth Report of the Committee on the Bill were as follows: 
(a)                Rationality of bringing Members of Parliame nt within the purview of the Lokpal, in
view of the Supreme Co urt judgement in the case  of Sh ri P.V. Narsimha Rao Vs. State,
wherein the court has held MPs and MLAs as  public servants who could be prosecuted
under the Prevention of Corruption (PC) Act, 1988; 
(b)               Views and recommendations  of the Committe e of Privileges of Lok Sabha regarding 
procedure to be followed by Lokpal in investigating cases of corruption against Members
of Parliament under the PC Act; and 
(c)                Views of Ethics Committee of the Rajya Sa bha wherein it had not favoured the idea o f 
subjecting the Members to the disciplinary authority of an agency outside the jurisdiction
of the House. 
3.1.3    He shared information regarding status of Report of the Committee of  Privileges (Eleventh Lo k
Sabha) ( under the Chairm anship of Dr. Mallikarjun) on “Ethics, St andards in Public Life,  Privileges,  
Facilities to Members and Other Re lated Matters” (1997) and First Re port of Ethics Committee   o f 
Rajya Sabha.  The Committee of Privileges was of the opinion that Lokpal ma y be empowered to deal
with only those complaints falling under the provisi ons of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.  Afte r
investigation on those com plaints, Lokpal may forward its Re port to the S peaker, Lok Sabha, who ma y

refer the same to the Committees on Ethics and Privileges for suggesting action.  The Committee in turn 
may report back to the Speaker  with its suggestion and actions in such matters.   The said report had not
yet been adopted by the Lok Sabha.   
3.1.4    In relation to First Report of Ethics Committee of Rajya Sabha, the Secretary had stated that the 
same  was presented to Rajya Sabha on 8 December 1988 and  had also been adopted by that House on 
15 December 1999.  The Committee did not favour the idea of subjecting the Members to any 
disciplinary authority of an agency outside the jurisdiction of the House.  Moreover, the Committee was 
in favour of  making the Ethics Committee  a permanent institution of the Rajya Sabha . 
3.1.5    In regard to the issue of  the rationality of bri nging MPs within the purview of Lokpal, the
Secretary informed the Committee th at the matter was de liberated upon by a Group of Ministers, which
recommended exclusion of the MPs  from the purview  of Lokpal  to the Government.  But the Cabinet
decided to retain the MPs alongwit h the Prime Minister wi thin the ambit of Lokpal.  However, the
Cabinet in conformity with the recommendation of Group of Ministers had agreed to delete clause 18 of
Lokpal Bill, 1998 which spoke about the declaration of assets by the Members of Parliament.              
3.2       The Secretary (Personnel) highlighted sa lient features of the Lokp al Bill, 2001 which were as
follows: 
(i)                  The composition of Lokpal would be three-one Chairperson and two Members, for a fix 
term of three years.  While the Chairpers on could be appointed from amongst serving o r
retired Chief Justice of India or a Judge  of Supreme Court, the Members could be
appointed from among the reti red or  serving judges of the Supreme Court  or Chie f
Justices of High  Courts; 
(ii)                The Chairperson  and other members shal l be appointed by the President by warrant
under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the Committee consisting of the Vice
President  of India as Chairman, Prime Minist er, Speaker of the House of the People, the
Minister in charge of the Mi nistry of Home Affairs in th e Government of  India, the
Leader of the House  other than the House in which the Prime Minister is a member, the
Leader of the Opposition in the House  of the People and  the Leader of the Opposition in
the Council of States as members.   
(iii)               The Chairperson and Members of Lokpal woul d not be removed from their  office 
except by  an order made by the Presiden t on the ground of proved misbehaviour o r
incapacity, after an inquiry ma de by a Committee consisting of  the Chief Justice of India
and two other Judges of the Supreme Court next  to the Chief Justice in seniority.  The
Chairman or Member, as the case may be, woul d be  informed of the charges against him
and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges. 
(iv)              The Lokpal would be  given the power of civil court in resp ect of summoning and 
enforcing the attendance of any person an d examining him on oa th, requiring the
discovery and production of any document and receiving  evidence etc. 
(v)                The Lokpal would enquire into complaints  against   public functionaries under the
Prevention of    Corruption  Act 1988 and the expression “public functionaries”  covers 
the  Prime Minister, the Ministers  a nd the Members of the Parliament.  The
constitutional functionaries  such as Judges of Supreme Court, the Election
Commissioner, etc.  have been kept out of ambit of Lokpal.      
4.0       Members raised a number of queries/issues  on the various provisions of the legislation while
expressing their respective viewpo ints on the Bill. Observations of the Members and their queries
centered around  the following points: 
(i)         The le gislation put more em phasis on corru ption b y public functionaries and

understressed  the issue of redressal     of public grievances, which was the rationale for the

(ii)                There was unanimous view on th e issue of not bringing the Prime Minister within the 
ambit of Lokpal but on the issue of keeping M.P.s within the purview of Lokpal differing
views emerged.  One strand of  opinion was that the MPs s hould  not be brought within
the ambit of Lokpal as  
(a)  it would subject them to  the authority of an agency, other than the  House, which
enjoyed broad autonomy under the scheme  of Constitution and may amount to
encroachment  upon the authority and autonomy of Parliament; 
(b)   it would lead to subjecting MPs to one more inquiring agency  in addition  to 
Ethics/Privileges Committees of the respective House and the Central Bureau o f
Investigation/Police,  while public serv ants committing offences  under PC Act, 
1988 were subjected to only one investigating authority i.e. CBI/Police; 
(c)    Lokayukta of States  have no jurisdic tion over MLAs.  Why MPs  should be 
brought within the purview of Lokpal? 
(iv)       The Bill provides for inquiry into  allegations of complain t under  PC Act, 1988.  The
view of the Committee was th at bribery and corruption cases  were cognisable offences 
and had to be investigated unde r the relevant provisions of Code of Criminal Procedure. 
It was pointed out that a pol ice investigation would be done  for a public servant charged
with a ‘corruption offence’ whereas in the case of Member s, it would only be inquired
into.  Further the Bill did not  provide  definition  of the inquiry. What would happen in a
situation when an individual goes to the Police instead of Lokpal against an allegation  of
corruption by a Member of Parliament under Sections, 154 and 200 of Cr. PC? 
(v)        While the inquiry is in progress with Lokpal, is not it possible for the MPs to file case o f
defamation under Sections 182 or 193 or 500 of the Indian Penal Code as many people
can fabricate evidence? Again,  when the matt er is pending with L okpal, a Minister can
ask the Attorney-General/Advocate-General/ Public Prosecutor to file a complaint o f
defamation  under Section 199 of Cr.PC. 
(vi)              Inquiry by Lokpal would be a public inquiry if otherwis e not required to be done in
camera.  How far is it practicable for Ministers/MPs to function fearlessly? 
(vii)             The Supreme Court can transfer  cases against the Ministers or MPs  to any other Court 
of Sessions under section 406 of  the CrPC as indicated in clause 22 of the Bill, which
will be embarrassing for them   
(viii)           The Supreme Court judgment in   JMM Bribery case which declares  MPs to be  public
servant is a divided  judgment (three-two),  which could be modified  by the Supreme 
Court  itself.  A point was raised that MPs were not whole time public servants.  They are
public servants only   to the extent of  putting questions, speaking in the House. 
Subjecting them  to Lokpal for the act done as part of his profession was not appropriate. 
Further,  the MPs are immunized for their act ivities  in Parliament under Art 105 (2) o f
Constitution which had also been upheld by the Supreme Court.

              Thereafter, the Committee took up the Lokpal Bill, 2001 for further consideration. 
6.0       The Chairman briefly outlined the histor y and evolution of the Par liamentary system in the
country and possible implications of the proposed legislation on the futu re of the system in the country. 
He made a passing reference to th e earlier Committees which had ex amined the said legislation in
depth.  He felt that the issue of  bringing the PM and the MPs within the ambit of Lokpal needed careful
and conscious consideration. 
6.1       He requested the Members, who were not present in the last meeting on Lokpal, to make thei r
observations on the Bill first.  Thereafter, othe r members might supplemen t their points expressed
earlier.   He advised the officers of the Ministries to take down poi nts and send their comments to the
Secretariat as early as possible.   
7.0       Members expressed their view- points/observations  on the  Bill  which inter alia  veered around 
the issue  (i) whether the Prime Minister should be  within the ambit of Lokpal ( ii) whether the
Members  of  Parliament should be subjected to multiplicity of authorities leading to double jeopardy as

be brought within the scope of Lokpal? 
7.1       Members were of the unanimous  view th at the Prime Minister shoul d not be brought within the
ambit of Lokpal as its  implications would shake   the foundation of Parliame ntary system built in the
last  fifty-two years.  They obser ved that how  the PM  who enjoyed the confidence of the House of the 
People could function  when allegati ons were brought to the notice of  Lokpal  and that body initiates
inquiry.  A Member opined that even if the PM wa s to be brought  within the scope of Lokpal, some
checks and balances should be provided in the Bill itself particularly in clause 23.  He suggested that the
Lokpal after making preliminary scrutiny  of the complaint against the PM should send it to the
President of India, who may sanction a full inquiry if deemed fit. 
7.2.0    As regards bringing MPs within the ambit of Lokpal, ce rtain Members felt that some
institution/body  to look  into the conduct of Member s of Parliament had beco me necessary as public
perception of the elected   representatives was an unhappy one.  But handing  over the matter to the
retired judges would mean that the constitutional framework was not working properly.  It was stated
that the MPs had been declared  as ‘public    servant’ by the Supreme Court a nd they were to be 
prosecuted  under the PC Act, 1988,  and thus the in clusion of the MPs in th e definition of ‘public 
functionary’  may  amount to double jeopardy and mul tiplicity of proceedings.        The propose d
legislation did not provide  safeguards nor did any sa feguard exist to protect the Members of Parliament
from double jeopardy.

7.2.1    In that context, a member  mentioned that judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Court  had
created safeguards for themselves with  the pronoun cement of judgement in th e K.Veeraswamy case, in
terms of which no FIR could be registered against a Judge of High Court, Chief Justice of High Court or
Judge of the Supreme  Court with out the clearance of the Chief Ju stice of India  and sanctions fo r
launching  prosecution against them  could not be  granted by the Presiden t of India without the
concurrence of the Chief Justice of India. 
7.2.2    That member further menti oned that there should be a law wh ich would entail the prosecuting
agency to take the concurrence of the Pr esiding Officer i.e. Hon’ble Speaker/Hon’ ble Chairman before 
proceeding further and the invest igation should be done by the officer not below the rank o f
Superintendent of Police.  Another member suggested  that the competent author ity in the case of the
MPs should be their re spective Houses which should send the comp laint against them either to a Joint
Parliamentary Committee or Priv ileges Committee or Ethics Com mittee which would decide about
action to be taken i.e. suspension, removal or criminal investigation by the investigating agency within a
particular time frame or the House could even also reprimand the MP at the Bar of the House.  He,
therefore, felt that the proposed legislation contained anomalies and if any law were to be made it should
be self contained and should be made  in consonance with the present sc heme of Law.  In the absence o f
proper law, the matter may be left to the House to ha ve its own mechanism to tackle cases of corruption
by the Members of Parliament. 
7.3       Some members desired that Judges and Chief Justices of the High Courts, Judges of the Supreme
Court and Chief Justice of India should also be brought under the cate gory of ‘Public functionaries’ as 
defined in sub-clause (g) of clause 2 of the Bill.  It was suggested that the President of India could be the 
sanctioning authority for inquiry in to conduct of judges of the High  Courts & the Supreme Court by
Lokpal, for which relevant provisions may be added in clause 23 of the Bill. 
8.0       Views were expressed that  the proposed legislation was an half- baked measure and contained 
serious anomalies.  Anomalies pointed out by the Members were as follows:- 
(i)         Connotations of two terms i.e. ‘Public  functionary’ and ‘complaint’ detailed   in clause 2 
of the Bill are incoherent with the sc heme of Law to the extent that complaint against the

(v)                The Lokpal has no nexus with Parliament as has been the Sw edish Ombudsman and

(vi)              The Legislation does not   a ddress public grievances; rath er focusses its attention on 
bribery and corruption at high places, 
Thus,  it was suggested  that effi cacious law  should be brought to tack le  corruption at high  places as
the Lokpal legislation  appeared to be insufficient. 
8.1       A Member solicited a comprehensive bac kground note in tablular fo rm detailing provisions o f
different Lokpal legislation, problems encountered by it and perspective of different legislation on
Lokayuktas and another note on how misconduct of the Members of Parliament were dealt with in USA,
European and Commonwealth countries.  He desired that  the clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill 
may be deferred till that time. 
8.2       Another Member   suggested that promin ent jurist having experience of social service may be
inducted to Lokpal, who could also be Chairman of the institution of Lokpal. 
8.3       Certain members favoured the passage of  the Bill in the presen t form and suggested that

2.0       The Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and made reference to the history of 
the legislation on Lokpal and Lokayuktas as also to the originater of the idea behind the legislation, who

2.1       Thereafter, he touched upon, in brief, following three major areas emerging out of the 
discussions held on the Bill in the meetings of the Committee so far:- 
(i)                  Whether Lokpal’s jurisdiction should be extended to cover the judiciary? 
(ii)                Whether the institution of Pr ime Minister being privy to so many secret and sensitive 
issues of national interest be brought within the purview of Lokpal? and  
(iii)               Whether MPs should be subjected to the juri sdiction of Lokpal in  view of Supreme
Court judgement declaring  them as public servant and its legal consequences?. 
He felt that those points should be considered b y the Committee at len gth.  He then re quested the

3.0       On the issue of extension of ambit of Lokpal to the Judiciary, some  members expressed  the
opinion that the Lokp al should be broad- based enough to cover judges including Chief Justice of India
as the judiciary was not as clean and as respectable as it used  to be in the past.   Another member while
invoking the concept of “quis custodiet ipsos custodes ?”  (who will guard the gua rdians?), referred to 
one of the observations of the Ad ministrative Reforms Commision that in the discretionary field, 
matters involving acts of justice or  injustice, corruption or favourtism were to be inquired into by the
Lokpal and suggested that since the judiciary had been at times passing orders in a discretionary manner,
it should be  brought  under the Lokpal.  In that c ontext, he informed the Committee that an amendment
to that effect had been submitted by him.  He furt her suggested that the Chie f Justice of India should be
brought within the ambit of Lokpal with some checks and balances i.e. by keeping the President of India
as sanctioning authority for granting permission for initiation of inquiry by Lokpal. 
3.1       Another member was of the view that sinc e the scope of scheme of the present Bill was only in
regard to public functionaries, there was a need to have in place a separate mechanism for the judiciary.  
3.2       A majority of the members were of the opinion that the Prime Minist er being privy to vital
information should not be brought unde r the jurisdiction of Lokpal, as a constitutional process i.e. no
confidence motion was available in the Lok Sabha fo r removing him.  A group of members  opined that
the PM was not above the law of the land and shoul d be brought within th e ambit of Lokpal,  as
envisaged  by the Bill. Another memb er suggested that the  issue  s hould be referred to the larger body
i.e. Parliament, for taking a view thereon.  He opined that in case, the Prime Minister  were to be
brought within the ambit of Lokpal, there should be some sort  of cheeks and balances – providing 
concurrence of the President of India for initiating inquiry against him by the Lokpal. 
3.3.0    As to the issue of keeping of the Members of Parl iament within the ambit of Lokpal, an opinion
was expressed that Members of Pa rliament were public servants sui generis  in accordance with the 
judgement of the Supreme Court.  A nother member expressed  reservations on  the judgement declaring
MPs as public servant as they di d not exercise any executive power  and desired that the Government
might be requested to instruct Attorney General for appealing the Supreme Court to review its decision. 
Another  member opined that  Members of Parliament were under th e discipline  of each  House and its
Privileges/Ethics Committee.  Putting the MPs under the Lokpal would make them subject to the
multiplicity of authoritie s and thus led to encroachment upon the priviledges, authority and  dignity o f
Parliament.  The MPs may be made to appear before Second Class Magistrate as the Supreme Court had
power to transfer cases from the  Lokpal to the Court of Sessions as per clause 22 of the Bill which may
hamper the dignity and privileges of  Members and thereby of the Ho use and suggested deletion of that
clause from the Bill.  Some ot her Members wondered how could the Lokpal have jurisdiction over the
MPs without amending Article 105 of the Constitution. and in th at context, wanted to know the position
of the Government with regard JMM case, wherei n five Supreme Court J udges unanimously had held
the  view  that Section 19 of PC  Act, 1988 be amended to give sa nctioning authority in relation to
prosecution of the MPs.  Anothe r strand of opinion expressed by Members was that Members o f
Parliament should not be subjected to multiplicity of authorities; rather  they should for under the
Privileges /Ethics Committees of th eir respective Houses as precedents  galore where  the functioning o f
those Committees were better than any Commissions of  Inquiry. 
3.3.1    Some members expressed the opinion that MPs should be under the Lokpal as inherent 
safeguards in the form of sanction by competent authority did exist in the Bill. 
3.4       A majority of the me mbers dubbed the   Bill as half – baked legislation, a whole heap o f 
anomalies and pointed out that the following inconsistencies needed to be addressed: 
(i)                  The term “public functionary”  in the Bill included thos e who had been declared as
‘public servant’ by the Supreme Court a nd rationale of usin g the term ‘public 
functionary’ in the place of ‘public servant’.

(ii)                The term ‘inquiry’ had not been defined in the Bill whereas the inquiry as defined by
Cr.P.C. meant inquiry by a Magistrate. 
(iii)               The definition of the term ‘complaint’ as given in the Bill en tailed only inquiry into the 
offence under the PC Act, 1988 which ought to be investigated. 
(iv)              Provisions in the Bill particularly in Clauses 10 to 17 were a queer mixture of provisions 
of Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 and Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.  It amounted to
civil trial of corruption cases  by an inquiry officer which ought to have been done by an
investigating officer. 
(v)                Inquiry into the complaint under the PC Ac t, 1988 by Lokpal as envisaged under clause 
10 of the Bill may creat a situ ation where two parallel authorities would be inquiring and
investigating into the same offence as the Magistrate and Police were not duty- bound to 
keep the complaint pending till the matter was finalised by the Lokpal and the provisions
of Chapters XII and XV of the Cr. P.C. could not be kept in abeyance during that period. 
(vi)              The Bill was silent as to what was to be done after th e charges were proved by the 
Lokpal. 
(vii)             Ranks of Officers to assist Lokpal in conducting inquiry were not specified in the Bill.

camera trial of the public functionaries by the Lokpal.  They felt that the Bill  required further study and

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
  
            In its interim report on the “Probl em of Redress of Citizens ’ Grievances” submitted in 
1966, the administrative Refo rms Commission recommended, inter alia , the setting up of an 
institution of Lokpal. 
             
2. To give effect to this recommendation of the Administrative Reforms Commission, a Bill, namely, the
“Lokpal and the Lokayuktas Bill, 1968” was introduced in the Fourth Lok Sabha in 1968.  The Bill was
considered by a Joint Committee of Parliament a nd the Bill, as reported by the Joint Committee, was
passed by the Lok Sabha in 1969.  While this Bill was pending in Rajya Sabha, the Fourth Lok Sabha
was dissolved and consequently, th e Bill lapsed.  In 1971, the Bill passed by th e previous Lok Sabha
was re-introduced in the Fifth L ok Sabha, namely, the “Lokpal and L okayuktas Bill, 1971”.  This Bill 
also lapsed on the dissolution  of the Fifth Lok Sabha. 
  
3. A fresh Bill calle d the “Lokpal Bill, 1977 ” was introduced in the Sixth Lok Sabha in 1977.  This Bill 
was referred to a Joint Committe e of Parliament which submitted its report in July, 1978.  When the
Bill, as reported by the Joint Comm ittee, was under consideration in the Lok Sabha, the Lok Sabha was
prorogued and was subsequently dissolved and consequently that Bill also lapsed. 
  
4. The Lokpal Bill, 1985 was introduced in the Eighth Lok Sabha and subsequently withdrawn.  The
Lokpal Bill, 1989 which sought to include the office of Prime Minister also within the jurisdiction of the
Lokpal which was to be a three Me mber body was introduced in the Lok Sabha and lapsed with the
dissolution of the Ninth Lok Sabha. 
  
5. The Lokpal Bill, 1996 was introduced in the El eventh Lok Sabha on 13- 9-1996. Thereafter, it was 
referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs for examination
and report.  The Standing Committ ee presented its report to the Pa rliament on 9-5-1997.   Before the 
Government could finalise its st and on the various recommendations of the Committee, the Eleventh
Lok Sabha was dissolved and the Bill also lapsed. 
  
6. The Lokpal Bill, 1998 was introduced  in the Lok Sabha on 3-8-1998.  Th ereafter, it was referred to 
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs for examination and 
report.  The Standing Committee pr esented its Report to the Parlia ment on this Bill on 25-2-1999.  
However, before the Government could take a view on the various recommendations made by the
Parliamentary Standing Committee, the Twelfth Lok Sabha was dissolved and consequently the Bill also
lapsed. 
  
7. The salient features of the proposed Bill are as follows:-   
  
(i) Setting up the office of Lokpal with a Chairperson and two Members for fixed tenure; 
  
(ii) With a view to en suring that the Lokpal is able to  act independently and discharge its
functions without fear or fav our, the Bill provides that the Chairperson or a Member o f
Lokpal shall not be removed from his office, except by an order made by the President on
the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapac ity after an inquiry made by a Committee
consisting of the Chief Justice of India a nd two other Judges of the Supreme Court next
to the Chief Justice in seniority in which th e Chairperson or Member, as the case may be,
had been informed of the char ges a gainst him and given a reasonable o pportunity o f
Page 53 of 6484th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/home_aff/84threport.htm

being heard in respect of those charges;
  
(iii) To enable the Lokpal to function effe ctively and in a quasi- judicial manner, the 
powers of the civil court in respect of summoning and enfo rcing the attendance of any
person and examining him on oath, requiring the discove ry and production of any
document and receiving evidence, etc., have been conferred on the Lokpal; 
  
(iv) The Chairperson and other Members shal l be appointed by the President by warrant
under his hand and seal on th e recommendations of a Comm ittee consisting of the Vice-
President of India, as Chairman, Prime Minist er, Speaker of the House of the People, the
Minister in charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs in the Government of India, Leader of
the House other than the House in which the Prime Minister is a member of Parliament,
the Leader of Opposition in the House of the People and Leader of Opposition in Council
of States as members. 
  
(v) The public functionaries directly or indirectly elected by and responsible to the public,
such as, Members of Parliame nt, Prime Minister and Ministers have been brought within
the purview of the Bill but other constituti onal functionaries such as Judges of the
Supreme Court, the Election Co mmissioners, etc., have been kept out of the purview o f
the Bill. 
  
  
(vi) The Lokpal will inquire into complaints alleging that a public f unctionary as defined
in the Bill had committed an  offence punishable under the prevention of Corruption Act,
1988 and the expression “public functionary” covers the Prime Minister, the Minister, the 
Ministers of State, the Deput y Ministers and the Members of  Parliament.  It seeks to
carry out in this respect the recommenda tions of the Admini strative Reforms
Commission for enabling the citizens to have  recourse to a conve nient and effective
forum for determination of complaints a nd thereby save them from pursuing thei r
remedies through the process of courts. 
  
  
(vii) The Bill also seeks to make special provisions for discouraging frivolous, vexatious 
and false complaints.

conditions of service, allowances and pension payable to him shall not be varied to his disadvantages.

his functions in certain circumstances.

inter alia, of any investigating agencies of the Government and of any other agencies. 
  
            Clause 10  deals with the jurisdiction  of the Lokpal Sub-clause (1 ) seeks to provide that the 
Lokpal may inquire into any matter involved in, or arising from or connected with any allegation made
in a complaint, Sub-clause (2) se eks to provide that the Lokpal may conduct an inquiry  into any act o r 
conduct of any person other than a publ ic functionary concerned  if it  considers necessary to do so fo r
the purposes of his inquiry into any allegation.  Sub-cl ause (3) seeks to provide that no matter in respect 
of which a complaint may be made  under the proposed enactment shall be referred for inquiry under the
Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952. 
  
            Clause 11  seeks to provide that the Lokpal shall not  inquire into any matter concerning any
person if the Chairperson or any ot her Member has any bias in respec t of such matter or person.  This
clause also seeks to provide that the Lokpal shall not inquire into any complaint made after the expiry of
a period of ten years from the date of the commission of the offence mentioned in the complaint.

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 
  
            Sub-clause (1) of clause 3 of the Bill provides for the establishment of the Lokpal consisting of a 
Chairperson and two other Members.  Sub-clause  (3) of clause 6 of th e Bill envisages that the salary, 
allowances and all other conditions of service of, the Chairperson shall be the same as those of the Chief
Justice of India and the Members as those of the Judges of the Supreme Court.  This sub-clause  also 
provides  that the salary payable to the Chairperson and other Members shall be reduced by any pension
and pension equivalent to other pensionary benefits to which th e Chairperson or a Member may be
entitled to in respect of any previous service under  the Government of India or under the Government of
a State. 
  
8.33     Sub-clause (1) of clause 9 provides that th e Lokpal shall, for the purpos e of assisting it in the
discharge of its functions under the Bill, appoint a Secretary and such  other officers and employees as
the President may determine, from time to time, in consultation with L okpal.  Sub-clause (2) of clause 9 
empowers the Lokpal to secure for the purpose  of  dealing with any comp laint or any classes o f
complaints, the services  of any of ficer or employee or investigating agency of the Central Government
or a State Government with the c oncurrence of that  Government or the servi ces of any other person o r
agency.  The terms and conditions of such officers, employees, agencies  and persons shall be such as
the President may determine, from time to time, in consultation with the Lokpal. 
  
8.34     Clause 18 of the Bill provides that the salari es, allowances and pensions payable to, or in respect
of, the Chairperson and Members of the Lokpal, shal l be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund
of India. 
  
8.35     At this stage, it is not possible to give precise details of the expenditure to be incurred on the
Lokpal.  It is, however, expected that the Bill, wh en enacted, will involve  a non-recurring expenditure 
of rupees seventy-five lakhs and a recurring expenditure of rupees one crore and fifty lakhs in a year. In 
case it becomes necessary to cons truct a building to house the establ ishment of the Lokpal, additional
expenditure of a non-recurring nature of the orde r of rupees one crore a nd fifty lakhs may also be
involved. 
  
8.36     The Bill, if enacted, is not likely to involve any other recurring or non-recurring expenditure.

INTRODUCTION
                        I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having
been authorised by  the Committee to submit  the Report on its behalf, do hereby present  this Eighty-fifth  Report of the
Committee   on “Law’s Delays: Arrears in Courts”.  This comprehensive  report dealing with the Judicial Reforms
purports to go a long way in improving our Judicial system.
2.0       The Indian Judicial System may be one of the best judicial systems in the world, but the figures, which follow,
raise questions which cause anxiety.  The bewildering statistics reveal the magnitude of the problem: over 20 million
cases pending in the District/Subordinate Courts;  3.5 million cases pending in High Courts; Madhya Pradesh, Patna,
Rajsthan, and Calcutta High Courts have cases pending since 1950, 1951, 1956 and 1955 respectively; percentage of
under-trials in India is 73% of our total jail population; inhuman conditions of women under-trials; no separate jail
rooms for women except in Tihar Jail in the entire country, to give only a few examples.  There are only 10.5  Judges per
million of our  population, and that is  one of the lowest in the world;  the number of vacancies in the Subordinate Courts
is  1900 against the total strength of 12500 (about 15% of the total strength) and  170  in High Courts as against  the total
strength of 647 (about 26% of the total strength). The budget allocation for judiciary is only 0.2 percent of the GNP, out
of which 50 percent i.e. 0.1 percent is realised from the court revenues.
2.1       The situation in Committee’s opinion is alarming. Preparing and implementing a blueprint of comprehensive
reform should be regarded as one of the highest priorities on our national agenda.
2.2       Considering the immense scope and the wide ambit of Judicial Reforms, it was necessary to identify a specific
problem area.  The issues which arose for  the Committee’s deliberations, included inter alia vacancies of judges;
pendency of cases in courts; specific action plans to tackle them; centrally sponsored scheme for infrastructural 
development  of the judiciary;  need for amendment in the  Memorandum of Procedure of Appointment  of Judges of
Supreme Court and High Courts; improvement  in the quality of judgements;  and the need to tune our  legal system  to
the  post-WTO and the international  patent  regime;  increasing the sanctioned strength of Judges  of High Courts and
Subordinate  Courts; setting up of benches of Supreme Court and High Courts; setting up of  tribunals  to decide 
disputes  relating to  matrimony, education, elections petitions, company matters; increase in the age of retirement of
High Court and Supreme Court Judges; adjournments; provision of loans to young lawyers  for libraries and computers; 
use of retired judicial human resource to dispose of pending  cases;  procedural  reforms  to curb delays;  providing
modern infrastructural facilities up to the subordinate courts;  alternative  dispute  resolution  mechanism;  introduction
of case management  system  in the courts; and  classification,  categorization  and bunching of cases.
3.0       To do justice to the subject of judicial reforms I, on behalf of  the  Committee on Home Affairs,  reconstituted
 the   Sub-Committee  on Judicial Reforms on 17 May, 2000 with Dr. L.M. Singhvi, a Member of the Committee and
Senior Advocate, as its Convenor and Shri Hansraj Bhardwaj, Shri Sangh Priya Gautam, Shri S. Ramachandran Pillai,
Shri Raj Mohinder Singh, Shri C.P. Thirunavukkarasu, Shri Kuldip Nayyar, Smt. Jayashree Banerjee, Shri P.H. Pandian,

 REPORT
1.         The dictum ‘Justice Delayed Is Justice Denied’ postulates that an unreasonable delay in the administration of
justice constitutes an unconscionable denial of justice.    The mounting arrears in the trial and appellate courts  coupled
with increased institution of court cases on account of the awareness of rights on the part of the citizens, enactment of
numerous laws creating new rights and obligations, industrial development in the country, increased trade and
commerce  and legislative and administrative measures touching  the lives  of citizens at all levels, have assumed 
serious proportions.   The total number of pending cases at present amount to a staggering 24 million [1]
 in all the courts
taken together in the country.  A large number of unfilled vacancies of Judges and a  low Judge-population ratio across
the board have caused a formidable accumulation of arrears and shockingly inordinate delays in the disposal of cases
with the result that at the zenith of its many outstanding achievements in aid of Democracy and Rule of Law, the Indian
judiciary is face to face with an incipient darkness at noon and with challenges which can only be met with constructive
cooperation between the three branches of the Government, the fourth estate, and we, the people of India.
 
Law’s Delays & Delays in Disposal of Cases
2.         The expression ‘Judicial Reforms’ involves a critical appreciation and assessment of the existing system of laws
and administration of justice with a view to make it more vibrant, receptive and enable it to meet the demand of the
time.  The courts in India function according to the procedure laid down in the Criminal Procedure Code, Civil
Procedure Code, Indian Evidence Act and procedures laid down in Parliamentary and delegated legislation.
 
3.0 A classic case, one among several cases,  which epitomizes the Law’s delays and delay in the disposal of cases is the
one related to assassination of late Shri  L.N.Mishra, the then Union Minister for Railways who was killed in an
explosion in a public meeting at Samastipur on January 2, 1975. Since the trial proceedings started the case has been 
transferred to as many as nine judges.  The trial court has so far been able to record the statements of only two accused
persons out of seven despite a court’s directive for a day-to-day hearing to expedite the matter. Many important
witnesses had to be dropped either because they remained untraced or because they did not come forward for deposition.
The protracted proceedings inevitably  create a tangled web of anomalies.2
 
3.1   To remove the bottlenecks arising out of the inherent deficiencies in law which results in the law’s delays and

SUB-COMMITTEE

accelerate the disposal of cases, there is a need to amend the existing statutes i.e. the High Court Acts and Rules, Civil
Procedure Code, Criminal Procedure Code, Indian Evidence Act and other procedural laws.  It is also imperative to
augment the strength of courts to provide them full physical and functional facilities, institute alternative modes of
disposal and provide modern information technology to courts.
 
Proposed Amendments in Criminal Procedure Code            
 
4.         The Law Commission of India in its 154
th Report (1996)  has made a number of  recommendations for speedy
disposal of criminal cases. The Committee requested the Ministry of Home Affairs to apprise it of the status of
implementation of the recommendations. The Ministry informed the Sub-Committee that the report was referred to all
the State Governments/Union Territory Administrations for their views/comments as the Criminal Law and Criminal
Procedure are on the Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule  to the Constitution of India and Criminal laws are
administered by the State Governments. After repeated reminders and convening regional meetings, views of the State
Governments may be summed up as follows:
 
(i)         Most of the States  appreciated the recommendations of the Law Commission contained in its 154
th
Report on the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.  Some of the States have set up Committees to consider the
implications of  the Law Commission’s Report.
 
(ii)
                On the point of separate investigating Agency, while the states commended the idea behind the proposal,
they expressed apprehensions as to its practicability on account of financial implications.
 
(iii)     Some States  expressed the view that the provisions relating to anticipatory bail should be restricted in its
application.  There should be no bar to arrest  the person by the police during the pendency of the application for
anticipatory bail.  After charge sheet  is filed, anticipatory bail should not be granted.
 
(iv)
              There was general agreement that many more offences be made compoundable.
 
(v)
                On the subject of maintenance of wife, children and parents, the proposal of the Law Commission to
raise the maximum ceiling from the present Rs.500 to Rs.5000 was welcomed by all except Meghalaya which
said that this proposed ceiling should be reconsidered.  One State expressed the view that some minimum amount
of maintenance should also be prescribed. However, in view of the cost of living index rising constantly,
retention of a maximum ceiling is not justified. If a ceiling is prescribed and retained, it would require periodic
revision taking into account the inflation and rise in the cost of living as well as amendment of provisions of the
Act from time to time. This would consume time. Accordingly the Government had introduced a Bill i.e. The
Code of Criminal Procedure ( Amendment) Bill, 2001, in the Rajya sabha on 7 August, 2001, to amend section
125 and make consequential changes in section 127 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to remove the ceiling in
maintenance allowance. This Bill has since been passed by Parliament and enacted as Act No. 50 of 2001. 
 
 
(vi)
              Concept of plea bargaining found favour with most of the States.[2]
 ( vii)  As regards victimology,  control of victimization  and protection of victims of crimes,   there was general
agreement, but it was considered necessary that nature of the crime, victim and amount of compensation for each
offence should be duly considered and laid down.
 
(viii) Some States expressed the view that for minor offences of regulatory nature, there need not be strict
separation between the Judiciary and the Executive.  The Executive Magistrates may be given the power to try
and dispose them of.  Such offences are generally victimless crimes.  One State suggested that cases of
maintenance may be given to Executive Magistrates, for granting interim relief after a short inquiry and
thereafter the case may be passed on to the Judicial Magistrate concerned.
 
(ix)              One State suggested that Section 9 of the Cr.P.C. be amended on the lines of Section 11 thereof with a

view to enable the State Government to establish Special Courts of Sessions Judges.  It further suggested that in
cases triable by Sessions Court, there should not be any committal proceeding of cases triable by them.
 
(x)                The concept of Nyaya Panchayat [3] was welcomed by most of the States.
(xi)              Almost all the States agreed on the concept of establishing independent Directorate of Prosecution. 
Most of them, already have them.  States were also of the view that the Directorate of Prosecution should be
neither under the police nor under the Home Department.  It should only be under the Department of Law to
ensure its independence.
 
(xii)      One State noting that the subject matter of penal law and criminal procedure is in the Concurrent List,
expressed the view that there need not be uniform law for the whole country.  States may have their own
amendments, suitable to their needs.
 
 5.        The Home Ministry further informed that some other  recommendations  of the Commission did not call for an
amendment to the Code and, accordingly, were referred to the State Governments for implementation in November,
1997.
 
6.       The Committee was further informed that in the meanwhile, the Government has constituted a Committee in
January 2001, under the Chairmanship of Shri Justice V.S. Malimath, formerly Chief Justice of Karnataka/Kerala High
Courts, to suggest measures to revamp Criminal Justice System.   The terms of reference of the Committee are :-
 
(i)
                  To examine the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence, including the
constitutional provisions relating to criminal jurisprudence and see if any modifications or
amendments are required thereto;
 
(ii)
                To examine in the light of findings on fundamental principles and aspects of criminal
jurisprudence as to whether there is a need to rewrite the Code of Criminal Procedure, the
Indian Penal Code and the Indian Evidence Act to bring them in tune with the demand of the
times and in harmony with the aspirations of the people of India;
 
(iii)
               To make specific recommendations on simplifying judicial procedures and practices and
making the delivery of justice to the common man closer, faster, uncomplicated and
inexpensive;
 
(iv)              To suggest ways and means of developing such synergy among the judiciary, the
prosecution and the police as restores the confidence of the common man in the criminal
justice system by protecting the innocent and the victim and by punishing unsparingly the
guilty and the criminal;
 
(v)
                To suggest sound system of managing, on professional lines, the pendency of cases at
investigation and trial stages and making the police, the prosecution and the judiciary
accountable for delays in their respective domains; and      
 
(vi)
              To examine the feasibility of introducing the concept of “federal crime” which can be put on
List I in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India.
 
  7.       The Committee has been informed that the Malimath Committee was asked to submit  its report within six
months. However, it has now been given extension up to 31 March 2002. The Committee welcomes the setting up of this
Committee to go into the revamping of the criminal justice system and  is hopeful that its recommendations would be far
reaching as far as revamping of the criminal justice system is concerned. The Committee would also expect of the
Government to speedily process the recommendations and thereafter implement those which are found acceptable.

Amendment in the Civil Procedure Code
 
8.0       The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which contains the law relating to the procedure in suits and civil
proceedings, has been amended from time to time. Of late, Parliament has enacted the Code of Civil Procedure
(Amendment) Act, 1999, with a view to cutting short the delays at various levels. After the Bill was enacted, the same
could not be brought into force in view of the lawyers’ protests and agitations. Subsequently the Government while
reconsidering the matter regarding reduction in delay in the disposal of civil cases, after consultation with legal
luminaries and Bar Council of India and other concerned, has proposed to further amend the Code of Civil Procedure,
1908 in the form of the Code of Civil Procedure, (Amendment) Bill, 2000, which was referred to the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home  Affairs, which has since presented its report to the Parliament on 20
November,2001.
 
8.1    The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 would be given simultaneous effect after the enactment of
the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000.  Both the legislations will go a long way in expediting the disposal
of cases.  Major provisions contained in the said Act/Bill are as follows:
 
(i)
                  No Letters Patent Appeal (LPA) against the decree pronounced by the High Court in the exercise of its
original power is permissible under section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure;
 
(ii)
                Introduction of  approved modern means of transmission (i.e. speed post, fax, courier, electronic mail)
for sending summons through the process server at the expense of plaintiff.  In addition, summons can
also be served by the plaintiff on defendants;
 
(iii)               Prescription of time limit of thirty days from the date of summons for submitting written argument by
the defendant in his defence, which could be extended upto the maximum period of ninety days by the
Court for reasons to be recorded;
 
(iv)              Requirement of filing document in support of evidence at the time of filing of suit.  New document can
be produced in support of evidence subsequent to commencement of trial with the leave of the Court;
 
(v)                Conditional amendments to the plaint after the commencement of trial in case of (a) change in law
subsequent to the framing of the issues and (b) new fact coming to knowledge of the applicant which
could not have been discovered by him with due diligence before framing the issue);
 
(vi)
              A few measures to check prolix oral argument:
(a)                submission of concise written argument by the party before the argument, which would form part
of record of the court and submitted to the opposite party;
(b)               no adjournment to be granted for filing written argument unless permitted by the court for reasons
to be recorded;
(c)                time limit to be fixed by the court for oral argument.
(vii)             Examination-in-Chief of a witness in the form of affidavit and the admissibility of the document filed in
affidavit lies with the court.  
 
9. Coming to the core theme of this report, a brief analysis of pendency of cases in various courts and their efforts,
successful or otherwise, to reduce it have been given in succeeding paragraphs.

10.       Long pendency of cases in Supreme Court, High Courts and Sub-ordinate Courts has become a matter of serious
concern.  A statistical presentation of number of pending cases relating to Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate
Courts and analysis thereof is given below:-

Pendency in the Supreme Court
 
11.       The pendency of cases in the Supreme Court has shown a downward trend.  The pendency of cases which was
1,04,936 as on 31.12.1991 came down to 58,794 in 1994 and further  down to 21, 995 as on 31 October, 2001.[4]
 
Supreme Court’s Tryst with Pendency
12.       The Supreme Court has taken certain steps which have resulted in a substantial reduction in accumulated arrears.
It has successfully implemented the cardinal principles of Active Case Flow Management Technique (ACMT) by
creating dual tracks, one for keeping abreast of current filings and the other to deal with old pending matters.[5]  It is a
model which commends itself to us and which can be replicated for dealing with the arrears in the High Courts and
Subordinate Courts.  A report on “Modernisation of Civil Justice System in India: Implementation Plan”, prepared by
The Study Team constituted by the National Judicial Academy and submitted to the Hon’ble Cheif Justice of India, may
be referred to for detail discussion on the monitoring, co-ordination and case-flow tracking.
 
13.       Another area where the Apex Court has concentrated its energy is on adjournments.  Adjournments have been
made an exception.  Adjournments in the Supreme Court can never be taken for granted and cases scheduled for a
particular date are invariably listed on that day.  Indeed, listing is entirely computer-managed, except for extremely
urgent listing required within less than 15 days for which a special oral mention has to be made to the Chief Justice.
 
14.       In the Apex Court, the cases listed for a day which were earlier adjourned owing to the absence of any Judge are
now immediately redistributed on the very day over the remaining benches and thus dealt with or disposed of on the
same day, despite an inevitably enhanced work load for each bench.
 
15.       Bench stabilization in the Apex Court over three-month or six-month periods ensures that the same or similar
subjects out of the 56 computer classified subjects go to the same benches as far as possible, thus expediting disposal.
 
16.       On the Human Resource front, the Apex Court has made efforts to streamline the distribution of work in all the
departments  in  such  a way  that  intra-departmental  and inter-departmental file movement can be minimized.  It has
reorganized the staff strength depending on the filings and pendency.
 
17.       The Apex Court has made use of the computer in the most effective way.  Computerization at every level in the
Department of Registry has considerably increased efficiency.  Maximum information covering numerous fields and
criteria are fed into the computer in respect of each case, thus ensuring maximum information retrieval at the touch of a
button and a Judis Programme has already incorporated all Supreme Court judgements into the computer.
 
18.       In addition, the following steps have also been taken in the Apex Court:
a)         More practical categorization and grouping of cases involving similar questions of law.
 
b)
                  No accumulation of defective matters;
 
c)                  Reservation of sufficient slots for old, pending, miscellaneous and SLP matters so that they are listed in
chronological order in sufficient numbers.

Vacancies of Judges
 
31.0   The following procedure was followed for filling up of vacancies of judges before the judgement of the Supreme
Court.: Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be  appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after
consultation with such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the States as the President may
deem necessary for the purpose.  In the case of appointment of a judge other than the Chief Justice of India, the Chief
Justice of India was always required to be consulted vide article 124 of the Constitution.
 
31.1     The Judges of the High Courts were appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India,
the Governor of the State and in the case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of the
High Court Vide article 217 (1) of the Constitution.
 
31.2     Pre-1993 Status: Before 1993, the process of appointment of Judges of High Courts and Supreme Court was
required to be initiated by the Executive i.e. Department of Justice, as far as possible  6 months prior to the date of
vacancy.  There were delays in filling the vacancies during that period also but the Government was answerable and
accountable to Parliament.
 
31.3 Post-1993 Scenario: After the Judgement of the Supreme Court in Advocates-on-Record Association vs. Union of
India and others on October 6, 1993, a proposal for appointment of a Judge cannot be initiated by the Government.
According to the Judgement of October 6, 1993, read with the Advisory Opinion of October 28, 1998, of the Supreme
Court of India, the initiation of the proposal for appointment of a Judge in the Supreme Courtmust be by the Chief
Justice of India and in the case of a High Court by the Chief Justice of that High Court.  For transfer of a Judge/Chief
Justice of a High Court to another High Court, the proposal has to be initiated by the Chief Justice of India. 
 
31.4     As per the Revised Memorandum of Procedure for the appointment of Chief Justices and judges of the High
Courts, the Governor, as advised by the Chief Minister,  was required to forward his recommendation to the Union 
Minister of Law, Justice and Company Affairs an as early as possible but not later than six weeks from the date of
receipt of the proposal from the Chief Justice of the High Court.  If the comments were not received within that time
frame, it was to be presumed by the Union Minister of Law, Justices and Company Affairs that the constitutional
authorities of the State (i.e. Governor or Chief Minister) have nothing to add to the proposal.  The Union Minister of
Law, Justice and Company affairs was then to consider the recommendations in the light of such other reports as might
be available to the Government in respect of the names under consideration.
 
31.5.   The complete material would then be forwarded to the Chief Justice of India for his advice.  The Chief Justice of
India would,  in consultation with two senior most Judges of the Supreme Court, form his opinion in regard to a person
to be recommended for appointment to the High Court.  The Chief Justice of India and the collegium of two Judges of

the Supreme Court were to take into account the views of the Chief Justice of the High Court and of those Judges of the
High Court who have been consulted by the Chief Justice as well as views of those Judges in the Supreme Court who are
conversant with the affairs of that High Court.  After consultations, the Chief Justice of India was expected to send his
recommendation to the Union Minister of Law, Justice and Company Affairs within four weeks.  The Union Minister of
Law, Justice and Company Affairs was required to put up as early as possible, preferably, within three weeks, the
recommendation of the Chief Justice of India to the Prime Minister who would then  advise the President in the matter of
appointment.
 
Inordinate delay in filling up of vacancies
           
31.6     After the Judgement of the Supreme Court in 1993, the Government is bereft of  role in initiating the process of
filling up of the vacancies.   The maximum the Government can do is to addresses letters to the Chief Minister of the
States and the Chief Justices of the High Courts, from time to time requesting them to make their recommendations for
appointment of judges in the High Courts to fill up vacancies expeditiously.   There appears to be a widespread non-
observance of any strict time frame at different levels in respect of filling up vacancies.
 
 
31.7     The judiciary in whom the power and the responsibility now vest has failed to fill up the vacancies in judicial
posts promptly and punctually and those vacancies of judges in all courts contribute to the huge pendency in a big way.
Though the vacancies in the Supreme Court have been filled up recently, but the situation has not improved in the High
Courts and Subordinate Courts. Tabular presentation of status of vacancies of Judges in Supreme Court, High Court and
Sub-ordinate Courts is given below.  It is for the judiciary to identify and rectify the causes of delay in the existing
system.  It may be that the modes of collegiate consultation have led to a peculiar species of “the politics of the
judiciary”.  Members of the collegium are prone to filed candidates of their choice.  The give and take in the collegiate
consultation has the potential of undermining merit.  It is also fraught with the potential of undermining the office of the
Chief Justice and his primacy.  On the other hand, the Executive is unable to secure due consideration of its own inputs
in respect of the personal and professional standing of the candidate.  More often than not a transferred Chief Justice in a
High Court is unfamiliar with the situation.  As a result, there are unacceptable delay witout the benefit of a higher
quality in the intake.  The challenge is for
the judiciary, the Parliament and the Executive is to find a viable solution within the framework of “independence” and
“accountability”.
