LEFT WING EXTREMISM
43.       Left wing extremism has been posing one of the biggest challenges on the internal security front.  Several States,
namely, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and two of newly
created States of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh have been bearing the brunt of violence unleashed by the protagonists of
this kind of extremism viz. CPML-PW and MCC.  These groups have been making concerted efforts to militarise their
cadres through formation of special guerilla squads and extend their activities over larger areas of the country.  Not just
that, they are now forging links with Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist).  These groups have even envisaged a Compact
Revolutionary Zone (CRZ) by linking up their strongholds spread across Telangana, Dandkaranya, Bihar, Jharkhand and
Chhattisgarh in India and areas of influence of Communist Party of Nepal (CPN-Maoist).  The violence unleashed by
these extremist groups has seen an upsurge in 2001 after having been in doldrums since 1996.  The Ministry of Home
Affairs has informed that some of the violent incidents occurred in 2001, were due to the protest actions of PWG and
MCC for declaring them as terrorist organizations under the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance, 2001. 
43.1     In reply to a query as to what measures had been taken to quell the spurt in the violence, the Ministry of Home
Affairs replied that ‘Public Order’ and ‘Police’ being State subjects, it was for the concerned State Governments to devise
various methods and take concrete steps to curb left wing extremist activities in the States.  However, keeping in view the
overall dimensions of left wing extremism, a Coordination Centre headed by the Union Home Secretary with Chief
Secretaries and Directors General of Police of the seriously affected States, as its members, regularly reviewed and
coordinated steps taken by the States to check left wing extremist activities, monitored the plan of action in respect of
each State and made recommendations both on development and security aspects of the problem.  Several important
decisions such as providing financial support from the Central Government for combating left wing extremist activities,
preparation of plans for development of affected areas, to tackle the problem in a holistic manner, sharing of intelligence
inputs, and providing assistance of para military forces on need basis, etc. had been taken by the Coordination Centre and
effectively followed-up.  CPML-Peoples War (PW) and Maoist Communist Centre (MCC) and their formations and front
organizations had been notified as Terrorist Organisations under the provisions of the Prevention of Terrorism (Second)
Ordinance 2001 to enable the States to take effective action against them.  In order to curb Maoist activities on the Indian
soil along Indo-Nepal Border, Special Service Bureau (SSB) personnel had been deployed in the border States of
Uttaranchal, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal covering the districts of Pithoragarh, Champawat, Udham Singh
Nagar of Uttaranchal, Pilibhit and part of Lakhimpur Kheri of Uttar Pradesh, Purbi Champaran, Madhubani, Piprakoti,
Kishanganj, Sitamarhi, Supaul of Bihar and Darjeeling in West Bengal.  State Governments had also been advised to gear
up their intelligence machinery for collection and sharing of intelligence from the field, particularly with regard to
possible plans of sympathizers of CPN (M) to hold meetings, raise funds and organize logistic support.  States had also
been advised that any attempts of Maoist elements to seek sanctuary would have to be firmly deterred and a close watch
kept on movement of arms, ammunition and explosives to and from Nepal.
43.2     The Home Secretary, in his presentation before the Committee, also informed that the magnitude as well as the
intensity of left wing extremist violence registered an upsurge for the first time since 1996 with 1208 incidents and 564

MONSTER OF COMMUNALISM
45.       Communalism has been the bane of modern India.  It acted as a midwife in the partition of India and even after
that it continues to plague the social fabric of the country.  It has acquired different forms and dimensions over the years. 
However, in the recent years it is rearing its ugly head in an organized manner much in the same way as it did in the years
preceding the partition.  There are several forces which work tirelessly to ensure that it does not lose it momentum.  These
forces are the real anti-national elements who are bent upon tearing the social fabric of the nation apart.  In their zeal to
gain foothold in their respective communities, these forces are stoking communal fire.  Their actions are spreading venom
in the society which threatens to be divided along communal lines.  These attempts to create a communal divide in the
society are one of the biggest challenges before the Indian polity.  Therefore, it needs to be nipped in the bud before it
grows too large to be controlled.  It is the considered view of this Committee that the Government must make honest and
sincere efforts to maintain the pluralistic character of the society and bring all right thinking elements of all communities
together to try and find ways to check the growing divide between them.
POLITICISATION OF POLICE FORCES
46.       Indian police system is a relic of the British colonialism.  Various Commissions and Committees set up from time
to time to suggest the measures necessary to purge the system have come out with a plethora of suggestions and
recommendations.  These recommendations have not at all been implemented  by some States and where they have been
implemented their letter and spirit has not been followed.  As a result of that, Indian police system continues to be
plagued by several ills.  Some of these ills were inherited by it from its colonial masters while some have crept into it as it
has evolved in the post-colonial period.  In the post-colonial period, it has been made to subserve the ruling elite.  This
has   raised  a  big  question mark over the  objectivity and
impartiality of the police.  Today we have a police which is politicized and politically polarized.  For it has become a
pawn in the hands of its masters.  In return, policemen get political patronage which has become essential for their
survival.  These days police personnel are found to be divided in camps with each camp having its own political leanings. 
This connivance of the police with the powers that be is giving rise to cynicism among people who are not only losing
faith in the police but also in the democratic principles of our polity.  These are, by all means, very dangerous signs for
the continuance and survival of democracy.  What can be more dangerous than a situation when people are losing faith in
as vital an institution as the police?
47.       In this backdrop, the Committee feels that there is need for a serious introspection by all concerned.  The
Government must act fast to stem the rot which has set in.  If immediate steps are not taken to set the house in order, there
are dangers of the system falling prey to these degenerating developments.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Government should make earnest efforts to depoliticise the institution of police before it becomes too late to retrieve it
from the morass of degeneration.  It must be ensured that police remains accountable only to the law of the land.

modernization of police forces is the primary responsibility of the State Governments.  However, the Central Government

police forces.  For, an efficient and modernized police is a sine qua non for proper maintenance of internal security.  With

REVAMP OF INTELLIGENCE APPARATUS
51.       Large scale intrusion of foreign mercenaries and Pak army regulars in Kargil in 1999 woke up the Indian
establishment to the need for a systemic overhaul of the intelligence set up.  Intrusions in Kargil proved a watershed
development for the overhaul of intelligence apparatus.  In the aftermath of Kargil war, a Group of Ministers (GoM) on
National Security was constituted to deliberate upon various issues and questions relating to the national security in a
comprehensive manner.  The report of the GoM was considered and accepted by the Government in May 2001.  The
Report focused on the areas of intelligence apparatus, internal security, border management and defence.  As regards
intelligence apparatus, the GOM has recommended the setting up of an Intelligence Coordination Group (ICG), a
Technology Coordination Group (TCG) and a National Technical Facility Organisation (NTFO).  The establishment of
these groups is aimed at ensuring better flow of intelligence inputs and providing strategic facilities and equipment.  In
addition to this, the GoM has also recommended the constitution of a Joint Task Force on Intelligence and a Multi-
Agency Centre in the Intelligence Bureau Headquarters as well as Inter-State Intelligence Support Teams and Multi-
Agency Centres in the States under the aegis of the Intelligence Bureau.  This entire paraphernalia is being put in place to
see that intelligence apparatus of the country is fully geared up, equipped and vigilant to ward off the nefarious designs of
divisive forces and the enemies.
52.       The Committee is satisfied to note the steps being taken to revamp the entire intelligence apparatus.  It hopes that
the new set-up will function smoothly.  However, with too many groups and agencies entrusted with different aspects of
intelligence, the real problem arises in regard to proper coordination amongst all of them.  The Committee hopes that all

53.       Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) has been marshalling all its resources to destabilize India.  In order to
set its sinister designs against India into motion, it has spun a web of its operatives across the length and breadth of the
country.  These operatives with the help of their local connections work ceaselessly not just to foment trouble but also to
aid and abet troublemakers.  As part of this strategy, ISI is providing financial assistance towards setting up of religious
fundamentalist institutions along Indo-Nepal border.  These institutions not only provide safe sanctuaries to ISI’s
handpicked men but also indoctrinate young minds to wage a holy war against India.  In other words, these institutions
have become breeding ground for anti-India elements.  The Ministry of Home Affairs, in response to a query as to

being misused by ISI activists for subversive activities against India.

call of the ISI to destabilize India.  The audacity with which ISI is using both Indian people and soil, that too for
destabilizing and disintegrating India, is really condemnable.  The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to
leave no stone unturned to root out such institutions and the activists being harboured by them   before any irreparable

said Committee made an in-depth examination of the report and furnished its recommendations to the Government on the
basis of which the Ministry firmed up its views on the various recommendations contained in BPR&D’s report.  The
Ministry further informed that the recommendations as accepted by the Ministry of Home Affairs would entail a huge
expenditure both in regard to creation of substantial number of additional posts and modernization of the force. 
Accordingly, Delhi Police had been advised to prioritise various schemes for strengthening of the Force so that the
accepted recommendations were implemented in a phased manner over a reasonable period of time.
63.       BPR&D’s report on manpower requirements and modernization needs of Delhi Police seems to have got trapped
in the usual bureaucratic quagmire. As a result of that the implementation of the report is lying in the lurch. The attitude
of the Ministry towards the report seems to be casual. Although it has accepted some of the recommendations as
contained in BPR&D’s report, it has not carried out any exercise to work out the cost of their implementation.  It has
merely stated that it would entail huge expenditure.  Similarly, it has not set any timeframe for the implementation of the
report.  By stating that the accepted recommendations would be implemented in a phased manner over a reasonable
period of time, the Ministry has given the impression that it seems to be groping in the dark.
64.       The manner in which the Ministry of Home Affairs is dealing with BPR&D’s report raises serious doubts over its
intentions vis-à-vis the implementation  of the report.  If the Ministry was really sincere about the implementation of the
report, it should have chalked out a concrete timeframe for its implementation after working out costs of its
implementation.  Instead, it has dropped the ball once again in the court of Delhi Police.  The whole exercise appears to
be aimed at putting the implementation of the report on the backburner.  In view of this, the Committee reiterates its
earlier recommendation as contained in its 73
rd Report that the Ministry of Home Affairs should first set a definite
timeframe within which the recommendations of BPR&D will be implemented.  Similarly, the estimated costs of
implementation of the recommendations should be worked out and necessary budgetary provisions be earmarked over the
period of implementation of the recommendations.
65.       While going into the details of traffic management in Delhi during the examination of Demands for Grants (2001-
2002), the Committee, in its 73 rd Report thereon, had recommended for setting up of a Unified Traffic Management
Authority in Delhi.  The Ministry of Home Affairs had referred the recommendations to the Government of NCT of Delhi
for obtaining their considered views to enable it to take the decision in the matter in its proper perspective.  In reply to a
query as to what follow up action had been taken by the Government of NCT of Delhi in regard to the setting up of the
recommended authority, the Ministry of Home Affairs informed that the Government of NCT of Delhi had with regard to
the recommendations for setting up of a Unified Transport Management Authority, informed that it was not possible for
them under the existing frame-work to bring about an integrated legislation for setting up of a Unified Transport
Management Authority as Delhi Legislative Assembly was not empowered to legislate with respect to matters connected
with “Police” and “Land”.  The Ministry further informed that it had, however, accepted the recommendation made by
BPR&D in its study report for setting up of a Traffic Advisory Committee under the Chairmanship of the Commissioner
of Police with the representatives drawn from the Government of NCT of Delhi, local bodies and Delhi Development
Authority to continuously monitor such aspects of road engineering and road furniture as help smooth flow of traffic.
66.       The proposal to set up a Traffic Advisory Committee under the Chairmanship of Commissioner of Police, Delhi
falls short of an independent Traffic Management Authority.  The idea behind setting up of such an authority was to
ensure that traffic management was viewed with an integrated approach.  However, that idea seems to have not gone
down well with the policy makers of the Ministry of Home Affairs.  By linking it with a somewhat identical
recommendation as contained in the report of BPR&D, the Ministry has sought to put the setting up of the authority also
on the backburner.  Therefore, the Committee strongly reiterates its earlier recommendation as contained in its 73
rd
Report that the Government should set up a Unified Traffic Management Authority vested with the powers of overall
planning and management of traffic in Delhi.
67.       The satisfaction level of residential accommodation for the personnel of Delhi Police continues to be static
primarily because of the inability of the PWD of Government of NCT of Delhi to satisfactorily cater to the requirements
of Delhi Police because of their commitments elsewhere.  To overcome this hurdle in raising the satisfaction level, the
Committee had recommended for setting up of a Housing Corporation for Delhi Police.  As the proposal did not find
favour with the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Committee endorsed the proposal of the Ministry to carve out a separate
dedicated wing out of the PWD to cater to the housing needs of Delhi Police.  However, this proposal too could not

of Home Affairs will raise the satisfaction level of residential accommodation for the personnel of Delhi Police.  It,
therefore, urges upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to come out with some concrete proposals to raise the housing
satisfaction level of Delhi Police in the next couple of years to a fairly satisfactory level.
SITUATION IN PUNJAB
68.       The Home Secretary, in his presentation, apprised the Committee that the recent inputs indicated that Pak based
terrorists of Khalistan Commando Force (Panjwar), Babbar Khalsa International, Khalistan Zindabad Force and
International Sikh Youth Federation (Rode) were desperate to undertake some sensational terrorist action in India because
of constant pressure from Pak ISI.  Attempts to resurrect terrorism in Punjab also became evident from the continued
recovery of large quantities of arms, ammunition, explosives and sophisticated timer devices in the State.  He informed
that the security forces arrested 31 terrorists while one surrendered before the police in 2001.  Similarly, 35 terrorists were
arrested and 3 surrendered in 2000.  He further stated that despite reverses and neutralization of some of their top rung
activists over the years, the Khalistani terrorists still retained the capacity and substantial fire power to carry out acts of
violence.
69.       In view of these developments, the Committee feels that there is a subtle change which is taking place at the
ground level.  Therefore, there is need for being vigilant to ensure that terrorism does not rear its head once again in the
State of Punjab.  The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to take all necessary preventive measures to
thwart attempts of Pak-ISI to revive terrorism in Punjab.
70.       In this context, the Committee also draws the attention of the Government to the concern expressed by Members
regarding the plight of 400 odd policemen of Punjab facing trial in various courts for their role in anti-terrorism
operations during the heyday of terrorism in Punjab.  The trial of these policemen may have a demoralizing effect on the
policemen in general and those fighting terrorism in particular.  It becomes even more demoralizing when persons, who
spearheaded the terrorist movement from their foreign bases, are not only being allowed entry into the country but also to
move freely.  Are these recently returned separatist leaders not a threat to the security and unity of the country? 
Ironically, those who indulged in terrorism are moving freely and in sharp contrast those who fought terrorism are going
through hell of an experience.  In view of this, the Committee urges upon the Government to consider the cases of these
400 odd policemen and simultaneously cautions it to keep a strict vigil on the activities and movement of the recently
returned separatist leaders so that they do not become once again, a potent threat to the security and unity of the country.
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
LEFT WING EXTREMISM
*          The Government has been adopting two-pronged strategy of focusing on security as well as developmental aspects
of the problem.  The Coordination Centre headed by the Union Home Secretary regularly reviews and coordinates
steps taken by the affected States to check the menace of left wing extremism, monitors the plan of action in
respect of each State and makes recommendations both on development and security aspect of the problem.  The
Committee notes that the efforts of the Government are not just focused on the security aspect, the development
aspect is also receiving due attention.  In this context, the concluding remarks of the Home Secretary made by him
in his presentation before the Committee may be worthwhile to recall.  He had stated, in the context of militancy
in Jammu & Kashmir, that since many members of terrorist outfits were our own people, albeit misguided ones,
we could not think of destroying them like the USA did to the Taliban and the Al Qaeda.  Given the logic of this
guiding principle, it may be presumed that it applied in case of left wing extremists too.  Therefore, without going
into the complexities of the causes that led to the origin of left wing extremism, the Committee is of the
considered view  that the Government should make sincere efforts to engage these extremist groups in a dialogue
so as not just to identify their problems and grievances but also to find ways and means to address them.  A
process of dialogue, at this stage, appears to be a step in the right direction because each passing day will add a

new dimension to the whole problem thereby worsening the situation
further.                                                                                                                      (Para 44)
MONSTER OF COMMUNALISM
*          Communalism has been the bane of modern India.  It acted as a midwife in the partition of India and even after
that it continues to plague the social fabric of the country.  It has acquired different forms and dimensions over the
years.  However, in the recent years it is rearing its ugly head in an organized manner much in the same way as it
did in the years preceding the partition.  There are several forces which work tirelessly to ensure that it does not
lose it momentum.  These forces are the real anti-national elements who are bent upon tearing the social fabric of
the nation apart.  In their zeal to gain foothold in their respective communities, these forces are stoking communal
fire.  Their actions are spreading venom in the society which threatens to be divided along communal lines.  These
attempts to create a communal divide in the society are one of the biggest challenges before the Indian polity. 
Therefore, it needs to be nipped in the bud before it grows too large to be controlled.  It is the considered view of
this Committee that the Government must make honest and sincere efforts to maintain the pluralistic character of
the society and bring all right thinking elements of all communities together to try and find ways to check the
growing divide between them.                                      (Para 45)
                                               
POLITICISATION OF POLICE FORCES
*          In this backdrop, the Committee feels that there is need for a serious introspection by all concerned.  The
Government must act fast to stem the rot which has set in.  If immediate steps are not taken to set the house in
order, there are dangers of the system falling prey to these degenerating developments.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government should make earnest efforts to depoliticise the institution of police before it
becomes too late to retrieve it from the morass of degeneration.  It must be ensured that police remains
accountable only to the law of the land.                                                                                                      (Para 47)
MODERNISATION OF POLICE FORCES
*          Although the Ministry of Home Affairs provides funds to the States for modernization of their police forces, the
Committee wonders what actual benefits will it accrue at the ground level?  There is all the more reason to be
apprehensive in the backdrop of total absence of a proper plan and a well thought out strategy.  Mere provision of
funds does not ensure that police forces will be modernized.  What is needed is a well chalked out plan of action
to be followed and implemented over a period of time with concrete goals in sight.  Though, a scheme is there, it
seems to be meant only for earmarking funds under a particular head as part of the annual budget making
exercise.  In view of this, the Committee is of the considered opinion that the Ministry of Home Affairs should
prepare a blueprint of a model police force to be followed by all States while drawing benefits from its scheme of
modernization of police forces.  A definite plan of action with a proper mechanism to ensure accountability is the
need of the hour.  It not only ensures accountability but also establishes unity of command and direction. 
                                             (Para 50)
REVAMP OF INTELLIGENCE APPARATUS
*          The Committee is satisfied to note the steps being taken to revamp the entire intelligence apparatus.  It hopes that
the new set-up will function smoothly.  However, with too many groups and agencies entrusted with different
aspects of intelligence, the real problem arises in regard to proper coordination amongst all of them.  The
Committee hopes that all the finer details vis-à-vis role, functions and structure of each and every functional group
and agency have been worked out so that there are least chances of overlap and conflict of functions.  In this
context, the Committee would like to lay emphasis on one more and equally important aspect of accountability. 
With so many functional units in place, there are situations when the proverbial game of passing the buck starts as
each unit points the finger towards the other to save its skin.    The Committee, therefore, is of the view that a
proper system of accountability should be evolved whereby it is easier to fix the responsibility and follow it up
with necessary action.                                             (Para52)

that it was mainly due to regional imbalances.  As regards left wing extremism, he was of the view that the problem
would continue as long as land reforms were not carried out honestly.

security forces and compulsory military training for youth.

Chairman invited Shri J.F. Ribeiro to make a presentation before the Committee.
 
6.         While welcoming Shri J.F. Reibeiro, the Chairman drew his attention to various aspects   of    internal    security   
situation  by way of a brief overview.  He then apprised Shri Ribeiro of the procedure to be followed during the course of
the meeting and requested him to send his written comments to the queries which may be raised, within a week’s time.

7.         Shri J.F. Ribeiro, in his presentation before the Committee,  submitted that the real matters of concern were cross
border terrorism, insurgency in the North-East, left wing extremism, religious fundamentalism, role of the ISI and the
nexus between drug trafficking and terrorist and insurgent groups.  While stating his views on these issues, he said that he
personally felt that terrorism finally had to be ended by the people themselves.  Another aspect on which he threw light
was that the army could not play the role of the police as it happened in Gujarat during 1985 riots which could not be
controlled by the army in five months whereas under his leadership as DGP it was controlled in a week.  He stated that
the main thing in such a situation was to deal with the persons who were fomenting the trouble.   He further stated that
fanaticism of any type should be put under control, whether it was majority fanaticism or minority fanaticism or any other
type of fanaticism.
 
7.1       Speaking on the bandhs and such type of political activity, he observed that a law was required by which the
person who called for bandhs or who called for procession or any kind of such political activity could be prosecuted.  If
the bandh turned violent then there should be a law to prosecute the persons who called for such type of activity.  He
stated that it was the police which had to face it.  To deal with it efficaciously, the police should be a professional force
and not highly politicized.   In this context, he highlighted the sufferings of the common man.   He was of the view that
what was needed now was to forget our selfishness or even our party interests and see to it that the police became
apolitical, power was not misused and that it was ensured that the police acted according to the law.  He concluded his
evidence by saying that we were still working on the fringes and the people had to help themselves otherwise their very
quality of life was being affected.
 
7.2       The Chairman and the members then sought certain clarifications from him and he was directed to send the
written replies to the queries.
 
8.         The Chairman then invited Shri Sankar Sen, to share his views on internal security situation. In his presentation
made before the Committee, Shri Sen stated that one of the biggest problems was the ineffectiveness of the police to
grapple with the internal security problems.  In this regard he cited his experience as the Director-General of National
Human Rights Commission.  The next problem according to him was the security of the tenure of the police chief which
was emphasized in the National Police Commission’s Reports and stressed upon by the National Human Rights
Commission too. He spoke about the need for operational autonomy of the police which had eroded significantly.  He
stated that in a public opinion survey, it was found that 80 per cent respondents strongly felt that political interference
with the police was a greater evil than corruption.
 
8.1       Referring to the recommendations of the National Police Commission, he said that fixation of tenure, institutional
mechanism to insulate the police as well as separation of law and order from the investigating wing were needed
forthwith.  In his view, these were the major factors responsible for the poor performance of the police. The other
problem was the inadequacy of training.  Citing his experience during his association with National Police
Academy(NPA) and later with BPR&D, he stated that there were no proper training institutions except NPA nor were
there any quality trainers.  He suggested for the structural changes which were also strongly recommended by the
National Police Commission. 
 
8.2       Another important point which he mentioned was the increasing lawlessness and escalating crime.  He later
referred to the percentage of the crimes registered.  Regarding organized crimes, he stated that an agency was required at
the national level to tackle this menace.  He said that during his tenure with the BSF, he felt the need for curbing the
illegal immigration which had the capacity of changing the demographic profile of some of the bordering districts.
According to him the scenario had dangerous portents.  The other aspect on which he drew the attention of the Committee
was the requisitioning of the army to deal with any law and order situation at the drop of the hat.  He touched upon 
several reasons responsible for the internal disturbances and the deteriorating law and order situation. The working of the
prosecutions, he believed, was also required to be thought over seriously. He suggested for a law to ensure greater
coordination between the prosecution and the police.  Lastly, while referring to the  Maharashtra  Control of Organised
Crime Act,  he emphasized the need for a special law to deal with the organized crime.
 
9.         The Chairman then welcomed Shri K.P.S. Gill and invited his views/suggestions on internal security situation in
the country. In his presentation before the Committee, Shri Gill made a few recommendations for changes in law which
dealt with the issues of terrorism and organized crime.  He stated that he believed in the efficacy of the police station in
tackling terrorism.  He stated that the size of the police force should be in manageable limits so as to maintain its efficacy.

In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred¨ the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 2001, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 31 August 2001 and pending therein, to the
Committee for examination and report.

The Press Communiqué appeared in the leading newspapers
on  24 September 2001.

                   iii) Shri VN Rai, Managing Director, Krishak Bharati Cooperative Limited

REPORT
 
            The Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 2001(see Annexure-I) seeks to amend the Companies Act, 1956 by way of inserting an additional Part (Part-IX-A) relating to the formation/registration of Producer Companies and all matters relating thereto.  The Bill, in effect introduces a new

89th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/89threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:51:19]
economic enterprise1 known as “Producer Company” in the Companies Act, 1956.
 
1.1       The principal aim of the proposed legislation is to provide for formation and registration of producer companies, whichhas unique blend of many features of a limited company with the principles and practices of mutual assistance and cooperation to operate under a regulatory framework
similar to that of private limited companies.
 
1.2       The Bill will also enable incorporation of cooperative as producer companies and conversion of existing cooperatives into producer companies.
 
2.0
              A producer company can be formed/registered by any of the following entities/manner: -
 
(i)                  any ten or more primary producers;
(ii)                any two producer institutions;
(iii)               a combination of ten or more primary producers and producer institution(s);and
(iv)              conversion of producer cooperative of inter-state nature, if two-thirds of its  members voluntarily resolve to do so.
 
2.1.0    The objects of a producer company inter alia include production, processing, manufacture and sale of primary produce as well as allied matters.  The owners/members of Producer Company have necessarily to be “primary producers”.  In nutshell producer company deal with produce of its
Members.
 
2.1.1    The Primary producers are those individuals who are engaged in an activity connected with or relatable to primary produce [Section 581 A (k)  Clause 2 of the Bill].
 
2.1.2    Primary produce as defined in the Bill [Section 581A(j) Clause2] includes products of agriculture, horticulture, floriculture, pisciculture, viticulture, forestry, forest products, revegetation, bee-raising, farming, plantation products, animal husbandry and related field as well as the products
of cottage industry, artisans, etc.
 
2.1.3    The differences between Producer Company and other Company are given in the accompanying Table:

3.0       The salient features of the proposed legislation are as categorized below: -
 
(i)
                  It enables primary producers to form specially structured Producer Company on the basis of principles of mutual assistance and provides purely a voluntary option for existing cooperatives to become Producer Companies.
(ii)                Ten or more natural persons who are producers, two or more producer institutions or a combination of both can also form Producer Companies;
(iii)               This act gives option to such of those inter-state co-operatives2 desirous of registering as Producer Companies to do so;
(iv)              In case of Company formed of individuals member shall have single vote irrespective of share holding, where the Company is formed exclusively by producer institutions the voting right may be computed on the basis of participation in the business, and incase of Company formed
of individuals and institutions there shall only be a single vote for every member;
(v)                In order to further its objectives the Producer Company may collaborate to form subsidiaries, joint ventures etc.
(vi)              Board of Directors of the Producer Company are elected by the General Body. Provision for co-option of expert Directors has been provided;
(vii)             The Board of Directors shall appoint the Chief Executive of the Producer Company.  Other employees of the company will be appointed by the Chief Executive in accordance with the powers delegated to him by the Board;
(viii)           The Board of Directors shall be responsible and accountable to conduct timely audit, election and general body meetings.
(ix)              Producer Company may provide provisions for “Special Users Right” to its active members in the articles of association;
(x)                Every member of a Producer Company must participate in the Company’s business.  The articles of association may establish minimal levels of the participation and may provide conditions under which those who do not meet those levels, or who cease to participate, may be made
ineligible to hold office, to vote or to continue their membership;
(xi)              Producer Companies will form their own articles of association suiting to their own business and operational needs; and
(xii)             Dispute settlement shall be by simple process of Arbitration and Conciliation.
 
4.0       The Bill is almost akin to the draft legislation formulated by the High Powered Committee for Formation and Conversion of Cooperative Business into Companies on the basis of its observations and recommendations.  The draft legislation was also annexed to its Report.
 
4.1.0    The said High Powered Committee was constituted in the background to the proposed legislation on 1 November 1999, which in turn submitted its Report on 15 March, 2000.
 
4.1.1    The Alagh Committee was of an eight member body headed by Dr. Y.K. Alagh.  The Committee had also appointed a five-member sub-Committee comprising of officers from Departments of Company Affairs, Legal Affairs, Rural Development and Agriculture and Cooperation to
recommend a draft legislation to it.
 
4.2.0    The Alagh Committee had observed that post-independence cooperatives have often become vehicles for Government programmes, operating with substantial government funds and personnel.  Government funding has often led to Government control leading to bureaucratization and
political interference.
 
4.2.1    In the era of liberalisation and globalisation of Indian economy, producer cooperatives are trying for its growth & development in competitive environment.  It is due to the fact that rural producer cooperatives are not equipped with resources, skill, opportunity,  they are not able to
withstand the competition.  Moreover, under the existing cooperative laws even the large producer cooperatives find it extremely difficult to face increasingly stiff competition from their corporate counterparts due to lack of a level playing field. The Committee, therefore, suggested Producer
Company as an alternative for those producer cooperatives, which opt voluntarily to operate effectively in a competitive environment.
 
5.0       In the liberalised economy, the producer cooperatives as an independent business entity are at a disadvantageous position as compared to other economic entities dealing with the same produce such as MNCs.  The factors attributed for the same by the Department of Company Affairs are
limited assets, resources, education access to advance technology and  bureaucratic control, etc. The Department of Company Affairs has stated in their background note that cooperative laws (both State & Central) vests enormous powers with Registrar of Cooperatives, which are often misused
thereby hampering growth and development of the cooperatives. Therefore Government feels the need to provide for option to the cooperatives to operate within the domain of Company Law.
 
5.1       The producer companies have to be registered with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956, even if the Producers Co-operatives are  registered bodies,  with Registrar of Cooperative Societies under Societies Registration Act, 1860 before becoming a producer
company.
           
6.0       The cooperative sector in India has emerged as one of the largest 3
 in the world with 5.28 lakh societies of various types with a membership of 22.8767 crore and working capital of Rs.285643.35 crores as on 31 March 2001.  Almost hundred per cent villages and sixty-seven of the rural
household are covered under the cooperative fold.  Their contribution in ushering in green and white Revolutions in the country is well known.
 
6.1       Producer Cooperatives form one-third of total cooperatives in India.  As per the statistics compiled by National Cooperative Union of India (NCUI), the total number of producer cooperatives is 150962 out of total cooperatives i.e. 528228.  [Source: Indian Cooperative Movement- A profile
2001: Indian Cooperative  Movement at a Glance (1999-2000)].
 
6.2       The National Policy on Cooperatives enumerates the development of cooperatives as institutions.  The first attempt to institutionalize cooperatives began in the year 1904.  Under the Government of India Act, 1919 the subject  of cooperation was transferred to the then Provinces, which
were authorised to enact their own cooperative laws.  Currently, “Cooperative Societies” is a State subject under Entry 32 of State List of the Constitution.  Accordingly,  almost all the States have their own laws on Cooperative Societies.
 
6.3       The Multi-Unit Cooperative Societies Act, 1942 was enacted by the Union Government to govern operations of cooperative societies where membership was from more than one province which was subsequently replaced by Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 1984.  The Multi-State
Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000 to replace the Act of 1984 is pending in the Lok Sabha to amend the Act of 1984.  The Multi-State Cooperative is in Union List  (entry No. 44)

6.4       The Alagh Committee had pointed out that in other parts of the World viz- Denmark, Switzerland, United States of America and Zimbabwe, cooperatives and similar forms of enterprises operate under Corporate Law which allows cooperatives the freedom to compete  with other economic
enterprises.
 
6.5       Some States (i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Bihar) have attempted to counter the problems inherent in their State laws on Cooperatives by enacting progressive parallel legislations.  Such a route will take too long to ensure that producer cooperatives have a viable
and sustainable place in the economy of the country.
 
6.6       The need for bringing in such legislations at Central level was felt owing to the rationale stated above.
 
7.0       The Committee in its meeting held on February 18, 2002 heard the views of the following representatives of the cooperative movement in the country:
   
               i)   Dr S.S. Sisodia, President, National Co-operative Union of India (NCUI)
              ii)   Dr Amrita Patel, Chairperson, National Dairy Development Board (NDDB)
             iii)   Shri V.N. Rai, Managing Director, Krishak Bharati Co-operative Limited (KRIBCO)
 
7.1       During his deposition, the President of NCUI had raised the following points:
 
(i)
                  The proposed legislation is not in the interest of cooperative movement and is also against its philosophy. It would send a wrong signal to the said movement across the country;
(ii)                Member’s control and participation which is the basic ethos of the cooperative form of organisation is absent in the Companies Act as voting by proxy is available therein. Therefore, it is most likely that the producer companies might be monopolised and hijacked by a few
individuals having large share holdings by misusing the provision of proxy vote available under the Companies Act;
(iii)               There is no provision in the Companies Act that provides for penalising a Producer Company that does not either follow the cooperative principles or flouts any of them;
(iv)              The Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000 does not have a corresponding enabling provision for conversion of cooperative societies into producer companies;
(v)                There is no need of the legislation as under clause 19 of the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000, societies can form their subsidiary institutions which may be registered under any other law including Companies Act; and
(vi)              The Alagh Committee neither held any consultations nor invited comments or responses of NCUI, which is an apex body of the cooperative movement in India on the subject of formation of Producer Companies under the Companies Act.
 
7.2.0    The Chairperson of NDDB was very emphatic in her presentation conveying that the Bill in question is very important for the growth and benefit of the cooperatives in the present liberalized economic scenario. She specifically narrated the experience of NDDB in promoting the dairy
cooperatives, the obstacles faced by them in view of the restrictive cooperative Acts, and the need for providing them a level playing field at a time when they were faced with increasing competition. She was of the view that the existing Cooperative Acts were based on a law formulated to meet
the needs of small village level cooperatives and were ill suited to the current needs of the cooperatives. She mentioned that although some States had taken the initiative to enact parallel cooperative laws meant for self-reliant cooperatives, the reforms in cooperative legislations had been
extremely slow. She also indicated that the proposed producer company legislation was extremely opportune and necessary if the impact of liberalization and globalisation was to be dealt with professionally and if the interests of our rural producers  was  to be protected.
 
7.2.1    She suggested to the Committee to consider bringing about the following two changes in the Bill:
(i)                  Omission of clause 581D(1)(c) which provides for single vote for every member of a Producer Company formed by a combination of producer institutions and individuals and other consequential changes explaining that such a provision is prone to misuse; and
(ii)                Need for suitable change in 581P(1)(6) qualifying the term expert directors to be co-opted on the board of a Producer Companies so as to prevent the misuse of the provision for co-option.
 
7.2.2    To a query by the Chairman of the Committee on whether the proposed Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000 will be able to meet the requirement of the cooperative movement instead of the Producer Companies Bill, she replied that the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000
will have limited utility. She said that it will benefit only those cooperatives which have members in more than one State whereas the Bill now being considered addresses the need of organizations whose objects extend to more than one state and thus will meet a different purpose.
 
7.2.3    Responding to the question whether there was any significant opposition to the Bill from certain quarters, she said that since the NCUI had expressed some concerns with respect to the Bill.  On the advice of the then Agriculture Minister Shri Nitish Kumar, the points raised by NCUI were
discussed with them.
 
7.3       The Managing Director of KRIBCO did not have any specific points to offer except categorically conveying KRIBCO’s support to the Bill.
 
 7.4      The Committee also considered replies/clarifications of the Department of Company Affairs on the apprehensions/comments/suggestions raised by the witnesses in the meeting of the Committee as well as in their subsequent memoranda and on the responses/suggestions received from
various organizations such as Co-operative Development Foundation (CDF), Hyderabad, Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (IIMA), All India Handloom Fabric Marketing Co-operative Society Limited and National Co-operative Dairy Federation of India (NCDFI) (see Annexure-II).
 
8.0       The Committee held threadbare discussions on various provisions of the Bill in the presence of the representatives of the Department of Company Affairs.  Points/queries made/raised in the meeting by the Members of the Committee were clarified by the Department   (see Annexure-III).
 
8.1       To a query about the differences between the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 2001 and the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Bill, 2000 the Ministry had submitted eight major differences between the two which are produced in the accompanying table:           
 
IMPORTANT DIFFERENCES BETWEEN COMPANIES (SECOND AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 & MULTI-STATE CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES BILL, 2000
 
Sl.No. Companies (Second Amendment)  Bill, 2001 Multi-State Co-operative Society Bill, 2000
1. Will benefit any co-operative whose objects by way of its business operations or activities extend to more than one State Only co-operatives whose membership extends to more than one State (at present only few hundred co-operatives) will be
benefited.  This is because ‘objects’ is narrowly defined as relating to membership.
 
2. Membership based on user-ship criteria and concept of active membership. Membership open to any individual.  No concept of active membership allowing mis-use of positions in many co-operatives. No
specific provision for special user rights, patronage bonus and other rights to encourage active membership.
 
3. No nominations by the Government.
 
                                                     
Powers of Government to nominate in co-operatives (one nominee if Government holds upto 26% equity, two if it holds upto
51% and three if more than 51% equity).
 
4. Appointment of Auditors by the Company itself. Appointment of auditors from out of a panel of auditors approved by the Registrar of Societies.
 
5. Intervention by Government in affairs of the Board similar to the procedure followed in respect of other companies under the
Companies Act.
 
Government has powers to supersede the elected Board in certain classes of cooperatives and in certain cases.
6. Elections to Board by the company itself. Elections as per rules framed by the Government.
 
7. Provision of patronage bonus. No specific provision for patronage bonus.
 
8. Concept of limited returns specifically provided.
 
No such concept specifically provided.

9.1       The Bill has only one substantive clause besides clause 1.  The clause has been divided into XII Chapters proposing to add to the Companies Act, 1956, sections 581 A to 581ZT, having sub-clauses under those.

9.3.6    The proposed section allows the investment of general reserves of any Producer Company in the approved securities, fixed deposits, units and bonds issued by the Government and cooperative or scheduled bank.
 
9.3.7    The Committee pointed out that the above provision restricts the investment of general reserves of the company in approved securities, Government units, bonds etc. and the investment in zero-risk areas may not entail much profit to the members of producer companies whereas wider
options were available for higher return.  Therefore, the Committee suggested that suitable changes may be considered in the proposed section and requested the Department of Company Affairs to consider the same.
 
9.3.8    In response to the Committee’s suggestion, the Department of Company Affairs has submitted their reply as following
 
The producer companies will be having generally the features of Co-operative Society.  As such the investment of co-operatives should not be made in a risky manner and may be invested as provided in clause 581ZL of the Bill. Similar provisions for investment of funds are there in other
Acts also such as the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 and the State Agricultural Credit Cooperation Act, 1968 etc. In addition to this we may add in sub-section (1) of Section 581ZL the following words – ‘or as may be prescribed by the Government.’
 
This will enable the Government to prescribe any mode in which the investment can be made by the producer companies in addition to the existing one proposed in the Bill.
 
9.3.9    The Committee considered the response of the Department and adopted the amendment to the Section as suggested by the Department.
 
Section 581ZN
9.3.10
    The Section deals with amalgamation, merger or division of producer company.
9.3.11  While discussing the section, the Committee pointed out that the norms in respect of valuation of assets at the time of merger and amalgamation was conspicuously absent in the Bill.  The Committee further wanted to know whether the provision relating to the jurisdictional aspect of High
Court in respect of  the cases relating to Producer Company was incorporated in the Bill.  The Committee directed the Department of Company Affairs to submit a note on those aspects for its consideration.
 
9.3.12  The reply of the Department of Company Affairs to these two queries of the Committee are as below:
 
Section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956, deals with power to compromise and arrangement with creditors and members in case of merger/amalgamation etc., no such valuation clause finds place (sic).  There are no rules for valuation of assets under the Companies Act, 1956.  As such it is
not appropriate to introduce any such new provision for the Producer Companies.  However, the assets of the companies are evaluated according to accounting principles and exchange ratio is arrived at.  This is a matter of mutual agreement between members and creditors.  The details
will be available to all concerned before they exercise their power to vote.  The company will follow the normal procedure for getting the assets evaluated for the purpose of arriving at exchange ratio. No specific clause is necessary.
 
Even in the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Bill, 2000 also no provision for valuation of assets has been provided. It is based on mutual agreement.  However, normal accounting principles and business ethics will have to be kept in view while considering the amalgamation.  In view of
these facts no amendment appears to be necessary. 
 
Passing of resolutions by the members as required is sufficient to give effect to the amalgamation and Registrar will act on the basis of such resolutions.
 
The appeal against the said amalgamation shall lie before High Court.
 
9.3.13   The Committee again  sought to know the  provision under which the appeal against amalgamation  shall lie before the High Court.  The position was ascertained from the Department of Company Affairs.  They have informed  that under section  581ZN (16)  of Clause 2 of the Bill, it has
been provided that the appeal  against amalgamation shall lie before High Court.
 
9.3.14  The Committee noted the replies of the Department and adopted the section without any change.
 
Clause 1, Enacting Formula and the Title
9.4.0    Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which are of consequential nature, namely, ‘2001’ and ‘Fifty-second’ to be substituted by ‘2002’ and ‘Fifty-third’, respectively.
 
9.4.1    The Committee recommends that the Bill be passed after incorporating official amendments in respect of  sections 581-O and 581-ZL in clause 2 of the Bill.
 
9.4.2    The Committee also recommends that the amendment suggested by it in the marginal heading to Section 581-J may be incorporated.
 
9.4.3    As regards, printing error in the marginal headings in respect of Sections 581 K&L, necessary corrections may be carried out therein.

2.0       The Chairman while initiating a general discussion on the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 2001 explained the background to the formulation of the Bill.   He inter alia stated that the proposed legislation would enable incorporation of producer cooperatives as companies, and
conversion of existing producer cooperatives into companies.  It avowed objective was to  accommodate the unique elements of cooperative businesses  within a regulatory framework similar to that of companies. The Chairman then  made observations  on the fundamental aspects on the Bill.
 
2.2       The Chairman then stated that there were  various types of cooperatives viz.  Central, State, District  and Primary Cooperatives  and made general  observations on the cooperative movement in certain States and the constributions made by the cooperatives in the economic development of
the country.
 
2.3       To a query raised by a Member whether co-operatives would be converted into producer – companies and ultimately taken over by the MNCs, the Chairman responded that the Committee could make a recommendation that the producer-companies should only be Indian companies. 
 
3.         A Member opined that if the proposed legislation was meant for freeing the cooperatives from  bureaucratic control, he was in favour of it, but if it was meant for corporatising the cooperative sector, he was not for it.  To buttress his point, the Member  referred  to the closing of  small-
scale industries in Faridabad after the introduction of  liberalisation.  Another Member  said that in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, cooperatives were a  very powerful movement.  Now, the country was becoming like South Korea, where the peasantry was in the doldrums.  The land
holdings were  divided.  There was lack of  facilities  in the rural  areas; no education, no drinking water.  Therefore, he  felt  that  the matter should  be dealt with cautiously.
 
4.         The Chairman pointed out that there were cooperatives in the powerloom, hand -loom and textile sectors in Maharashtra.  The sugar cooperative was facing hardships.  The monopoly procurement benefited the farmers as well as the consumers.  The monopoly procurement  price system
had collapsed.  The cooperatives used to receive their sustenance, in the  form  of lower rates of interest or institutional support from the subsidies provided by the Government.  Since the Government’s capacity to provide subsidies had declined the cooperatives could not sustain themselves. In
such circumstances, an alternative had to be found.  On the other hand, if the entire production machinery and the production tools went into the hands of others, their was the danger of having another colonial economy.
 
5.0       Another member observed that the cooperatives were in a situation of economic and investment deadlock.  There was however a need for a detailed analysis of the extent to which the voluntary route  or option prescribed in the Bill would hamper,  or distract  or derogate  the cooperatives
from their mission.  If it helped them to remould, recast, reinvigorate  and rejuvenate, the same ought to be examined.  The member further observed that no objective study had been made of the setbacks suffered by the cooperatives and the  need to revive them.
 
5.1       However, the Committee would want to know for sure that this Bill would help cooperatives which were on a plateau of development.  That member further observed that the Bill was an approach of form rather than of substance.  So, a deeper study of how this legislation would help
cooperatives was needed.

6.0       The Chairman then summed up the points raised by the members.  He apprised  members  that the  Alagh Committee was  set up at the initiative of  Ministry of Agriculture  which held discussions with the cooperatives and recommended amendments to the Companies Act,  1956.
 
6.1       He  then  drew the attention of the Secretary, Department of Company Affairs, to the observations made by the President of the National Cooperative  Union of India on 18.2.2002 with regard to the Multi-State Cooperative Societies  Bill, 2000 and  asked him in that Bill  could be further
amended  to  address some  of the  problems that were sought to be remedied by the amendments to the Companies Act and remove the deficiencies and inadequacies in the existing cooperative structure.  He asked the Secretary to clarify whether the piece of legislation under consideration of the
Committee, would create a new category of companies, in addition to the private limited,  the public limited the trusteeship and the nidhi companies.  He  also wanted the Secretary  to react to the apprehension  that if the option to form a producer company by any ten persons was available,  its
impact at ground  level would be detrimental to the cooperative movement.
 
6.2       Referring to the term “any body corporate” in sub-clause (3) of Section 581ZL,   the Chairman  asked the Secretary the meaning of  that term and whether the provision could be utilised for controlling the producer companies.  Bringing to the notice of the Secretary Section 581ZN relating
to amalgamation, merger or division, transfer of shares, etc.,  he expressed a view that  these provisions could be cleverly manipulated to have an overall control over the producer companies. 
 
6.3       Referring to Section 581ZT, the Chairman observed that Government would assume omnibus powers to  modify the Act in its applications to the producer companies and wanted the Secretary to explain the real intent  of the Government and the manner in  which it would exercise the
power.  He also stated  that it appeared  that the Expert Committee did not make any recommendation for inclusion  of such a clause.
 
6.4       The  Chairman asked the Secretary whether the Government considered it necessary to have larger consultations, in order to  allay  the misgivings that were cropping up in relation to the Bill under consideration of the Committee.  He wanted the Secretary also  to explain the urgency for
enacting this piece of legislation. He wondered whether any  harm would be done  to the poor farmers and other producers in the rural areas, in the absence of this legislation.
 
7.0       The Secretary, Department of Company Affairs responded to the questions/queries of the members.  He appealed to the Committee to view the Bill  with a fresh mind.  He explained  that the Bill was designed to help rural artisans, the cooperative movement, as distinct  from the
cooperative societies.  He further explained that under the present law only a cooperative society could be formed.  However, if the proposed Bill was enacted, then three options would be available to the cooperative institutions, viz, they could form a cooperative society, multi State Cooperative
Society  or a producer company.
7.1       The Secretary explained to the Committee that the  primary objective of forming such a producer-company was to take care of the interests of the producers in the rural areas, who did not enjoy the benefits that were available to the producers in the urban areas, as the people in the urban
areas had the option of forming a private limited company or a public limited company or a registered society.
 
7.2       In response to the Chairman’s query as to why the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act would not serve the purpose, the Secretary  stated  that there were eleven major differences in opting for this Act and be a part of the producer-company as against being a part of the co-operative
societies.  The Secretary further pointed out that this legislation had  the active inputs of all the members of the high-level body constituted, under the Chairmanship of Dr. Alagh, the Department of cooperation and the cooperators.  The Group of Ministers considered/reconsidered the Bill and
approved it.  It was the collective  wisdom  of the Law Ministry, Agriculture Ministry and all the stakeholders
 
7.3       In response to the Chairman’s query regarding Section 581ZL, the Secretary clarified that there was no danger of any producer-company being taken over by a multinational company,  as the clause clearly stated that the shareholder could only be a producer-individual or a producer-
institution.  As regards Section 581ZT, he informed the Committee that this clause was incorporated, based on the High-Power Committee’s Report.  As per this clause, the Central Government, by notification, could exempt a producer-company from other provisions of the Companies Act, but
not from the provisions of this particular Part, which  was being added  through this amendment.    The Secretary added that if the Government felt that some of the provisions of the Companies Act, say, relating to audit or any other matter, were  too burdensome or it wanted  to have a simplified
structure, like a producer company, it could then issue a notification and provide this exemption.
 
7.4       On the Chairman’s apprehension that the Government would still have control over these companies, by making use of the provision under Section  581ZA, the Secretary said that the Government would have all the powers  to inspect and intervene in the affairs  of producer-companies, in
extraordinary circumstances.  This authority, he explained, would always vest with the Government, as the provisions contained in the Companies Act would hold good for this  part as well.  But the Government had always ensured that this intervention was not a strong intervention and that there
was a level playing field.
 
7.5       As to the urgency for bringing in this piece of  legislation, the Secretary explained that this legislation was a reform measure, and that  a large number of cooperatives which were  feeling stifled  because of the State Cooperative Societies Act, had sought early enactment  of the new law.
 
8.         A Member of the Committee felt that there was  lack of adequate safeguard in the Bill to ensure the producer  companies  would not be taken over by the multinationals.  His apprehension was that, in the name of forming a joint venture, the Indian industry would be colonised by  the
multinationals. 
 
9.         The Secretary pointed out  that there was a clear  provision in the Bill  that the share of a  producer company could only be owned by producer individuals or producer institutions, and it would be left to the individual company to enter  into any  kind of joint venture that would benefit
them.
 
9.1       The representative of the Ministry informed the Committee that of the nine reservations expressed by the President,  National Cooperative Union of India, six had been accepted; and one more suggestion, namely, re-conversion into a multi-State Co-operative Society, had been agreed to by
the Law Ministry, and this would also be incorporated in this legislation.   He stated that only two of his submissions, namely, that the name ‘producer-company’ should be changed to ‘co-operative companies’, and having a regulatory mechanism for ensuring compliance with the Memorandum
and Articles of Association, had not been accepted by the Legal Department.   So, the suggestions  that had  been incorporated/accepted  include-(i) provision of proxy voting to be omitted; (ii) Annual General Meeting to be held only at a place where  the producer company  suggests ; (iii) the
delay in holding the Annual General Meeting on account of extraordinary circumstances, like in the event of natural calamities, shall not adversely affect the term of the Board of Directors; (iv) provide for audited accounts  in the AGM; (v)  include  the provision of ‘one-member-one-vote’ and
(vi) not to provide for mandatory external debt ratio.
 
10.0     The Chairman thanked the Secretary, Department of Company Affairs for his lucid and exhaustive  responses.   He  requested the Secretary to furnish to the Secretariat  of the Committee, his responses in a written form.
 
10.1     The Chairman then informed the Members that since some Members  were not present either because of the elections  in certain States or due to other reasons, and since it was an important piece of legislation, there would be another round of general discussion so that there was a broad
consensus on the legal procedural and substantive  issues.  After that,  the Committee would take up clause-by-clause  consideration of the Bill. 
 
11.       A summary of the proceedings was kept.
 
12.       The Committee then adjourned at  1.00  P.M.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            During the last decade, changes have taken place in the Indian economy, in the communication and transportation infrastructures, as well as in the method of commerce, banking and international trade.  Liberalization of the economy is in the process of changing the terms of trade between
rural and urban, labour and industry, finance and commerce.  Biotechnology, the information revolution, computerization can all be used to raise the standard of living of the rural asses and ultimately link this economic with regional, national and global demand.  Institutions are needed to link the
rural economy with the emerging new opportunities.  Rural producers are at a potentional disadvantage given their generally limited assets, resources, education and access to advanced technology.  In the present competitive scenario, if cooperative enterprises are to continue to serve rural
producers, they require an alternative to the institutional form presently available under Law.
            2. Keeping all this in view Government constituted a Committee consisting of experts led by Dr. Y.K. Alagh, Economist, former Union Minister to examine and make recommendations with regard to (a) framing a legislation which would enable incorporation of cooperatives as companies
and conversion of existing cooperatives into companies and (b) ensuring that the proposed legislation accommodates the unique elements of cooperative business within a regulatory framework similar to that of companies.  The Committee had a series of meeting during which it interacted with,
and received responses from various cooperatives, institutes and individuals.
 
            3.  On the basis of the recommendations of the Committee the present Bill has been prepared with the main objective of facilitating formation of cooperative business as companies and to convert existing business into companies.  The salient features of the Bill are:
          (i)           to offer a statutory and regulatory framework that creates the potential for producer-owned enterpirses to compete with other enterprises on a competitive footing.  The Companies Act envisages and provides for various forms of Companies including private limited, public limited,
trusteeship companies and nidhis, each with specific and appropriate provisions applicable to them.
 
           (ii)         to provide for the formation and registration of producer companies which include the mutual assistance and co-operative principles within the more liberal regulatory framework afforded by the Company Law with suitable adaptations.
         
           (iii)        to provide an opportunity to cooperative institutions to voluntarily transform themselves into the new form of producer companies.
 
            (iv)       Under the Bill conversion of co-operatives to producer companies is purely voluntary.
 
(v)
                Member equity may not be publicly traded, but may only be transferred, with the approval of the producer company’s Board of Directors.  Producer Companies would not be vulnerable to the takeover by multinationals or other companies.
 
(vi)
              The conversion option by co-operative society to producer company can be exercised only if two-thirds of the Members of the concerned society vote in favour of a resolution to that effect.
 
(vii)             The new form of Company is designated as “producer company” to indicate that only certain categories of persons can participate in the ownership of such Companies.  The members of the Producer Company have necessarily to be “primary producers”’ that is persons engaged in
an activity connected with, or relatable to, primary produce.
 
(viii)           The objects of a producer company have been defined to include, among other things, production, processing, manufacture and sale of primary produce as well as allied matters.
 
4.  The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been
authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninetieth Report on the
Representation of the  People (Amendment) Bill, 2001·
.
 
2.         In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred¨¨ the Representation of the People  (Amendment) Bill,
2001, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 5 December, 2001 and pending therein, to the Committee on 10 December
2001 for examination and report.
 
3.0.      The Committee considered the Bill in 4 sittings held on 11 December 2001,4 February, 17 June and 5 July 2002.
 
3.1       The Committee in its sitting held on 11 December 2001 decided to issue a Press communiqué inviting
suggestions/comments on the Bill from individuals/institutions/organisations interested in the subject matter of the Bill
by 7 February 2002.  The Press communiqué appeared in the leading newspapers on 7 January 2002.  
 
3.2       The Committee heard oral evidence of the Secretary, Legislative Department (Ministry of Law, Justice and
Company Affairs) on the Bill in its sitting held on 4 February 2002.
 
3.3       In its sitting held on 17 June, 2002, the Committee held further deliberations on the Bill.
 
3.4       In its sitting held on 5 July 2002, the Committee considered the draft Report on the Bill and adopted the same.
 
3.5       In the sitting held on 5 July 2002, the Committee also decided that the evidence tendered before the Committee
may be laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament.
 
4.0       In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill received form
the Legislative Department (Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs), replies of the Legislative Department to the
queries raised by the Members in the sittings of the Committee and comments of  Legislative Department on memoranda
received from individuals/organisations. The list of individuals/organisations and gist of their memoranda together with
comments of Legislative Department thereon is placed at Annexure.
 
5.         For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been
printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
